News.title: Major fire at Canada military base leaves four dead, dozens injured
News.content:
Four members of the Canadian military have died and dozens were injured in a major fire at a base in the province of Alberta.

Addressing the nation on Sunday from Ottawa, Prime Minister Mark Carney described it as "one of the worst tragedies for the forces on Canadian soil in peacetime".

The fire broke out at about 16:00 local time (22:00 GMT) on Saturday at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, one of the country's busiest military training bases, and is now contained. Its cause is still unclear, but officials said it did not appear tied to "terrorist activity".

"The nation is in mourning for those brave members of our armed forces who we have lost," said Carney.

The BBC has confirmed that Sgt Morgan Wong, Pte Shaun Farrell, Pte Aidan Goulding and Pte Hayden Lykkemark have died.

Of the 39 injured people being cared for in hospital, at least 19 are in a critical condition, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said at a press briefing on Sunday evening.

Fire and rescue teams are remaining at the scene to contain any potential flare-ups, Wainwright Mayor Bruce Pugh told the BBC.

Members of the infantry had been conducting "high-intensity combat training with live munitions" at a grenade range and attack range, where 10 soldiers practise attacking a simulated enemy, Maj-Gen Wade Rutland told reporters at the briefing.

"There was a multitude of ordnance moving through the Wainwright training area," he said, including a grenade launcher, grenades, small arms and ammunition.

A grass fire ignited about 1km (0.6 miles) away, with the cause currently under investigation, and moved toward the attack range.

"What I would say is there was multiple training activities happening throughout the training area at the time," he said. "Uncommonly strong winds caused the fire to spread rapidly and shift direction towards the range administrative area."

Cannon fire had been heard coming from the base on Saturday before it suddenly stopped, Mayor Pugh told the BBC, noting it's not uncommon to hear cannons being fired there.

News then came through that local emergency services had been deployed to an "all hands on deck" situation.

Carney said military and emergency crews fought the flames throughout the night in "some of the worst conditions imaginable".

The people who were hurt were on the attack range and included reservists and soldiers from the Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry, officials said.

In a statement early on Sunday, the Canadian Armed Forces said that "while the incident remains under investigation, at this time, there are no indications that it was the result of any terrorist activity".

Rutland told the briefing: "We do not believe this [incident] to be a result of any oil and gas infrastructure nor any outside interference".

News.title: Polanski says he will not overturn Green Party's 'Zionism is racism' motion
News.content:
Zack Polanski has said he will not overturn a motion passed by Green Party members that declared Zionism a form of racism.

The Green leader told Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that, while he would like to make amendments, it would be party policy until 2028.

The motion, passed at the party's conference earlier this month, described Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state in historic Palestine to the exclusion and/or domination of the non-Jewish population".

It divided the party and sparked a major backlash from MPs, Jewish campaigners, the government and the European Green movement, with the equality watchdog writing to the party for more information on it.

The fallout from the motion overshadowed the final days of Polanski's campaign in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, in which he came second to Labour, and threatened his leadership.

He came under criticism for not voting on the motion which was passed by 1,022 votes to 813 - a small fraction of the party's 230,000 members - in Brighton earlier this month.

The motion also asserted the party's backing for "a single democratic state throughout historic Palestine", a full arms embargo on Israel and a commitment to Palestinian liberation.

Asked if he would now step in as leader to overturn it, Polanski said: "I'm not going to try to overturn it.

"At the first available opportunity, I do want to amend it - I want to move away from one state, towards saying that Israelis and Palestinians should decide that future for themselves."

He said this would not be until 2028 as "you can't [amend it] within the rules, so when you vote on something in our party conference that's then policy for two years".

Kuenssberg asked if he would therefore change the rules as leader, but Polanski said: "I think if members have made a decision, then I respect the democratic will of our members."

Former Green Party co-leader and current MP Adrian Ramsay responded by calling for action to be taken sooner.

"I don't think it's tenable for us to continue the next two years with this policy that's been adopted given the huge political distraction that it's been for our councillors across the country," he told the BBC News Channel.

"One way forward could be to have a ballot of all party members to establish very clearly where does the party as a whole stand - my view is we would see a different answer."

Polanski had previously said he would not have voted for the motion without two amendments.

The first of these would have avoided "determining there was a single democratic state", and the other would have specified that the motion should not be used to discipline Jewish Green members who attend synagogues that consider themselves Zionist.

Both of these amendments were voted down by members at the party's conference.

Green MPs, including Ellie Chowns, have called for the party's member-led decision-making procedures to be reviewed given how few people took part in the vote.

News.title: A wave of homemade, synthetic drugs sweeps US and deepens crisis
News.content:
Warning: This story contains descriptions of drug-taking from the start and discusses suicide

The few grains of fentanyl sit in the silver foil as a straw, held between Mike's lips, hovers above, with a cigarette lighter below. The 48-year-old army veteran is crouched low in an alleyway in Columbus, Ohio's Linden neighbourhood.

"This drug will damn near make you do anything, unfortunately," he says.

The hit he's smoking cost three or four dollars.

"You can snort too much and you can't take it back. Kind of like a gunshot. Can't call the bullet back," he says.

He burns the foil and inhales. As the opioid takes hold, he grips the fence behind him. He sways as a low moan comes from deep in his throat - he could be humming a tune.

We've spent a few days with Mike - he's been our guide through the neighbourhood's back streets. Everyone seems to know him and he's regarded fondly. He helps out at a local pawn shop and gas station, and that's how he feeds his 20-year-old opioid addiction.

Synthetic opioids are more powerful and in plentiful supply, and they have transformed the drugs landscape.

Fentanyl, which is entirely man-made, is 50 to 100 times more powerful than heroin, which is cultivated from poppies. It is now often cut with synthetic tranquillisers, which make reviving overdose victims more difficult. These are homemade threats, where cocktails of synthetics can be made in American basements and bathtubs.

News.title: Home sellers cut asking prices on 3,000 properties a day
News.content:
Home sellers cut asking prices on more than 3,000 properties a day on average in Britain during September, according to figures from Rightmove shared exclusively with the BBC.

The property website said the total was the highest of any month for 15 years and was driven, in part, by a glut of homes on the market and some sellers setting unrealistic expectations.

The proportion of listed homes that eventually had a price cut peaked in 2023 and has remained relatively high since.

Property portals say buyers are now having to be choosy, with many working to a tight budget as mortgage rates have risen to three-year highs.

"Once a home has been on the market for a while and then has a price reduction, some buyers start asking questions, even when there is nothing wrong with the property," said Colleen Babcock of Rightmove.

"In a market with so much choice, first impressions matter."

News.title: Ending corridor care in hospitals for children a priority, says health secretary
News.content:
The health secretary has asked the NHS to draw up urgent plans to speed up ending hospital "corridor care" for children.

Yvette Cooper told the BBC there would be new standards for caring for children in A&E in England, with figures collected on corridor care by age for the first time.

She was speaking on Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg where the programme highlighted the case of two-year-old Finlay Roberts who died in 2024 after spending hours in a hospital corridor before being discharged.

The health secretary has announced Â£140m to improve urgent care in England ahead of what she said would be a "more difficult" winter than usual.

The government has already pledged to end corridor care for all patients by the end of this parliament, and now Cooper has said eradicating it for children would be prioritised.

Corridor care refers to patients receiving treatment or waiting in corridors, waiting rooms or other hospital areas due to a lack of appropriate space.

The health secretary was also asked if the government would meet a key manifesto pledge that 92% of patients would start treatment within 18 weeks of booking a hospital appointment by 2029.

"That remains our manifesto commitment and of course we're going to keep working towards it," Cooper said.

Pushed further on whether the target was achievable, she replied: "The whole point about having the targets is about having something stretching that we work towards."

The 18-week target has consistently not been met for more than a decade.

Cooper said that the NHS was dealing with a number of challenges after record A&E admissions following heatwaves over the summer.

According to the latest figures for England, an estimated 7.37 million treatments were waiting to be carried out at the end of August, relating to 6.24 million patients.

On the programme the story of Finlay Roberts, was highlighted. He died after being discharged from hospital in 2024 following hours spent in an A&E corridor in north London.

Finlay's father David told the BBC the situation was a "terrible mess", with the family moved into a room with a bed before being moved back into the corridor.

"He just clung to me, as we now know, slowly dying," he said.

Liz Roberts, Finlay's mother, said corridor care "robs people of their dignity when they are at their most vulnerable". She recalled being told to administer a suppository to her son in the corridor.

Cooper apologised to Finlay's parents on behalf of the NHS, saying: "No child should be treated in a corridor. No patient should be treated in a corridor."

News.title: Suspects hunted after police officer injured in shooting
News.content:
Detectives are searching for two suspects who fled after a police officer was shot in Nottingham city centre.

Nottinghamshire Police said the officer had approached two suspects in Angel Row shortly before 04:50 BST on Sunday.

The officer is in a stable condition in hospital, where he is receiving treatment for a wound to his foot, the force added.

Detectives said a man and a woman had fled the scene and that a firearm, which could be seen within the cordon, had been found.

Angel Row remained closed by a large police scene until Sunday evening.

Police cars were parked along the road, which is lined by fast food stores and shops, and orange traffic cones had been laid out alongside items left on the road.

The cordon had also been extended to St James's Street, where an officer is standing guard.

The force said there would be a heightened police presence as the investigation continued.

News.title: Photos show luxury boat with 50m pool and water slides near Kim Jong Un's summer retreat
News.content:
An 80m (263ft) luxury vessel has been repeatedly spotted in satellite images off North Korea's Wonsan coast from July to mid-October this year.

What stands out is the 50m swimming pool along the deck, with a cluster of waterslides at one end.

After sitting idle for months at a maintenance facility, it relocated in early July to waters off a strip of coastline known as the Kalma Peninsula.

This is close to Wonsan, a seaside resort with a sprawling villa used by North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and his family.

It was not the only large vessel on the move. A handful of others were also repeatedly seen near Kim's villa, in satellite images analysed by the BBC.

The vessels are widely believed to be used by Kim and his family. Former North Korean officials, defectors and experts say it would be difficult for anyone unconnected to the regime's leadership to own or freely use vessels of this size.

News.title: There's a crackdown on sports piracy but is it already out of control?
News.content:
"Football's Gone Round the Spend!" screamed The People newspaper one Sunday in July 1995. It reported breathlessly that three clubs between them were set to pay out more than Â£20m on new players.

The highlight that summer was the transfer of Stan Collymore from Nottingham Forest to Liverpool for a British record fee of Â£8.5m.

That number might not seem too impressive today, in an age when Â£100m transfers are almost commonplace. But at the time it was seismic stuff, and it symbolised the conversion of football from sport into big business.

All of this had been made possible in the early 1990s by the creation of the Premier League, and its initial TV deal with the broadcaster Sky, which paid more than Â£300m for five years of rights. The agreement put live top-tier football behind a TV paywall for the first time.

It was a lucrative model, one that other leading championships in motorsport, rugby, golf and cricket would later seek to replicate.

But now, that model is coming under pressure. Piracy has become endemic in British sports: around half of sports fans now admit to using what they might euphemistically call "alternative" means to watch paywalled material, according to the consultancy Ampere Analysis.

News.title: Man, 80, who died in light aircraft crash near Loch Lomond named
News.content:
An 80-year-old man who died in a light aircraft crash is understood to be flying instructor Ian Haggis.

He and a 16-year-old boy died when their plane came down near Loch Lomond. The teenager's identity has not been released.

The pair had flown out from Glasgow Airport at 16:17 and stopped transmitting at 16:37, a few miles north east of the village of Drymen near Stirling.

Emergency services were called to the crash at about 16:45 on Friday.

Both of them were pronounced dead at the scene.

Temporary airspace restrictions are currently in place over the area while the Air Accidents Investigation Branch (AAIB) carries out its inquiries.

Old Drymen Road, near the scene of the crash, remains closed with vehicles being turned around and hillwalkers rerouted.

News.title: NHS data breaches a disgrace, health secretary says
News.content:
NHS staff accessing the medical records of the Nottingham attacks victims and possible breaches over a man killed by a tiger is a "disgrace", the health secretary has said.

Speaking to the BBC, Yvette Cooper said she expected action to be taken against staff who had breached NHS data and privacy standards.

Her comments came after Nottingham University Hospitals (NUH) NHS Trust confirmed it had sacked a total of 15 members of staff and Yorkshire Ambulance Service said William Chapman's medical records may have been accessed illegitimately.

Dr Manjeet Shehmar, NUH medical director, previously said there was "simply no excuse for accessing the records of a patient without a legitimate reason".

Speaking to the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Cooper said "there's got to be proper respect for patients" from NHS staff.

"Let me be really clear about this," she said. "There are proper data and privacy standards across the NHS."

Students Barnaby Webber and Grace O'Malley-Kumar, and grandfather Ian Coates, were stabbed to death on 13 June 2023 by Valdo Calocane, who was diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 2020.

NUH said in May that it had sacked 11 members of staff for inappropriately accessing the victims' medical records, and had informed the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) and Nottinghamshire Police of the investigation.

At the time, the ICO told the BBC it would "assess any evidence provided by the trust in due course and consider our next steps", while police said there was "no criminal investigation".

In its update about further dismissals on Friday, NUH said it had taken action against "doctors, nurses, registered healthcare professionals and other staff", and that independent regulators such as the Nursing and Midwifery Council and General Medical Council, the ICO and Nottinghamshire Police had been informed.

NUH added a new system, currently under testing, was being implemented to protect patient records in future and alert the trust to potential breaches.

News.title: Man and woman in their late teens die in collision
News.content:
Two people in their late teens died in a collision involving two cars, Suffolk Police said.

Officers were first called by the ambulance service to Debenham Road near Little Stonham at 10:15 BST.

Fire crews and the air ambulance were also called to the incident that involved a red Peugeot 107 and a silver Volkswagen Passat.

Police said a male passenger in the Peugeot died at the scene. The female driver was taken to Addenbrooke's Hospital in Cambridge by land ambulance, but has since died as a result of her injuries.

The occupants of the Passat suffered minor injuries, the police spokesperson added.

The road was expected to reopen later in the evening.

News.title: West Midlands Police officer who accessed police records 2,000 times sacked
News.content:
An officer who inappropriately accessed police records more than 2,000 times has been sacked for gross misconduct.

A West Midlands Police misconduct hearing acknowledged PC Shannon Parsons felt "isolated and disconnected" due to working part-time and returning from maternity leave, but had breached standards of professional behaviour.

Parsons had claimed there was a policing purpose to her searches, the panel said, and was seeking to "keep herself up to date, informed and was often in a position to support and assist other colleagues in operational matters".

However, chair of the panel Debra Tedds concluded the searches were carried out for the officer's "own personal benefit".

As a result, Parsons was dismissed without notice and barred from future work in policing.

The searches took part over a period of about five years, the panel heard, and many included incidents near her home address.

Parsons had an otherwise unblemished career in policing in the West Midlands, lasting 13 years, but was said to show no insight or remorse "as to the potential harm that has been caused by accessing the amount of information over a significant time period," according to the panel's report.

News.title: BBC pauses civil service secondment scheme
News.content:
The BBC says it will pause secondments of government statisticians to its fact checking service, BBC Verify, and review their roles.

Since 2018 the BBC has offered six-month secondment opportunities for up to two civil servant statisticians to work for BBC News's head of statistics.

A BBC spokesperson said: "All BBC journalism and editorial decisions are made by BBC journalists and editors, in line with the BBC's editorial guidelines, so the statisticians never make editorial decisions."

Those currently on secondment would not be involved in the publication of news or content during the review and the current round of recruitment will be paused while the role is reviewed, the corporation added.

The decision follows a report in The Telegraph which said embedded civil servants had been engaging in editorial tasks and raised questions about a breach of impartiality rules.

The spokesperson added that the BBC "takes independence and transparency incredibly seriously, and we must ensure we are meeting the highest standards".

They said although statisticians' work had sometimes been recognised with their names on the BBC website, "they never made editorial decisions".

According to The Telegraph, external, a job advert for the 2027 secondment said a successful candidate would have "the ability to influence decision making, working with credibility and proactively with customers to share knowledge and information".

A now-removed blog post written by one civil servant about their placements showed a secondee describing how they had drafted copy for the news website.

Under the scheme, it is understood that statisticians explain data in writing that can be incorporated into stories, but they do not write the copy itself.

Secondees' contributions can be incorporated into journalism that scrutinises the current government, as well as all political parties.

The seconded statisticians also have to adhere to the Civil Service Code of Practice for Statistics. It requires them to present and use data and statistics objectively and not to withhold or misrepresent data due to political or commercial influence.

News.title: Man arrested after boy, 16, dies in crash
News.content:
A man has been arrested after a 16-year-old boy was killed in a crash in Birmingham.

Police said the teenager was in a white Seat Ibiza which was understood to have hit railings on Shaftmoor Lane at about 20:30 BST on Saturday.

A second passenger, a boy in his teens, was taken to hospital with a serious arm injury.

A 19-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of causing death and serious injury by dangerous driving and failing to provide a breath specimen, West Midlands Police said.

The force stated the 16-year-old boy who lost his life was pronounced dead at the scene, in the Acocks Green area, despite the best efforts of paramedics.

It appealed for information, adding specialist officers from the serious collision investigation unit were asking anyone who had dashcam footage from around the time of the crash to get in touch.

News.title: 'Learning to read in my 80s has changed my life'
News.content:
An 86-year-old man said learning to read has enabled him to read his and his wife's anniversary cards for the first time in 65 years.

Alan Hannay, from Dibden Purlieu, learned to read through the charity Read Easy, which helps adults across the country who struggle with the skill many of us take for granted.

Hannay told BBC Radio Solent: "It's changed my whole life, my confidence, changed my family life and everything around me.

"It's one of the best experiences I've ever had in my life."

Hannay said he now reads every morning for about an hour and a half and goes to the class twice a week.

"I enjoy it so much now," he said.

The charity said Hannay is an "inspiring example of determination and courage".

It said he asked his local library in Hythe, Southampton, about learning to read, which led him to the charity and his reading coach, Angie.

During his working life as a professional chauffeur, he relied on his memory to drive his clients around London, and at the age of 70 he attended evening classes to improve his reading.

However, he found the group situation difficult.

News.title: House that looks like boulders to be built on moor
News.content:
Plans for a house designed to look like rocks on a famous Yorkshire moor have been approved.

The contemporary structure, which has large irregular-shaped windows and a natural outdoor pool, looks similar to the landmark Cow and Calf Rocks in Ilkley, West Yorkshire.

The house will be built on green belt land which is the garden of a home off Heber's Ghyll Drive, and will be eco-friendly, to an ultra-low energy standard called Passivhaus.

Harrogate-based architects Shaw & Jagger said the scheme was eventually passed by HM Planning Inspectorate through the country house clause, which allows development on green belt for buildings of "exceptional quality".

The architect Matt Masserella-Gill was commissioned to design the home by the landowner David Rasche.

He said the design was "arguably the most complex country house application ever made in this country".

The house has been named Fomorian - meaning a supernatural race of giants in Irish mythology - taking inspiration from the mythical giant Rombald who is told to have lived on Ilkley Moor.

Masserella-Gill said: "The design approach was to propose a scheme that is intrinsically linked to the spirit of its place. Fomorian is of its place, part of the moors, its geology and its spirit.

"We took cues from local folklore, the surrounding rocks; ancient carvings, standing stones and escarpments that are synonymous with the landscape."

News.title: Anthropic commits 5% of its stock to a new 'public benefit' fund
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Anthropic said Sunday it is committing 5% of its shares to a new “public benefit” fund, with the fund's worth potentially increasing as its shares grow in value.

The shares will go to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, a new entity within the company.

The fund “will have increased flexibility and scale, enabling us to pursue our mission in new ways: for example, we might explore large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations,” Anthropic said in a blog post. It gave labor market impacts as an example, saying that while it has already committed $200 million to study the effects of artificial intelligence, “given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed.”

CEO Dario Amodei and the company’s five other cofounders established Anthropic as a public benefit corporation, a designation that for-profit companies select to balance financial goals and social impact.

They have also pledged that they will donate 80% of their wealth. An equity donation match program, in which about half of the company's employees participate, lets workers pledge equity that Anthropic matches.

When combined with Sunday’s announcement, Anthropic said roughly 20% of its shares will be dedicated to the “public good,” plus any additional percentage that could be added if the company’s valuation reaches specific milestones.

Anthropic is planning a massive initial public offering as soon as November.

News.title: Massachusetts GOP lieutenant governor candidate suspends campaign after arrest in car crash
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The Republican candidate for lieutenant governor in Massachusetts dropped out of the race on Sunday hours after he was arrested in a suspected drunk driving crash.

Shawn Oliver, a city councilor in New Bedford and a corrections officer, said in a post on X he was ending his campaign because "the election is too important to be overshadowed by personal matters.”

The move came after his running mate, Republican gubernatorial candidate Mike Minogue, said he asked Oliver to immediately suspend his campaign and that "when elected, I will formally ask for his resignation.”

“I am extremely disappointed,” Minogue said on X. “There is no excuse for driving under the influence.”

Police said Oliver, 42, was arrested after he was involved in a car crash late Saturday involving a vehicle that struck multiple parked vehicles before turning over.

He was taken to the hospital for injuries and arrested on suspicion of operating under the influence of alcohol, negligent operation of a motor vehicle, a marked lanes violation and speeding, police spokesperson Holly Huntoon said in an email. The arrest was first reported by The New Bedford Light.

New Bedford Mayor Jon Mitchell, a Democrat, said the allegations against Oliver were “deeply concerning” and that the public deserves to hear from him about what happened.

A phone message seeking comment was left for Oliver, who was born and raised in the city of 100,000 people about 60 miles (97 kilometers) south of Boston and was elected to the city council in 2023.

Minogue, a businessman and military veteran, faces incumbent Democratic Gov. Maura Healey on the November ballot. The Democratic candidate for lieutenant governor is incumbent Kim Driscoll.

The lieutenant governor's position in Massachusetts is seen as largely ceremonial, but the officeholder is first in line to become governor if the governor resigns or dies.

Oliver has been placed on restricted work duty at his job at the Massachusetts Treatment Center “while all facts and circumstances are reviewed,” Lindsay Corcoran, a spokesperson for the state's Department of Correction, said in an email. The medium-security facility houses sex offenders and people civilly committed as sexually dangerous persons.

News.title: Trump keeps his doctor on a short leash. A new report reveals just how short
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Donald Trump’s personal physician must stay no more than three minutes away from the president at all times, according to a report published by The Wall Street Journal.

While round-the-clock medical proximity is standard protocol for the commander-in-chief — former White House physician Dr. Jeffrey Kuhlman previously noted keeping a doctor and critical care nurse within two minutes of past presidents — the rule highlights the tight boundaries surrounding the oldest elected president in U.S. history.

The arrangement, overseen by Navy Captain Dr. Sean Barbabella, comes as Trump receives glowing medical reports and routinely ignores his doctors’ advice, all while under constant emergency-ready care.

Barbabella, a 56-year-old military physician who served in Afghanistan prior to his White House post, is responsible for conducting the 80-year-old president’s health evaluations and drafting his public reports.

A person familiar with Barbabella’s White House routine told The Wall Street Journal that aides typically left the room during consultations between the doctor and Trump, characterizing the physician’s bedside manner as “low-key and direct.”

open image in gallery Donald Trump’s personal doctor must remain within three minutes of the president at all times, according to a Wall Street Journal report ( Reuters )

Although the physical proximity is routine, Barbabella’s public summaries of the president’s health have drawn attention for their flattering details. In a May 2026 report, Barbabella wrote that “AI-enhanced electrocardiogram (ECG) analysis estimated his cardiac age, an established measure of cardiovascular vitality, to be approximately 14 years younger than his chronological age.”

Despite Barbabella advising weight loss, diet modifications, increased exercise, and a lower aspirin intake, the doctor offered an unqualified endorsement of the president’s physical state.

open image in gallery Dr. Sean Barbabella, a 56-year-old military physician who served in Afghanistan prior to his White House post, is responsible for conducting the 80-year-old president’s health evaluations and drafting his public reports ( AP )

“President Trump remains in excellent health, demonstrating strong cardiac, pulmonary, neurological, and overall physical function,” Barbabella reported. “His demanding daily schedule, including multiple high-level meetings, public engagements, and regular physical activity, continues to support his overall well-being. Cognitive and physical performance are excellent.

“He is fully fit to carry out all duties of the Commander-in-Chief and Head of State.”

The glowing report continues a long tradition of flattering health evaluations for Trump. In 2015, Dr. Harold Bornstein, who served as Trump’s personal doctor from 1980 to 2018, issued a statement declaring that Trump’s “physical strength and stamina are extraordinary” and claiming he would be “the healthiest individual ever elected to the presidency.”

Bornstein later admitted to CNN in 2018: “He dictated that whole letter. I didn’t write that letter, I just made it up as I went along.” Bornstein died in 2021.

open image in gallery A former personal doctor later confessed that a famous 2015 letter declaring Trump the healthiest president ever was written entirely by Trump himself ( AFP/Getty )

Questions also linger over how much medical counsel Trump actually accepts. Addressing a rally crowd in Ohio last week, Trump spoke openly about overriding his doctors’ recommendations regarding his high daily dose of aspirin, which Barbabella addressed in his recent report.

“I take an aspirin a day,” Trump told supporters. “I don’t know if it works, but psychologically I need it. They said, ‘Sir, you don’t need that!’

“I said, ‘Do me a favor, I’ve been doing okay for 35 years. Leave me alone.’”

News.title: UK must rejoin EU to combat growing threat from Russia and Trump, Burnham warned
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Escalating Russian aggression and an unpredictable Donald Trump mean Andy Burnham should aim to regain full membership of the European Union, a major new report has warned.

Being part of the EU is necessary to protect the UK’s prosperity, security and democracy and the prime minister should work to build a national consensus in favour of re-entry, the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) argues.

But the Labour leader should “stop talking about Brexit” and recognise that the EU is a very different entity from the one the UK left in 2016, shaped by a series of different threats and challenges, including Vladimir Putin’s war on the edge of Europe, it said.

The stark message by the leading think tank, which has close links to Labour, is bolstered by new polling, commissioned by IPPR and Persuasion UK, which found that, there was a 64–36 split in favour of regaining membership to the bloc, among those expressing a view.

open image in gallery Prime minister Andy Burnham ( AFP/Getty )

Even among Labour voters considering switching to Nigel Farage’s Reform, 54 per cent want to join the EU, compared with 36 per cent who want to stay out, the poll found.

Harry Quilter-Pinner, IPPR executive director, said: “The government has made important progress in repairing relations with Europe, but a series of individual deals will not be enough. There is one option which is best for the UK’s relationship with Europe – membership of the EU. That does not mean announcing another referendum tomorrow. But this means starting work to move towards this destination, building political support at home and in Europe.”

Former Labour leader Neil Kinnock, who previously told The Independent that rejoining the EU is the “only patriotic thing to do” for Britain and that Mr Burnham would be the man to do it, endorsed the IPPR’s call.

He said: “As the IPPR says and every sensible citizen knows, the world has changed traumatically in 10 years. That reality, together with our proximity to our biggest market, says that the rational course is for the UK to join the EU again in the national interest. Patriotism, prosperity and security all propel the UK in that direction.”

The prime minister recently said it was “possible” Labour’s next election manifesto could include an in-out referendum on EU membership, in his strongest signal yet of his intentions to repair the damage caused by the UK’s departure.

But he also announced at his party’s annual conference last month that he would look at other options that would take Britain closer to the bloc.

Europe: The Way Back We’re campaigning to rebuild Britain’s future in Europe JOIN US HERE

The report finds that Russia’s invasion of Ukraine means “the EU is being transformed” and the bloc that Britain would join is fundamentally different from the one it left.

Increasingly a major security alliance, it is ramping up defence spending across the continent, a move that also has deep implications for industry and supply chains. Yet, it warns, British politics is still debating its relationship with the EU of a decade ago.

Laura Chappell, associate director at IPPR, said: “It’s time to stop talking about Brexit and focus entirely on the future. A lot has changed over the past decade. The prime minister has said his mission is to give people back control, but Britain can’t do that alone anymore.

“Whether it's protecting households from swings in the cost of living, restarting industry, or keeping us secure, we lack the weight to act alone. In today’s world, we can’t take back control while being an outsider in Europe.”

The IPPR calls on the government to work with the EU to, among other things, create a European Defence Alliance, with the UK offering capabilities that would allow Europe to rely less heavily on the US, including satellite communications.

Just last week, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s said Mr Trump had betrayed Ukraine by curbing its access to a vital Starlink satellite communications system at a crucial time in the Russian invasion.

Elon Musk’s Starshield – the military version of Starlink – has provided a lifeline to Ukraine in helping to defend against incoming attacks, as well as striking Russian targets. But Ukrainian officials on Wednesday began reporting issues with it following another souring of relations between Mr Trump and Ukraine, after he announced a deal to waive sanctions on Russian diesel and called for Mr Zelensky to be replaced.

Reacting to the IPPR report, Nick Boles, the former Tory minister who helped to prepare Labour for office before it entered government in 2024, said: “At last a report that recognises how much has changed in the world since Brexit.”

He added that it was “clear that we need a much closer relationship with our European allies so we can tackle together the defence and security challenges we face as well as the economic opportunities and threats posed by AI and unfair competition from China.”

Dr Mike Galsworthy, chair of pro-EU group, European Movement UK, said: "The Brexit vote may have been cast just a decade ago, but in geopolitical terms it feels like a previous age. The IPPR are quite right that we are in a new era with new urgent demands and new solutions available. There is also a new mood in the country about where we belong in the world, reappraising the responsibilities and opportunities we should be picking up. So the past needs to be buried and the future embraced.”

Naomi Smith, chief executive of Best for Britain, which campaigns for the UK to restore its EU membership, said the UK was “worse off, less secure, and increasingly isolated” as a result of Brexit, and it was “only right as we look forward to the next decade that we ask ourselves what course we want to chart”.

“Prioritising being safer, better off and back around the table with our reliable allies and close neighbours is the only acceptable option for the UK: we either tackle the multi-crises facing us all, together, or continue on a hiding to nowhere, down a path of non-existent growth, diminishing influence, and worryingly fading security,” she said.

A government spokesperson said: “We are building an ambitious, close relationship with the EU that will strengthen our economy and create more opportunities for young people and communities across the whole UK."

Persuasion UK polled 3,039 people from 11–15 June and 2,907 people between 25–30 June.

News.title: UK house prices jump by thousands in October as market faces mortgage squeeze
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

House prices across Britain rose by more than £3,500 month-on-month in October, according to Rightmove, though the property market remains price sensitive with values "virtually flat" overall compared to the previous year.

Figures from the real estate platform show the typical asking price of a newly listed property increased by 1.0 per cent, or £3,575, compared to September.

This pushed the national average asking price up to £371,015, representing a minor drop of 0.1 per cent from 12 months ago.

In London, asking prices experienced a sharper monthly increase, rising by 2.5 per cent to average £673,942.

Rightmove noted that this autumn bump in the capital comes after a notably subdued summer, allowing vendors to recover some of their lost ground.

Despite the monthly surge, the typical asking price in London remains 1.7 per cent below the level seen a year ago. Rightmove added that the capital usually sees stronger seasonal price growth at this time of year, as sellers capitalise on a traditional rise in autumn buyer activity.

open image in gallery Rightmove said the number of new potential buyers contacting agents about properties is 9 per cent lower than a year ago, and the number of new listings coming to market is 3 per cent higher. ( AFP/Getty )

Colleen Babcock, a property expert at Rightmove, said: “The rapid rise in mortgage rates is really beginning to hit buyers’ budgets.

“We’re now seeing mortgage rate rises feed through to seller pricing in many of the cheaper parts of Great Britain, where prices had been more resilient this year.

“It’s an early sign that higher mortgage costs are putting pressure on affordability even in markets with lower property prices, affecting the areas and types of property that buyers can afford.

“This is a stark reminder of how price sensitive the market is, and the message from agents, backed up by our data, remains the same – that competitive pricing from day one of marketing is critical to capitalise on initial buyer interest.”

Rightmove said the number of new potential buyers contacting agents about properties is 9 per cent lower than a year ago, and the number of new listings coming to market is 3 per cent higher.

The total number of homes available for sale remains at its highest level for this time of year since 2014, with the high volume of homes for sale contributing to muted new seller asking price growth, the website said.

Ms Babcock added: “Higher mortgage rates are putting pressure on affordability across Great Britain, but sellers appear to be responding in different ways.

“Some have room to lower their expectations, while others need to hold firm on price to make their next move add up, even if that means waiting longer for a buyer.

“In such a price-sensitive market, the guidance and expertise of a local agent are paramount.”

open image in gallery Rightmove noted that this autumn bump in the capital comes after a notably subdued summer, allowing vendors to recover some of their lost ground ( AFP/Getty )

Matt Smith, a mortgage expert at Rightmove, said: “It’s been a difficult few weeks for home buyers who have been watching mortgage rates rise quickly, particularly for those who had worked out what they could afford based on lower rates earlier in the year.

“Some buyers will understandably be reassessing their budget and what they can afford or feel comfortable borrowing.”

Michael Donnachie, director at Michael Anthony Village Estates in Aylesbury, said: “With mortgage rates rising buyers are having to be more considered about what they can afford and what represents good value.

“That makes getting the asking price right from day one incredibly important.”

Marc von Grundherr, director of Benham and Reeves in London, said: “There’s certainly an element of seasonality at play, with the summer firmly behind us and the London market gearing up for one final push before Christmas.”

Nathan Emerson, chief executive of property professionals’ body Propertymark, said: “Looking ahead, much will likely depend on how inflation, interest rates and mortgage affordability evolve over the coming months and into the new year.”

The research was released as a survey from Barclays indicated that a quarter (24 per cent) of homeowners would be open to downsizing. One in 10 (10 per cent) said they have downsized.

open image in gallery In London, asking prices experienced a sharper monthly increase, rising by 2.5 per cent to average £673,942 ( PA )

On average, homeowners said they would need to release around £108,516 from their property sale for downsizing to feel worthwhile.

Costs were found to be an obstacle to downsizing, with 27 per cent of homeowners saying stamp duty costs would put them off and 21 per cent highlighting moving costs. A fifth (20 per cent) highlighted renovation or adaptation costs and 19 per cent mentioned legal or conveyancing fees.

Jatin Patel, head of mortgages, savings and insurance at Barclays, said: “Downsizing can give homeowners the opportunity to find a property that better suits their needs, reduce household costs and strengthen their financial resilience.

“However, the decision is rarely as simple as moving to a smaller home.

“Significant upfront costs and a shortage of suitable options can make a move difficult to justify, even for those who are open to it.”

Opinium Research surveyed 2,000 people across the UK in August for Barclays.

News.title: Ticket resale giant slams Raye’s ‘absurd’ manual checks as they urge crackdown against touts
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Resale site Viagogo has described singer Raye’s decision to assess ticket applications by hand as "absurd", arguing that automated bots can only be tackled by opening up the primary sales sector to form a "fairer" system.

Attributing the surge in touts employing bots to primary ticket outlets, the secondary platform has urged the government to examine the wider industry to establish a level playing field.

It follows criticism from Raye last week against touts who "overwhelmed" registration for her 23 October performance at the Royal Albert Hall, generating "hundreds of thousands of fake registrations".

In response, representatives for the ‘Where Is My Husband!’ artist undertook the rare step of sifting through the list by hand to spot "real fans" and thwart the automated attempts.

A Viagogo spokesperson told the Press Association: “It is absurd that artists and their teams have to manually sift through hundreds of thousands of registrations to identify real fans.

“Fans deserve a fair chance to access the events they love.”

open image in gallery Viagogo is pushing for an ‘open distribution’ model that allows sports and live entertainment tickets to be sold through more than one firm

They added: “Criticism of the resale market often frames bots as a secondary-market problem.

“However, bot activity occurs on primary ticketing platforms.

“We need an open and interconnected ticketing market to tackle the problem at its source.”

Viagogo is pushing for an “open distribution” model that allows sports and live entertainment tickets to be sold through more than one firm.

The company – which operates under the StubHub brand in the US – wants the industry to adopt an airline-style ticketing model, which it believes would boost competition for fans, help drive down prices and crack down on ticket-buying by bots.

The group told PA: “The ticketing system is broken and fans continue to face the same systemic issues.

“Bots target tickets when they first go on sale, on primary ticketing sites.

“Tackling this requires primary sellers to share information with regulators when their systems are breached.

“We strongly support UK anti-bot legislation and have proposed a solution built on industry-wide collaboration.”

open image in gallery Raye condemned ticket touts last week, saying they 'overwhelmed' sign-ups for her live show at the Royal Albert Hall on 23 October, creating 'hundreds of thousands of fake registrations' ( AFP/Getty )

It added: “Open ticketing would allow authorised primary and resale platforms to share technology and ticketing information, helping identify bots and suspicious activity, verify tickets and give fans greater choice and protection.”

It is already competing with primary ticket sellers in the US and markets globally, and is expanding this into the UK to shake up the market dominated by the likes of Ticketmaster.

Raj Beri, chief business officer of StubHub North America and Viagogo, told PA the group had already seen a 400 pe rcent jump globally in events where it is the primary ticket seller over its third quarter.

The push comes ahead of a planned crackdown in Britain on reselling tickets for profit, with a proposed new law to make it illegal for tickets to be resold above face value, plus unavoidable fees.

While the government has yet to come back with concrete plans for the ban and how it would work, Viagogo is urging ministers to review the entire sector and pave the way for reforms to allow more competition.

The firm said: “We’re ready to work with the government on practical, pro-competitive reforms to create a fairer ticketing industry.

“Real progress means tackling the problem across the whole ecosystem, starting with open ticketing.”

News.title: Dog owners urged to do this one thing now before Bonfire Night
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Dog owners ought to begin desensitising their pets to firework noises ahead of Bonfire Night, a charity has recommended.

To help owners gradually introduce their animals to these sounds, Guide Dogs has released The National Fireworks Archive, a free training video made from public footage.

The tool was created after the organisation discovered that the average UK adult keeps seven minutes of firework clips on their mobile phone.

According to research by Guide Dogs, firework anxiety impacts nearly two thirds (63 per cent) of dogs across the UK, equating to an estimated 9.9 million animals.

Yet, 79 per cent of owners state they do nothing to prepare for Bonfire Night, with 35 per cent admitting they did not realise dogs could be desensitised to fireworks.

The charity plans to enlarge the archive using a wider array of videos filmed at different distances and settings, capturing the crackles and whistles of screechers and Catherine wheels alongside the sharp bangs of rockets and major displays.

Those who are able to contribute to the archive can email videos to press@guidedogs.org.uk.

Dog owners should begin de-sensitising their pets to the sound of fireworks now, in preparation for Bonfire Night, Guide Dogs has advised ( PA )

Haley Andrews, a Guide Dogs expert, said: “Fireworks night is just round the corner but there’s still time to start desensitising beloved pets now.

“It’s straightforward, relatively easy to do and can help avoid the heartache, expense and disruption so many dog owners experience in the weeks running up to and even after Bonfire Night on November 5.

“By introducing the sounds gradually, at a level their dog can cope with, owners can give their pet, and their household, the best possible chance of having a calmer Bonfire Night.”

Guide Dogs recommended that owners start early with desensitisation, beginning at the lowest volume and keeping sessions short at about two to five minutes, once or twice a day to begin with.

The volume can be increased only when the dog remains relaxed, and different sounds should be introduced carefully.

Households should create a quiet, cosy den with blankets, toys and familiar scents, with treats hidden inside throughout the day so the dog learns to associate it with feeling safe.

On the night itself, owners should take their dog out for a final toilet break before dark, close the curtains, turn on the TV or radio, prepare a food item and let the dog choose where to settle.

News.title: UK profit warnings jump to highest since 2024 ahead of Budget
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Profit warnings by UK-listed firms jumped to their highest level for almost two years in the latest quarter, according to new data.

Research by advisory firm EY indicated that UK firms have come under pressure from rising costs and subdued consumer sentiment ahead of the first Budget since Andy Burnham’s appointment as Prime Minister.

EY’s latest profit warning report showed that 65 UK-listed companies warned over profits in the three months to the end of September.

It represents an increase from 59 in the previous quarter and marks the highest reading since the final quarter of 2024, when 71 warnings were issued by firms.

The research found that policy change and geopolitical uncertainty was the leading cause of profit warnings in the third quarter, being linked to 54% of warnings.

Meanwhile, 38% of warnings specifically referenced the impact of the conflict in the Middle East.

More than a third of warnings, 35%, cited rising costs as a leading factor, pointing towards inflationary pressures and higher business costs weighing on firms.

Almost a fifth of list companies, 17%, have issued at least one profit warning over the past 12 months.

Jo Robinson, EY-Parthenon partner and UK&I financial restructuring leader, said: “The latest figures show the variety of structural changes and challenges that companies are currently navigating.

“This is not a conventional economic cycle.

“For much of the post-war period, the economy followed a familiar demand-led boom-and-bust pattern but, since the pandemic, supply-side disruption including material and labour shortages, energy shocks, tariffs and wider geopolitical disruption has become far more significant.”

The data comes less than two weeks ahead of the autumn Budget, amid calls from industry for the Government to avoid business tax increases following cost pressures linked to recent budgets.

Ms Robinson said: “With the autumn Budget around the corner, profit warnings linked to policy change and uncertainty – once concentrated around fiscal events or elections – have become a regular feature of our data.

“Businesses have shown considerable resilience, but the pace of policy change is making forecasting, investment and capital allocation much harder.”

News.title: Arsenal late show keeps heat on Man City
News.content:
In the ordinary course of a Premier League season, you would say Manchester City have applied pressure on Arsenal by opening up a six-point lead before the champions play at Nottingham Forest this afternoon.

This is not a normal Premier League season though, and we await to discover if the top of the league table is simply a mirage.

Regardless, Mikel Arteta and his Arsenal players have their own motivations to accumulate as many points as possible before January as they seek to retain the title for the first time since the 1930s.

Arsenal have struggled at the City Ground, drawing 0-0 on their last two Premier League visits. They also lost at Forest in May 2023, a result which confirmed Manchester City as champions at Arsenal’s expense, and were knocked out of the FA Cup by Forest in January 2022.

Forest are yet to score a home league goal under Oliver Glasner, another data point suggesting this will be a low-scoring game.

That might not be the full story though, with Forest creating a hatful of chances in their defeat at Crystal Palace last week and Arsenal also playing a more inventive, technical game with the ball so far this season.

Arsenal have yet to score from a non-penalty set-piece, and their percentage of goals from open play is now the highest in the Premier League.

Morgan Gibbs-White is a doubt after sustaining what Glasner described as a “minor muscle injury” at Palace and his involvement in the game will be a last-minute call. With the exception of Christos Tzolis, Piero Hincapie and long-term absentee William Saliba, Arsenal’s squad is in pretty good health. Bukayo Saka, Martin Odegaard, Kai Havertz, Riccardo Calafiori and Ben White could be recalled to Arteta’s starting XI after starting the Champions League win over Lille on the bench.

Full team news on the way shortly.

News.title: Slow and dull Man Utd are just not good enough
News.content:
Manchester United are like John Toshack’s duvet. You fix one problem – being far too vulnerable to conceding goals – only to create another – lacking the threat to score. It is all very Meh United not Man United. The indisputable fact is they are just not very entertaining to watch. They are slow and dull.

In the end it also points to another thing. The thing highlighted in midweek by Lisandro Martínez after the Champions League defeat at Atlético Madrid: they do not have the strength in depth to compete.

What they do have appears to not be fit for purpose. Certainly Michael Carrick, the under-pressure manager, is struggling to get the best out of the resources he has.

“It’s like a duvet,” Toshack, the former Real Madrid and Wales manager, famously said of football. “If you pull it up, your feet get cold. If you pull it down, your shoulders get cold.”

There will have been times in the last few days, with the intense criticism and scrutiny over his future, when Carrick will have simply felt like dragging that duvet up over his head and keeping it there.

Defeat by Leeds United would have been unthinkable. It would have put Carrick under potentially intolerable pressure in what appears to be a pivotal week, with Como away in the Champions League and a home Premier League fixture against Bournemouth in the coming days.

Was this a lifeline or the tightening of the noose for Carrick? Time will soon tell. The relief of avoiding defeat was tempered by the reality of it now being just one win in their opening seven league games – at home to newly promoted Ipswich Town – and they are down in 13th place. It is six games without a win in all competitions.

News.title: Pierre Sage fears for his Crystal Palace future after Brighton humiliation
News.content:
Pierre Sage has admitted that he fears for his future at Crystal Palace, adding that he felt “shame” after his side slumped to their joint-heaviest defeat by rivals Brighton and Hove Albion.

Sage replaced Oliver Glasner as manager in June but since then Palace have won just two league matches with him in at the helm. The south London club have taken seven points from seven Premier League games and have already conceded 17 goals, the most of any team in the league.

“I don’t know,” Sage said when asked if he will get enough time to rectify Palace’s slump. He admitted that his shame was about how Palace were overwhelmed, leaking three goals within the first nine minutes of the game before eventually losing 5-0.

“We are not at the level we expected, and I’m really sorry for that,” the 47-year-old said. “I just want to apologise to the fans because it’s not normal to show this face.”

The Frenchman said that he took full responsibility for the 5-0 defeat, and understood why hundreds of Palace fans left well before the final whistle.

News.title: Ruthless Daniel Dubois dispatches Fabio Wardley in just two rounds
News.content:
Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Daniel Dubois vs Fabio Wardley.

When Wardley dragged himself out of the ring at Manchester’s Co-Op LIVE Arena, the physical damage was obvious, but the psychological sting was far deeper. Wardley had Dubois severely hurt early on, flooring the Londoner twice and teetering on the verge of a career-defining stoppage. Instead, he let the knockout slip away, allowed Dubois to find his rhythm, and was ultimately broken down and halted in the 11th round - surrendering his WBO heavyweight belt in a dramatic comeback victory.

Now, just five months after that gruelling night, the two heavyweights meet again at London’s O2 Arena in an immediate rematch that carries potentially massive implications for the entire division.

For Wardley (20-1-1, 19 KOs), the decision to trigger his rematch clause was instant. Dismissing concerns over the severe punishment he absorbed down the stretch, the Ipswich man is motivated entirely by redemption and the belief that his early success proved Dubois is beatable.

Dubois (23-3, 22 KOs), however, views things very differently. Entering as The Ring’s No. 1 heavyweight contender and a proven two-time world champion, Dubois has brushed off Wardley’s power, claiming his rival “punches like a baby” and insists Wardley threw away his one and only chance at glory in Manchester.

With Oleksandr Usyk approaching the final chapter of his career and the Anthony Joshua vs. Tyson Fury blockbuster looming just eight weeks away, this London clash is far more than a personal grudge match. The winner won’t just walk away with the WBO strap; they will stake an undeniable claim as the torch-bearer for the heavyweight division’s next era if they can land another title fight in short order.

News.title: Newcastle jeers tell Matthias Jaissle his ‘vertical’ football is not working
News.content:
Newcastle United look like a poor team playing badly. The evidence is increasingly damning after Matthias Jaissle’s side were loudly booed off at the end of this limp defeat.

This has all the makings of a long, hard season. Anger is already rising to the surface, even though Jaissle claimed Newcastle deserved more from a game they “controlled” in the first half and “dominated” in the second. Those comments jarred with what we had just seen.

After four years of enjoying an upward trajectory under Eddie Howe, the team faded last season, sold their best players in the summer, lost the manager and there is no evidence yet they have replaced anything with better.

This was supposed to be a reaction to the embarrassing 4-1 thrashing at Coventry City, but it led to another loss and, in the first half at least, another abject display. Aston Villa were always the more fluent and more threatening. They should have won by more than just Johan Manzambi’s first-half header.

News.title: Liverpool’s £400m front line clicks but win at Brentford turns on red card
News.content:
Only time will tell if Liverpool’s £400m front line can ever justify the extraordinary amount of money that was spent on them, but this was at least a significant step in the right direction. In a gritty victory away to Brentford, all four of Alexander Isak, Florian Wirtz, Bradley Barcola and Victor Muñoz either scored or assisted goals.

Admittedly, the task was made significantly easier by the major turning point of this game: a red card for Brentford’s Yehor Yarmoliuk. At the time of Yarmoliuk’s “headbutting action” towards Liverpool defender Jeremy Jacquet, the visitors were trailing 1-0 and looking worryingly short of ideas in attack.

But as the context of the match changed, so did the level of threat from the visitors. Against 10 men, with more space in which to operate, Liverpool’s forwards looked increasingly dangerous. Wirtz began to pull the strings, Barcola started to cause problems, Muñoz stretched the Brentford defence and Isak became a lurking menace.

News.title: Steely Chelsea triumph despite losing Martinez to head injury
News.content:
This was the afternoon when Xabi Alonso’s Chelsea went from swashbuckling to stoic, thrilling to tenacious.

For all Alonso’s attacking vigour at the start of his reign, there can have been no more symbolically satisfying victory under the new coach than this resolute win at Everton – the most vivid example of an increasingly impressive transformation.

This was what Alonso described as “winning in a different way”. A triumph amid the adversity of losing goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez to what appears to be a serious injury after a head collision with Jarrad Branthwaite is just one facet of why the joyous visiting supporters might consider this an early turning point.

Where recently they wilted, on Saturday they thrived in securing a first Premier League clean sheet for nine months.

Much more of this and the adjectives which were splattered across Chelsea during the golden years of José Mourinho – solid, robust and dogged – will be part of the Stamford Bridge lexicon once more.

“Just one day,” Alonso warned, both acclaiming the importance of the win while wisely preaching caution. “It will be key when we manage 10 clean sheets, even though this one feels good. We need to repeat it again and again, but the mentality was very good. Sometimes it is not to play nice, it is to play good – to win second balls, and to be efficient. We needed one of these: a clean sheet and a win.”

Asked about Martinez’s condition, Alonso said: “It was a concussion, but beyond that I do not know. I have only seen one clip of the incident, so we need to wait.

“What we know is that he left the stadium conscious and is now in hospital undergoing precautionary tests.

“We need to wait. Hopefully it will not be too serious, but at the moment we just have to wait.”

News.title: Wallabies humiliated in ‘unacceptable’ thrashing by New Zealand
News.content:
New Zealand blew Australia off the field in an extraordinary first-half display in Sydney as they claimed a 13th successive win against the Wallabies and completed a 2-0 Bledisloe Cup clean sweep.

The annual series had already gone New Zealand’s way for a 24th successive year at Eden Park last weekend, but Australia did enough in a highly competitive first half in Auckland to suggest they could give the All Blacks a game on their home turf. And in a breathless opening six minutes in Sydney, it looked as if they might.

The ball-in-play time during that opening spell was incredible as both teams committed to fast, attacking rugby, offloading from everywhere. Like two heavyweights going toe-to-toe in the opening round of a boxing contest, throwing haymakers to see who would get knocked out first.

Ryan Lonergan produced an excellent turnover for the Wallabies to trigger an Australia counter, and the irrepressible Peter Lakai responded with one for the visitors, as the ball travelled from one end of the pitch to the other in one long unbroken spell.

But after New Zealand wing Josh Moorby finally crossed the whitewash, it was Australia who found themselves out on their feet, punch drunk.

Sports.title: Watch Jude Bellingham assist Kylian Mbappe as Real Madrid score stunning ‘Fifa Street’ goal against Sevilla

Sports.title: Arsenal star Ethan Nwaneri shown red card by MISTAKE as ill-fated Dortmund loan takes bizarre turn
Sports.content:
Next

ETHAN NWANERI was shown a red card in the first minute of Borussia Dortmund’s 0-0 draw at Union Berlin on Saturday.

But match referee Daniel Schlager swiftly corrected his decision and opted only to book the Arsenal loanee.



Nwaneri, 19, was selected from the start for BVB’s Bundesliga clash in the German capital.

Just 17 seconds into the contest the attacking midfielder scythed down Union ace Tom Rothe.



To Nwaneri’s shock, the referee pulled out his red card following the incident.

Schlager, however, had brandished his red by mistake and had actually meant to only book Nwaneri.

The confusion was quickly cleared up and the young Gunner was allowed to continue.

Despite his reprieve, the teenager struggled to leave an imprint on the game.

And boss Niko Kovac opted to hook him for ex-Wolves flop Fabio Silva on 62 minutes.

The move did not pay dividends, however, with the game going on to finish 0-0.



BEST FREE BETS AND BETTING SIGN UP OFFERS

After the match, Kovac was left frustrated by how blunt his side were going forward.

The former Bayern Munich boss, 55, said: “We need to play much more accurately, much more precisely, and much more automatically in the final third.

“Union defended well, but we also didn’t play the way I would have liked.

“Because it would have been possible to attack behind the opponent’s defense to ultimately break through their line.



“We need to get back to doing that quickly, because you can only win games by scoring goals.”

Nwaneri, who was an unused substitute during Arsenal’s 3-0 opening day win over Coventry, has played five times in the Bundesliga for Dortmund.

The England youth international laid on an assist on debut but that is his only goal contribution for his loan club to date.

Nwaneri has also featured in Dortmund’s Champions League clashes with Villarreal and Bodo/Glimt so far this term.

Sports.title: What is wrong with Bruno Fernandes? Carrick tries to throw fans off scent as concerns over Man Utd captain grow
Sports.content:

BRUNO FERNANDES is in a funk – no matter how much boss Michael Carrick tries to throw us off the scent.

The Old Trafford skipper was a shell of himself again during Manchester United‘s third straight 1-1 Premier League draw.



Carrick, of course, insisted it was business as usual, projecting calm as the public face of the club after a rocky week dominated by the fallout from Lisandro Martinez‘s outburst.

Carrick told journalists at Elland Road: “No, he’s all right, no, it’s not a big deal. He is absolutely fine.”



But Carrick also said United’s sixth game without a win was a “fresh start” for the club hitting 13th in the table with two wins from ten.

He stretched it even further by dubbing it a “quiet week behind the scenes,” apparently assuming nobody noticed Martinez apologising for publicly torching the board’s transfer policy.

Man Utd ratings v Leeds MAN UTD went six games without a win after a 1-1 draw with rivals Leeds United. Bryan Mbeumo’s 35th minute goal was cancelled out by Dominic Calvert-Lewin swiftly after the break. Here’s how SunSport’s Katherine Walsh rated the United players at Elland Road.

Twice this week Carrick has spoken of a Fernandes “injury niggle” but stressed there was nothing to worry about on Sunday.

But their talisman’s performances before and since have suggested otherwise.

Yet Carrick again kept the out-of-sorts club captain on the pitch until the final whistle for the seventh successive league game. Such is Fernandes’ ability to pull something out of nothing.

The mention of an injury was perhaps an attempt to deflect the mounting scrutiny facing the reigning Prem player of the season.

The 32-year-old was crowned the best of the best in the most scrutinised league in the world, chalking up 21 assists to break the all-time record held by Thierry Henry and Kevin de Bruyne.

Yet at the start of what was meant to be a new United era, the midfielder’s form has become an unexpected problem for Carrick, an avatar of where United sit.

Anybody with eyes can see that Fernandes is well off it.

He has gone five Prem matches without scoring or assisting – his longest run since April-May 2025.

Carrick denied that his positional changes, with Fernandes being shunted to the right wing in the 2-0 loss at Atletico Madrid midweek and as a false nine at Leeds, have affected his mood or form. But he would say that.



Kobbie Mainoo’s injury has prompted a reshuffle, pushing Youri Tielemans into Fernandes’ preferred No 10 role while new signings Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba lined up in midfield.

Tielemans has enjoyed his best week since joining after facing criticism for his ability to cover ground from deep during the first eight games.

The fact Fernandes stayed on all match is a concern, a sign that Carrick is forcing square pegs into round holes to keep him on the pitch.

Carrick said: “He was through the middle today and played a slightly different position in midweek, but apart from that, it’s pretty much as usual.



“He’s an important part of our team. He has been for us for some time, and that’s not changing.

“There was a freshness to the group. You look at the midfield with Carlos and Andrey, that’s a pretty fresh spine of the team, through the middle of the pitch. Both young players are adapting to life at this football club. They were terrific today.”

Yet a five-minute compilation could be made of all of Fernandes’ head-loss moments at Leeds.

Booked on 17 minutes for mouthing off at ref Darren England after a late challenge on Leeds star Tarik Muharemovic, the hot-head kept sulking.



Daniel Farke’s players clocked that the more tackles they made, the more United’s fuming skipper would combust.

There was still time for one final complaint, as he screamed to the gods after a stepover didn’t come off late on.

United have long tolerated his on-pitch petulance, but his dedication had never faced serious scrutiny—until now.

There is a suggestion that he appears fed up with false promises made by the club’s recruitment department and ambition shown in the summer.

Entering his final year with a club-held option to extend it by a year, Fernandes is in a contract stalemate.



He has stepped back from press duties to dodge mounting speculation over his Old Trafford future. He would be right to question the direction of the club.

Eagle-eyed fans caught him failing to celebrate Bryan Mbeumo‘s goal against Spurs last Saturday before he left Old Trafford in a hurry while reporters were still waiting for player interviews backstage.

Although he reacted to Mbeumo’s strike across the Pennines on Sunday, underlying issues remain readily apparent.

Sports.title: Former Premier League club’s abandoned 30,000-capacity stadium now used as an allotment following demolition

SWANSEA are dreaming of a stunning return to the Premier League – but their former home is now unrecognisable.

The Welsh side are top of the Championship despite suffering a 1-0 defeat to fellow promotion chasers West Ham on Saturday.



They set a new attendance record at the Swansea.com Stadium when 20,973 fans turned up to see the showdown with the Hammers, who were relegated from the top-flight on the final day of last season.

But the Swans’ beloved Vetch Field, which they walked away from in May 2005, has been given a huge makeover.



Parts of the abandoned arena have remained intact for more than two decades – including the pitch’s original centre circle and players’ tunnel.

And some of the land where Vetch Field once stood has been transformed into an allotment following the demolition of the stadium.



It has allowed Swansea fans to grow vegetables where they once saw club legends spearheading their side to wins.

The decision was made to put together a community garden despite initial plans being drawn up to build four blocks of flats.

Vetch Field closed its gates for the final time when Swansea notched a 2-1 win over Welsh rivals Wrexham in the FAW Premier Cup final.

And the Swans posted their record attendance at the stadium – with more than 30,000 supporters flocking to see an FA Cup defeat to Arsenal in February 1968.

NONI MADUEKE hailed Arsenal for showing a “champion’s spirit” to squeeze past Nottingham Forest.

The winger came off the bench and was the Gunners’ hero by scoring the winner with 10 minutes to go.



The goal was Arsenal’s only shot on target – but Madueke loved the way the reigning champs ground out a 1-0 win to keep pace with Manchester City.

The England forward said: “We showed grit, determination and a champion’s spirit – I’m really pleased.



“At times maybe last year this game might not have gone for us as it did at the end. We have that extra belief, that extra mentality now.

“We know we are the champions and we can pull it out of the bag wherever we go. I’m just delighted we were able to do that.



“The Premier League can shock you – we had a shock versus Brighton and it was up to us to get back to the drawing board, regroup, go again and show everyone why we are the champs.”

Arteta was delighted with Madueke’s impact after bringing him on at half time for Eberechi Eze.

Madueke ultimately made the difference and his deflected strike off defender Jair Cunha meant Arsenal won to close the gap on Prem leaders City to three points.

Arteta said: “Noni is just a special guy. I saw an interview where they were asking a few of our players who would you call if you have a problem?

This was the third Prem game in a row where a player has come off the bench to score the winner for Arsenal and Arteta is thrilled by his substitutes contributing so much.

He said: “At the end I had the belief that the physical level [of Forest] was going to drop.

Sports.content:
Howard Webb discloses double Man Utd contact after major VAR error

The referees chief has spoken about the incident which resulted in Man City's winning goal against Manchester United earlier in the season

View 2 Images Howard Webb has revealed that he contacted Manchester United following Erling Haaland's goal. (Image: Michael Regan - The FA, The FA via Getty Images)

Referees chief Howard Webb has said that he has contacted Manchester United twice to acknowledge an error in the Manchester Derby earlier this season. Erling Haaland's goal was the difference between the two sides.

‌



‌



The goal was one of the more controversial moments of the season. After originally being ruled out for offside, a VAR review found that Haaland wasn't in an offside position; however, they didn't acknowledge the impact of Enzo Fernandez, who was in an offside position.

‌



After the game, Pro Ref confirmed an 'error of judgement', and contacted United over the incident. Webb has now revealed that he personally contacted the club on two occasions.

‌



Speaking to The Times, he said: "I called [director of football] Jason Wilcox and Rebecca [Britain, the club secretary], acknowledging the error.

"People can't believe it when they see it. It's like the gorilla," he said. "The gorilla banging his chest when the kids are playing basketball, hiding in plain sight.
