World.title: Mbappe scores brace as Real Madrid thrash Sevilla 4-1
World.content:
Real Madrid’s French forward #10 Kylian Mbappe celebrates with teammates scoring his team’s third goal from the penalty spot during the Spanish league football match between Real Madrid CF and Sevilla FC at the Santiago Bernabeu stadium in Madrid on October 18, 2026. (Photo by Oscar DEL POZO / AFP)

Kylian Mbappe scored twice including one brilliant individual goal as Real Madrid thrashed Sevilla 4-1 on Sunday to climb into third in La Liga.

Arda Guler netted a spectacular opener before Mbappe’s double and a rocket from Yan Diomande as Jose Mourinho side moved above Real Betis, who lost 5-2 to league leaders Barcelona on Saturday.

Mbappe’s first was a sensational strike, involving a roulette on the edge of Sevilla’s box, and his second a chipped Panenka penalty.

Champions Barca are six points ahead of Real Madrid before next weekend’s Clasico at Camp Nou, with Atletico Madrid second, sandwiched between Spain’s giants.

Mourinho lined up with Diomande on the left in place of suspended Brazilian winger Vinicius Junior, and brought Guler in as part of the midfield pivot.

Vinicius’s red card for hair-pulling last weekend provoked ire in the Spanish capital at officiating in Spain.

Madrid fans at their Santiago Bernabeu stadium chanted and held up banners against La Liga president Javier Tebas, after he said the club’s strategy of trying to discredit referees was similar to the techniques of Nazi propaganda chief Joseph Goebbels.

Los Blancos and their new coach Mourinho have complained bitterly about Spanish refereeing in recent weeks, and more generally over the past two seasons, in which they have failed to win a major trophy.

On this occasion it was Sevilla who had more to complain about in terms of officiating as Madrid eased to victory.

A quiet start was disrupted when Madrid midfielder Guler appeared to elbow Sevilla’s Peque, which went unpunished midway through the first half.

Sevilla had resisted the probing of Madrid’s attacking stars early on, but were undone by a moment of magic from Guler himself after 30 minutes.

Jude Bellingham played the ball out to the flank where record signing Diomande received it and fed Guler on the edge of the box.

The Turkish playmaker lofted a superb strike across Sevilla goalkeeper Odysseas Vlachodimos and into the top corner.

– Mbappe skill –

Mbappe came close to adding a second with a lightning-quick burst down the pitch, but his low effort was saved.

The French superstar soon got his goal, one of the best of the season.

Bellingham backheeled the ball into Mbappe’s path and the forward produced a dazzling roulette turn into the area, before showing more skill to rapidly sidestep the goalkeeper and roll home.

Mbappe extended the lead from the penalty spot after he went down under a light touch from Andres Castrin in the area.

The forward, who hopes to be crowned the best player in the world at the Ballon d’Or ceremony later in October, dinked home his ninth league goal of the season.

Sevilla pulled one back with a neat strike from Manuel Bueno, but there was no fightback on the cards.

Ivorian winger Diomande thumped home from outside of the box for his second goal since joining this summer from RB Leipzig, Madrid’s next opponents in the Champions League.

Earlier, Real Sociedad rose to fifth with a thumping 5-2 win at bottom side Malaga, Celta Vigo defeated Alaves 2-1 and Osasuna beat Racing Santander 2-0.

Vanguard News

World.title: 2027: Kano governor assures Tinubu of northern support
World.content:
Gov. Abba Yusuf

Kano State Governor, Abba Yusuf, has assured President Bola Tinubu of Northern Nigeria’s support for his re-election in the 2027 general elections.

The governor gave the assurance in a statement issued on Sunday in Abuja by his Director-General of Media and Publicity, Mr Sunusi Tofa.

Yusuf said the North had confidence in Tinubu and remained committed to supporting his second-term ambition.

He said the inauguration of the Arewa for Asiwaju (A4A) campaign office in Abuja further demonstrated the region’s commitment to the President’s re-election bid.

According to him, the movement will mobilise support across Northern states and strengthen political engagement ahead of the 2027 elections.

Yusuf said Kano, which he described as the North’s largest vote-producing state, would lead other states in driving massive voter turnout for Tinubu.

The governor expressed confidence that the state would play a leading role in securing victory for the President.

The A4A movement, led by former Minister of Defence, Badaru Abubakar, aims to promote Tinubu’s achievements and mobilise support for the Tinubu-Shettima ticket in 2027.

World.title: Ibori hails Dele Cole’s role in resource control struggle
World.content:
By Dapo Akinrefon

Former Delta State Governor, Chief James Ibori, has mourned prominent Niger Delta leader Patrick Dele Cole, praising his commitment to the struggle for true federalism and resource control.

Cole, who was born on August 4, 1940, in Abonnema, in the Kalabari Kingdom of present-day Rivers State, died in London at the age of 86.

In a statement titled “PDC: So Long My Leader,” Ibori described the late Cole as a steadfast advocate of the Niger Delta cause who remained loyal to his roots despite the political implications of his position.

He said Cole played a significant role in the region’s struggle for true federalism and resource control, adding that his commitment to the aspirations of the Niger Delta people remained firm even while he served as a special adviser in the administration of former President Olusegun Obasanjo.

According to Ibori, Cole’s dedication to the region demonstrated his willingness to stand with his people at a time when doing so could carry considerable political costs.

He added that the late leader’s political choices were guided by his commitment to the interests and legitimate aspirations of the Niger Delta people.

“He was a prominent leader in the Niger Delta who stood firmly with us in our struggle for true federalism and resource control. Even while serving as a special adviser in President Olusegun Obasanjo’s administration, he remained committed to his people and their legitimate aspirations,” Ibori said.

He added that Cole’s actions reflected deep loyalty to his roots and an unwavering commitment to the Niger Delta cause.

“At a time when such a stance could carry significant political costs, he chose to stand with his people,” he said.

Ibori urged the family of the late statesman to take solace in God, saying Cole’s contributions to Nigeria’s development, particularly in the Niger Delta, would remain cherished.

World.title: Police arrest 56-year-old man over wife’s death in Ogun
World.content:
By James Ogunnaike, Abeokuta

The Ogun State Police Command has arrested a 56-year-old man, Madarikan Emehinola, in connection with a suspected arson incident that claimed the life of his 40-year-old wife, Igbagbo Erobe, in the Igbo-Edu area of Ogun Waterside Local Government Area.

The command disclosed this in a statement issued on Sunday by the Police Public Relations Officer, DSP Oluseyi Babaseyi.

According to the statement, the incident was reported at the Abigi Divisional Police Headquarters after information was received that a house had been set ablaze, resulting in the woman’s death.

“The Ogun State Police Command has a 56-year-old man, Madarikan Emehinola, in custody in connection with a suspected arson incident that claimed the life of his 40-year-old wife, Igbagbo Erobe,” the statement said.

The police said the deceased’s body had been deposited at a mortuary for a post-mortem examination to establish the circumstances surrounding her death.

The command added that arrangements were being made to transfer the case to the State Criminal Investigation Department (SCID), Eleweran, Abeokuta, for further investigation.

The Commissioner of Police in Ogun State, Bode Ojajuni, assured the public that the case would be investigated thoroughly and professionally in accordance with the law.

Ojajuni also reaffirmed the command’s commitment to protecting lives and property and ensuring that allegations involving serious crimes received appropriate investigative attention.

The police urged members of the public to report suspicious activities promptly and provide credible information that could assist crime prevention and ongoing investigations.

The circumstances surrounding the fire and the woman’s death remain under investigation. The suspect’s arrest does not establish guilt.

World.title: Aiyedatiwa renames Ondo Event Centre after Mimiko
World.content:
Left to Right: Tolu Adegbie, Representative of Finance Minister; Dayo Akinlaja, SAN; Special Adviser to Ondo State Governor on Special Duties, Ayo Obe Coordinator of the Young Professionals; Oddo State Governor, Lucky Orimisan Aiyedatiwa; Dr Olusegun Mimiko; Captain Idris Wada, Fmr Kogi State Governor; Oba Ajibade Gbadegesin Ogunoye, Olowo of Owo; Otunba Bademosi, representing the Osemawe of Ondo and Senator Dayo Faduyile

Tunji-Ojo hails ex-governor’s mentorship of young people

By Dayo Johnson, Akure

Ondo State Governor, Lucky Aiyedatiwa, has renamed The Dome International Event and Cultural Centre after former governor Olusegun Mimiko in recognition of his contributions to the state.

The facility will now be known as the Dr Olusegun Mimiko Cultural and Event Centre.

Aiyedatiwa announced the decision on Saturday in Abuja at an event tagged “An Evening of Celebration and Conversation with Mimiko”, organised by young professionals to mark the former governor’s 72nd birthday.

In his goodwill message, Aiyedatiwa commended Mimiko’s contributions to healthcare, education and other sectors, highlighting initiatives such as the free shuttle bus scheme for students.

He also praised the organisers of the event and urged them to remain worthy ambassadors of Ondo State and Nigeria.

Speaking during a fireside chat, Mimiko urged young professionals to prioritise hard work, personal development and preparation for leadership.

He said effective leadership required capacity building, stressing that young people must first develop themselves and build strong personal character before aspiring to lead others.

On national issues, the former governor described the Nigerian Education Loan Fund (NELFUND), introduced by President Bola Tinubu’s administration, as a major intervention capable of widening access to higher education.

He urged young people to support Tinubu’s re-election bid to sustain and expand the initiative.

“You are bustling with energy and zeal and have access to readily available, knowledge-enhancing information. You therefore have to make the best of the opportunities available and maximise your chances,” Mimiko said.

Earlier, the coordinator of the event and former Speaker of the Nigeria Youth Parliament, Ayo Obe, said the celebration was inspired by Mimiko’s moral, intellectual, political and material support for young people over the years.

The Minister of Interior, Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo, described the young people mentored by Mimiko as his most enduring legacy.

“The best of all the achievements of Dr Olusegun Mimiko are the young people he built through mentorship,” Tunji-Ojo said.

He urged political leaders to invest in mentoring the next generation, stressing that their legacy should include people equipped to sustain their contributions after they leave office.

“For every entry, one day, there will be an exit. But when the exit comes, who will be there to hold your hands?” he asked.

Representing the Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Tolu Adegbie commended Mimiko for his achievements despite the limited resources available to his administration.

Adegbie noted that states now had access to more resources following the economic policies of the Tinubu administration.

The Olowo of Owo and Chairman of the Ondo State Council of Obas, Oba Ajibade Gbadegesin Ogunoye III, and Otunba Bademosi, who represented the Osemawe of Ondo, also praised Mimiko’s contributions to healthcare, education and infrastructure.

Other dignitaries at the event included former Kogi State Governor, Capt. Idris Wada; Senator representing Ondo South, Dayo Faduyile; member of the House of Representatives, Fessy West Adediranye; Joseph Akinlaja; and other serving and former federal lawmakers from Ondo State.

World.title: Obi urges Nigerians in diaspora to help build new Nigeria
World.content:
Peter Obi, presidential candidate of the National Democratic Congress (NDC), has urged Nigerians at home and abroad to take collective responsibility for building a better country, blaming corruption and leadership failures for Nigeria’s slow pace of development.

Obi made the call in a statement posted on his X account on Sunday after an impromptu meeting with Nigerians in Manchester, United Kingdom.

He said the interaction provided an opportunity to listen to the concerns of Nigerians in the diaspora and discuss their hopes for the country’s future.

Obi said he was encouraged by their passion and determination to contribute to building a Nigeria that works for all citizens.

“The task of building a New Nigeria remains our collective responsibility, and there is no better time to roll up our sleeves and get to work than now,” he said.

The former Anambra State governor warned that the country faced serious challenges that required urgent and collective action.

“Our nation is standing on the brink of a precipice, and we must not shrink from the arduous task ahead of us,” he added.

Obi identified corruption and years of leadership failures as major obstacles to Nigeria’s progress, arguing that the country’s abundant resources should have placed it among the world’s most developed nations.

He maintained that Nigeria’s development depended largely on the character, competence, capacity and commitment of those entrusted with political leadership.

According to him, the forthcoming general elections should be approached as a defining moment for the country rather than a routine political exercise.

“No nation, as I have always maintained, can rise above the character, competence, capacity and commitment of those entrusted with its leadership,” he said.

Obi described the task of rescuing the country as a collective struggle and called on Nigerians to work towards what he termed the birth of a “New Nigeria” that is possible.

World.title: ·         THE CBN’S RATE RESET
World.content:
· It was a well-taken decision, argues

· TOPE FASORANTI

· The decision by the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) on September 22, 2026 to reduce the Monetary Policy Rate (MPR) by 350 basis points, from 26.5 per cent to 23 per cent, was the right call. It was decisive and well-timed. Its real significance, however, lies beneath the size of the cut, and it rewards closer examination than the headline has so far received. Assessed through the effective policy stance, the real interest rate, a standard policy rule and the mechanics of liquidity management, it stands out as a carefully calibrated decision, anchored in sound economics and built for the next phase of Nigeria’s monetary framework.

· I argued recently that the price stability gains of the past two years would soon face a tougher test in reviving credit and growth. The September decision meets it with care.

· Start with the effective operating rate. When a banking system holds surplus liquidity, as Nigeria’s has for much of this year, overnight rates gravitate towards the floor of the policy corridor, because banks holding surplus reserves have the option of placing them at the deposit facility. Under the previous corridor of plus 50 and minus 450 basis points, that floor, the Standing Deposit Facility (SDF), stood at 22 per cent, and interbank pricing settled close to it. The new corridor of plus 50 and minus 300 basis points places the SDF at 20 per cent. The floor has therefore fallen by 200 basis points, well short of the headline 350, and the market has followed it. According to Cordros Research, the overnight rate closed the week to September 25, 2026 at 20.77 per cent. The rest of the cut realigns the official signal with rates already prevailing. A large headline move paired with a modest change in market conditions is the mark of a central bank adjusting with caution.

· The real interest rate reinforces this reading. A central bank that holds its nominal rate unchanged while inflation falls is tightening passively, because the real interest rate rises with every month of disinflation. In August 2025, the MPR stood at 27.5 per cent against headline inflation of 23.14 per cent on National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) data, a backward-looking real rate of about 4.4 percentage points. Today the MPR of 23 per cent sits against headline inflation of 15.39 per cent, a real rate of about 7.6 points. The comparison holds on the effective rate. In August 2025, the corridor of plus 500 and minus 100 basis points placed the SDF at 26.5 per cent, about 3.4 points above inflation. Today’s SDF of 20 per cent sits about 4.6 points above it. On either measure, real rates remain higher than a year ago. The cut returns only part of the passive tightening that disinflation has delivered. The CBN has described the decision as an operational recalibration and not a change in its underlying stance, and the real-rate evidence is consistent with that description.

· A simple policy rule offers a useful benchmark. The Taylor rule, a standard reference for central banks, sets the policy rate according to the neutral real interest rate, current inflation and the distance between inflation and its target. Applying it across the 6 to 9 per cent target the Bank has signalled for its inflation-targeting regime, assuming output is broadly close to potential, a neutral real rate of 2 to 4 per cent and either headline or core inflation, gives an illustrative range of roughly 17 to 24 per cent. The new MPR of 23 per cent sits within it, towards the cautious end. The Bank has calibrated its move on the side of prudence while disinflation completes its course.

· International comparison places this calibration in perspective. Measured against August inflation, the real policy rate stands at about 2 percentage points in Kenya, where the Central Bank Rate is 8.75 per cent and inflation 6.6 per cent, and close to 3 points in South Africa, where the repo rate stands at 7.25 per cent after its September increase and inflation at 4.4 per cent. In Egypt, whose policy corridor of 19 to 20 per cent sits against urban inflation of 14.5 per cent, it is about 5 points. Only Ghana, at roughly 9 points with a policy rate of 14 per cent and inflation of 5 per cent, holds a higher real rate, the result of the same passive tightening as inflation there fell faster than policy adjusted. Within this group of Africa’s leading economies, Nigeria’s monetary stance remains among the most restrictive in real terms after the reset.

· The timing rests on the quality of disinflation as much as its pace. Persistence in core inflation is what typically keeps central banks on hold, because it signals second-round effects in wages and services. NBS data show that core inflation has moderated for three consecutive months, from 16.82 per cent in May to 13.29 per cent in August, and core prices declined slightly on a monthly basis in August. The CBN’s September Inflation Expectations Survey, published after the decision, adds a supporting signal: households and firms assessed future inflation considerably less adversely than current inflation, with the expectations index at 25.1 points against 43.1 for perceptions. Because monetary policy acts with long and variable lags, a forward-looking central bank must act on the trajectory of inflation.

· The credit cycle supports the decision too. CBN money and credit statistics show that private sector credit rose for a third consecutive month in August to 84.55 trillion naira, but its nominal annual growth of 11.4 per cent remains below headline inflation, implying that credit to the private sector is still contracting in real terms. With real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growing by 4.43 per cent, a measured adjustment supports a nascent recovery in lending. The public finances benefit too, as lower rates on new Treasury bills reduce the cost of government borrowing each time maturing debt is refinanced.

· On transmission, a bank’s lending rate combines the policy rate, a term premium, a premium for credit risk and the cost of regulation. The reset acts directly on the first, and over time it can reinforce itself through the third. Lower borrowing costs ease debt-service burdens and strengthen the balance sheets of firms and households, which reduces the probability of default and the risk premium lenders charge. Economists call this the financial accelerator, and in an improving macroeconomic environment it adds to the direct benefit of lower rates.

· The decision to retain the Cash Reserve Requirement (CRR) at 45 per cent for deposit money banks has a further consequence. When a large share of each deposit is held as unremunerated reserves, the effective cost of funding a loan from deposits is the deposit rate divided by the share that can be lent. On that simple arithmetic, and holding other costs unchanged, every percentage point decline in deposit rates at a CRR of 45 per cent lowers the funding cost of a deposit-funded loan by about 1.8 points. How far lending rates actually fall will depend on banks’ funding structures and pricing decisions. The same arithmetic means a high reserve requirement raises the level of lending rates, which is why its gradual normalisation would be a natural next phase once disinflation is fully embedded. The sequencing is prudent. Adjusting the price-based instrument first avoids releasing liquidity into a system already in surplus, which would press market rates against the floor and weaken the signal the Bank has just restored.

· Finally, the reset is an investment in institutional credibility. An inflation-targeting regime requires a policy rate that serves as a clear operating target. Having secured substantial disinflation through a period of firm monetary restraint, the CBN now has room to recalibrate. Preserving credibility will depend on continued progress towards price stability, supported by steady food supply, a stable exchange rate and transmission to lending, the natural markers to watch in the months ahead.

· The weight of the evidence therefore favours the committee’s judgement. The effective adjustment is moderate, real rates remain higher than a year ago and high by regional standards, and the new rate sits within the range a standard policy rule suggests. In an economy seeking to convert stability into sustained growth, the September reset gives monetary policy a sharper instrument and offers the real economy measured relief at a well-chosen moment.

· Dr. Fasoranti is an Economist, Banker, and Enterprise Transformation Strategist.

World.title: HOWEVER BAD THINGS GET, MAY THE MILITARY NEVER RETURN!
World.content:
We must not allow disappointment with civilian government to blind us to the dangers of military rule, argues

GODWIN SOGOLO

·

· Under difficult circumstances, we continue to give thanks to God in the recognition that things could have been much worse. Although this belief cannot be empirically verified, it remains both logically conceivable and practically meaningful. Indeed, the recognition that our circumstances could have been worse constitutes one of the fundamental premises underlying human faith and religious belief.

· At the individual level, the thought that “things could have been worse” offers consolation rather than satisfaction with our present circumstances. It invites us to envisage a possible world in which our situation is less favourable than it is in reality — a world that is logically conceivable, even if it does not exist. This perspective helps us appreciate that, however unpleasant our present condition may be, circumstances could have been even less favourable. While we pray that our situation does not deteriorate further, our ultimate aspiration remains to overcome the challenges we face and improve our lot in life.

· At the broader socio-political level, however, this way of thinking can serve purposes that go beyond personal consolation. Politicians frequently appeal to the fear of a worse alternative to persuade citizens that their policies, decisions, or continued stay in power are preferable to the consequences of choosing otherwise. The argument is simple but powerful: whatever the shortcomings of the present administartion, changing it might produce something even worse. The possibility of a greater disaster thus becomes an instrument of political persuasion, and sometimes a convenient means of defending an otherwise indefensible situation.

· The crucial question, however, is whether the possibility that things could have been worse is sufficient justification for accepting things as they are. More importantly, does the fact that one situation might have been worse establish that the alternative is necessarily better? These questions are particularly relevant to the debate over military intervention in African politics and, indeed, beyond.

· Examples of political leaders invoking the prospect of a greater disaster to justify controversial decisions abound in contemporary international politics. President Donald Trump of the United States, for instance, has justified military action against the Islamic Republic of Iran on the grounds that it was necessary to protect America and the wider Western world from the potentially catastrophic consequences of Iran acquiring and using nuclear weapons. The underlying argument is that the costs and dangers of military action must be weighed against the potentially catastrophic consequences of failing to act. In such reasoning, war is presented not necessarily as a desirable outcome in itself, but as a means of preventing something worse.

·

· Military apologists in Africa employ similar reasoning to justify the intervention of the armed forces in the political systems of African states. Their arguments rest, broadly, on two principal claims. The first is that democratic institutions, largely inherited or adapted from Western political traditions, are structurally ill-suited to the socio-cultural realities of African societies. According to this view, liberal democracy does not adequately reflect Africa’s indigenous political traditions, communal values, historical experiences, and patterns of social organisation. It is argued that the transplantation of such institutions onto African soil has contributed to political instability, electoral manipulation, corruption, and ineffective governance.

· The second argument, which follows from the first, is that the military – by virtue of its hierarchical structure, discipline, organisational coherence, and capacity for decisive action – is better equipped to govern than civilian politicians. Advocates of military rule often invoke the failures of civilian administrations – particularly corruption, abuse of power, ethnic and religious divisions, electoral fraud, and economic mismanagement – to suggest that military intervention, however undesirable in principle, may be necessary to rescue a nation from political and economic collapse. The underlying reasoning is familiar: if civilian democracy has brought a country to the brink of disaster, military rule may be justified as the lesser evil, preventing circumstances from becoming much worse.

· Both arguments, however, rest on assumptions that require critical examination. The first argument requires us to distinguish between the historical origins of democratic institutions and their suitability for African societies. The fact that certain democratic institutions were developed in the West does not, in itself, establish that they are incompatible with African values or political traditions. Nor does it follow that Africa must choose between an uncritical adoption of Western models and a wholesale rejection of democratic governance. The more pertinent question is how democratic institutions can be adapted to the historical, cultural, and socio-political circumstances of individual African states while preserving the principles of accountability, popular participation, and the rule of law.

· The second argument – that military governments are inherently better equipped to govern – also rests on questionable assumptions. Military organisations may be highly effective in maintaining internal discipline and executing commands, but the qualities required to command an army are not identical to those required to govern a complex, pluralistic society. A country is not a military barracks, and its citizens are not soldiers expected to obey orders without question.

· Similarly, the claim that military governments have performed better than civilian administrations cannot be sustained merely by pointing to the shortcomings of particular civilian governments. Military regimes are not immune to corruption, authoritarianism, economic mismanagement, or the abuse of public power. Indeed, the concentration of political authority in the hands of military rulers may weaken the very mechanisms of accountability needed to prevent such abuses. The suspension of constitutional government may therefore replace one set of political problems with another, sometimes more serious, rather than resolve the difficulties that originally prompted intervention.

· The crucial issue, therefore, is not whether military rule might – under particular circumstances – appear preferable to a failing civilian administration. It is whether military intervention provides a sustainable solution to the underlying problems of governance or merely postpones, compounds, or reproduces them. Here, the familiar argument that things could have been much worse becomes a convenient instrument of justification: the military presents itself as the force that has saved, or must save, the nation from a greater disaster. Yet the possibility that civilian rule might have deteriorated further does not, by itself, establish that military intervention was necessary, legitimate, or beneficial. A convincing defence of intervention must demonstrate not merely the failures it claims to prevent, but also the legitimacy, effectiveness, and long-term consequences of the alternative it proposes.

· In assessing previous administrations, whether military or civilian, we must also recognise a psychological tendency that can distort our judgement of the past. Every generation is susceptible to the belief that things were better in earlier times and that the present is inferior to what came before. Accompanying this tendency is often an uncertainty about, and fear of, the future. The past becomes a refuge from the anxieties of the present, while the future is perceived less as an opportunity for improvement than as a source of impending danger. The growing global concern over the actual and potential dangers posed by the uncontrolled development of artificial intelligence (AI) provides a good example.

·

· Psychologists have several concepts that help explain this tendency, including rosy retrospection, the inclination to remember past experiences more favourably than they were, and nostalgia, the sentimental longing for an earlier period. A related phenomenon is status quo bias, the tendency to prefer a familiar arrangement to an uncertain alternative. These concepts may help explain why some Nigerians, particularly among the older generations, increasingly look back with nostalgia at the years of military rule.

· Ultimately, nostalgia for military rule may be understood, at least in part, as an expression of popular disappointment with the performance of democratic institutions. When citizens perceive that democracy has become an instrument for the enrichment of the political elite rather than a mechanism for promoting public welfare, they may begin to romanticise an authoritarian past. Yet such nostalgia can be misleading if it encourages people to confuse the visible execution of developmental projects with good governance in its broader sense. Roads, bridges, and public buildings are important, but so too are accountability, the rule of law, respect for human rights, and the freedom of citizens to choose and remove their leaders.

· The lesson, therefore, is not that Nigeria should return to military rule, but that democratic governance must demonstrate its capacity to deliver tangible improvements in the lives of ordinary citizens. A democracy that fails to translate public resources into public welfare risks undermining its own legitimacy and creating conditions in which authoritarian alternatives begin to appear attractive. What Nigerians should yearn for is not the return of the military, but the return of purposeful leadership, fiscal discipline, accountability, institutional integrity and a genuine commitment to national development.

·

· However bad things may get, we must not allow disappointment with civilian government to blind us to the dangers of military rule. Our objective should not be to find comfort in the thought that things could have been worse, but to build a political system in which they can genuinely become better.

·

·

Sogolo is an Emeritus Professor who has taught and conducted research in Philosophy for over five decades – at the University of Ibadan, Cardiff University of Wales and currently at the National Open University of Nigeria.

World.title: DSS Arrests: Why Intelligence Must Drive Nigeria’s Fight Against Insecurity
World.content:
By Olufemi Lawson

The recent arrest of five suspected kidnappers linked to the abduction of 20 prospective National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) members, alongside the arrest of fugitive Faisal Maina, represents a significant achievement by the Department of State Services (DSS) and a welcome development in Nigeria’s fight against insecurity.

Beyond the arrests themselves, these operations reinforce the importance of intelligence gathering, strategic surveillance and coordinated security operations in confronting terrorism, kidnapping and other organised crimes threatening the country.

The rescue of the abducted prospective corps members and the subsequent arrest of five suspects demonstrate the value of sustained intelligence work beyond the immediate scene of a crime. Similarly, the reported arrest of Faisal Maina, who had been on the run since 2020, underscores the importance of intelligence in tracking fugitives and ensuring that nobody remains permanently beyond the reach of the law.

As I argued during a television interview yesterday, Nigeria must invest significantly more in intelligence if the country is to achieve lasting success in its war against terrorism, kidnapping, banditry and other criminal activities.

While military operations, weapons and personnel remain important, security cannot be sustained through force alone. Intelligence enables security agencies to identify criminal networks, anticipate attacks, track perpetrators and dismantle their operational structures before they inflict further damage.

Intelligence must therefore become the backbone of Nigeria’s national security strategy.

The Federal Government must prioritise modern intelligence technology, digital forensics, personnel training, secure communication systems and improved operational logistics. Investing in prevention through intelligence is ultimately more effective and less costly than continually responding to attacks after lives and property have beecommend

I particularly commend Mr. Adeola Oluwatosin the Director-General of the DSS for the renewed emphasis on the service’s traditional national security responsibilities, especially intelligence gathering, threat assessment and the prevention of threats to national security.

In my assessment, this renewed direction represents a welcome departure from what critics had perceived in previous periods as a diversion towards unconventional approaches that risked overshadowing the service’s core intelligence mandate.

The DSS occupies a critical position in Nigeria’s security architecture, and its effectiveness should be measured by its capacity to uncover threats, disrupt criminal networks and provide actionable intelligence that protects lives and national interests.

The latest arrests demonstrate the practical value of a focused intelligence service. I salute the Director-General for his leadership and, more importantly, the officers and men of the DSS whose vigilance, professionalism and dedication contributed to these successes.

However, the remaining suspects linked to the NYSC abduction must be tracked down, and all those found culpable must face the law.

The successes also raised the need for greater synergy among the DSS, the military, the police, the EFCC and other relevant security and law-enforcement agencies.

Criminal networks exploit gaps in coordination and information sharing. A more integrated security system, supported by joint intelligence operations and timely exchange of credible information, would significantly improve the country’s ability to prevent attacks and apprehend offenders.

The Federal Government must also increase funding and operational support for the DSS to strengthen its technological capacity, personnel welfare, intelligence infrastructure and field operations.

Adequate funding, accompanied by accountability and effective oversight, will enable the service to respond more effectively to evolving security threats.

The arrest of the suspected kidnappers and Faisal Maina sends a strong message that intelligence-led operations can deliver tangible results. Nevertheless, the ultimate measure of success must be the prevention of future crimes, the dismantling of criminal networks and the restoration of public confidence.

I urge the Federal Government to sustain its support for the DSS and other security agencies while ensuring that investigations and prosecutions are conducted in accordance with the law.

Nigeria cannot afford to treat intelligence as a secondary component of national security. It must be recognised as a strategic national investment.

I once again salute the Director-General and the officers and men of the DSS for their latest achievements. Their efforts deserve commendation and sustained institutional support.

With stronger intelligence capabilities, improved inter-agency cooperation and adequate funding, Nigeria can make meaningful progress towards defeating terrorism, kidnapping and organised crime.

*Comrade Olufemi Lawson, National Secretary of the Campaign for Democracy (CD), writes from Lagos.

World.title: Troops Disrupt Illegal Arms-Trafficking Network in North-central, Arrest One Over Alleged Kidnapping, Sexual Assault
World.content:
Linus Aleke in Abuja

The Nigerian military has said that troops of the Joint Task Force, North-Central Operation Enduring Peace, have uncovered, tracked and disrupted an illegal arms-trafficking network in the North-central region, particularly in Plateau State. The troops also dismantled kidnapping networks in the state.

The Director of Defence Media Operations, Major General Michael Onoja, made this known during his weekly update on the operational activities of troops of the Armed Forces of Nigeria (AFN) across the country.

He also revealed that troops of the Joint Task Force, North-West Operation Fansan Yamma, apprehended a suspect identified as Yusuf Iliya Sani at Maraban Kakini over his alleged involvement in kidnapping, extortion, sexual assault and killings in Birnin Gwari Local Government Area (LGA) of Kaduna State.

He said: “Troops of Operation Enduring Peace maintained operations to disrupt illegal arms trafficking, identify suspected perpetrators of violent crime and dismantle kidnapping networks in Plateau State.

“To this end, troops conducted a covert operation in Mangu and Barkin Ladi LGAs of Plateau State and arrested a suspected arms fabricator at Heipang, Barkin Ladi LGA. Three other suspects were also arrested over their alleged involvement in illegal arms trafficking. Troops recovered one locally fabricated revolver rifle, one fabricated pistol, one fabricated AK-47 barrel, one AK-47 magazine and 42 rounds of 7.62mm × 54mm rimmed ammunition.

“On 10 October 2026, troops arrested a suspect, Yusuf Suleiman, at Barkin Ladi Main Market. He was allegedly linked to the attack on Kassa community on 24 September 2026, as well as kidnapping, armed robbery and the killing of a resident, Mr Gyang, on 16 April 2026.

“Also, on 14 October 2026, troops raided a suspected kidnappers’ hideout at Ruga in Methodist Kisahyip, Agingin, Bassa LGA of Plateau State, and arrested two suspects.”

Recounting the operational activities of troops of Operation Fansan Yamma on 9 October 2026, General Onoja said troops operating around the Galadimawa area sighted three suspected terrorists fleeing with a kidnapped person.

He further explained: “Troops engaged the suspects and forced them to abandon the victim.

“On 10 October, troops responded to reports that a local resident travelling from Dogon Dawa to Takama Village in Birnin Gwari LGA of Kaduna State was under attack by an unknown armed group. On arrival, the responding troops engaged the assailants and recovered an AK-47 rifle with 15 rounds of 7.62mm ammunition.

“Following continued tracking and monitoring, troops apprehended a suspect identified as Yusuf Iliya Sani at Maraban Kakini on 10 October 2026 over his alleged involvement in kidnapping, extortion, sexual assault and killings in Birnin Gwari LGA of Kaduna State.”

Onoja said the operations conducted across all operational theatres had sustained the AFN’s efforts to ensure a safe and secure environment and restore security across the country.

The Chief of Defence Staff, General Olufemi Oluyede, commended the resilience of all security personnel, urging them to maintain operational momentum, remain highly vigilant and deny criminal elements any freedom of action.

The Defence Chief also called on all security agencies to strengthen their collaborative intelligence-sharing frameworks to enhance operations against criminal elements across the country.

He said national security was a collective civic responsibility, adding that through unwavering unity and resolve, the military would secure a peaceful and prosperous future for Nigeria.

World.title: Peter Obi Media Office Faults Shettima Over ‘Diminished Obi’ Remark
World.content:
* Says political leaders should debate records, policies not personal attacks

Sunday Aborisade in Abuja

The Peter Obi Media Office has criticised Vice-President Kashim Shettima over his description of the presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Peter Obi, as “diminished,” urging political leaders to focus on candidates’ records, policies and ideas rather than personal attacks.

In a statement issued Sunday by its spokesman, Idris Zekeri Jnr, the media office described the remark as inconsistent with the standards of political engagement expected of leaders, particularly at a time when political parties are positioning themselves ahead of the 2027 general election.

The office took exception to what it considered a contrast between Shettima’s call for northerners to respect former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar, an opposition figure, and his description of Obi, another opposition leader.

“Although Shettima has the right to oppose Obi, it is difficult to understand why he would demand respect for one opposition leader while casually dismissing another,” the statement said.

It added that political disagreements should not prevent public officials from recognising the contributions and political standing of their opponents.

The media office said Obi had maintained a campaign focused on issues and had avoided abusive language against political opponents.

“As a man of great decency, our candidate has conducted his campaign professionally and decorously. He has consistently focused his remarks on issues and has neither discussed nor used abusive language against anyone,” it said.

The statement also drew attention to the records of Obi and Shettima as former governors of Anambra and Borno States, respectively, arguing that their respective performances should be assessed against verifiable evidence rather than political rhetoric.

“However, Obi’s performance in Anambra State across key areas of governance surpassed Shettima’s record in Borno State, as demonstrated by performance statistics and the awards he received,” the office said.

It cited Obi’s record in fiscal management and investments in education and healthcare as areas that, in its view, distinguished his administration.

The office, however, did not provide comparative statistics in the statement to substantiate its assessment of the two former governors’ performances.

It challenged the vice-president and other political opponents to interrogate Obi’s record using verifiable facts and figures if they disagreed with the assessment.

“If Shettima contests any aspect of Obi’s record, he should present the facts rather than resort to political name-calling,” the statement added.

The media office said the controversy raised broader questions about political civility, the treatment of opposition figures and the responsibility of public officials to sustain issue-based debate in Nigeria’s democratic process.

It also appealed to political leaders from the South-east, including those in the All Progressives Congress (APC), to distinguish political loyalty from their responsibility to uphold mutual respect among political actors.

The statement urged South-east political leaders who support the APC to reflect on the implications of the exchange, particularly where they believe that criticism of an opposition politician from their region is inconsistent with the treatment accorded other political figures.

It said disagreements over party affiliation should not become grounds for tolerating what it considers disrespectful language against fellow Nigerians.

“We urge Igbo leaders in the APC and all Nigerians to draw the appropriate lesson from this episode and note that political loyalty must never justify tolerating disrespect towards a fellow Nigerian,” the statement said.

The office maintained that political competition should provide an opportunity for candidates and their supporters to examine competing records, policy proposals and governing philosophies.

“Those who oppose Obi should scrutinise his ideas and record rather than resort to personal abuse,” it said.

“Nigeria needs a contest based on records and ideas, not selective respect and political denigration.”

The media office further argued that Obi’s political relevance should ultimately be determined by voters rather than by comments from political opponents.

“The Nigerian people, rather than Shettima’s rhetoric, will determine Peter Obi’s political relevance,” it said.

The statement, dated October 18, 2026, was signed by Zekeri on behalf of the Peter Obi Media Office.

The development comes as political parties and their leading figures intensify their positioning ahead of the 2027 general election, with the conduct of political campaigns, the credibility of candidates and the tone of public debate expected to feature prominently in the contest.

While political leaders are entitled to criticise opponents and challenge their records in office, the exchange underscores the importance of substantiating political claims with evidence and maintaining a distinction between legitimate criticism and personal disparagement.

For the NDC presidential candidate and his supporters, the central argument is that Obi’s record as a former governor should be judged on its merits. For his political opponents, the challenge is to present competing evidence and policy alternatives capable of persuading voters.

Ultimately, the debate over the records of former governors and their suitability for national leadership is likely to remain part of the broader political contest as the 2027 election approaches.

World.title: 2027: Abia Youths Declare Support for Tinubu, Deputy Speaker Kalu, Plan One-Million-Man March in Aba
World.content:
A group of youths comprising artisans and Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) owners under the umbrella of “Great Aba Men” in Abia State has declared support for the re-election of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu and the Deputy Speaker of the House of Representatives, Rt. Hon. Benjamin Okezie Kalu.

The declaration was made during a courtesy visit to the Deputy Speaker at his country home in Bende on Saturday.

Speaking on behalf of the group, its leader, Prince Okwudiri Uche, said Abia youths will give President Tinubu the highest number of votes in the South East in the 2027 presidential election.

He said: “From today, we have declared for Mr. President. We will support Mr. President and Rt. Hon. Benjamin Okezie Kalu. Asiwaju is the next President of the Federal Republic of Nigeria.

“There is no way we will have the Deputy Speaker of this federation from Abia State, supported by Mr. President, and not return the President. It will not happen. Rt. Hon. Sir, we will make you proud because we will deliver President Tinubu. Abia youths will make it happen. He will go for a second term. Aba people will not let you down”.

The group, which congratulated the Deputy Speaker on his appointment as Director-General II (South) of the PBAT/APC Presidential Campaign Council, requested him to serve as its Grand Patron.

It also revealed plans to organize a one-million-man march for President Tinubu in Aba.

In his remarks, Kalu commended the group for declaring support for President Tinubu and himself.

He noted the President’s love for the people of the South East, particularly Abia State, stating that the President who supported a son of Abia to emerge as Deputy Speaker deserves to be repaid with gratitude.

“From today, you have become Mr. President’s foot soldiers and will take the message of Renewed Hope to every nook and cranny of Aba. I declare you the sons of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu. We are starting a movement that will go beyond January 16, 2026,” Kalu said.

He promised to support the group with a campaign bus for the planned march, charging them to mobilize across the State and take the message of Renewed Hope Agenda to the hinterlands.

“Every street will come out to show that we are supporting President Bola Ahmed Tinubu. In Bende, the President will harvest all the votes because the Deputy Speaker is from this Local Government. So, go and put up your strategy. We will show that Great Aba Men are behind the President. We must make sure the President wins in Aba. I want you to be very visible in Aba and take over Aba. Let’s comb the city to announce our presence,” he said.

World.title: FG Tasks VCs to Prioritize High-demand Degree Programmes
World.content:
* Reaffirms commitment to establishing autism centres across six geopolitical zones



Kuni Tyessi in Abuja

The Federal Government has called on vice-chancellors of Nigerian universities to prioritise degree programmes that address critical manpower shortages, respond to emerging societal needs and equip graduates with specialised skills for professional practice and employment.

It said such programmes should include degrees in Audiology, Occupational Therapy, Speech and Language Therapy, Clinical Psychology and Medical Social Work, noting that expanding training in these fields would help bridge gaps in specialised healthcare and social services while creating more career opportunities for young Nigerians.

Minister of Education, Dr. Tunji Alausa, also reaffirmed the Federal Government’s commitment to establishing autism centres across the six geopolitical zones to improve access to specialised care and support for persons on the autism spectrum and their families.

Alausa stressed that universities must align their academic offerings with national workforce needs and the growing demand for specialised professional services.

He noted that developing these programmes would strengthen Nigeria’s capacity to provide essential services locally, reduce gaps in specialist care and build a skilled workforce capable of meeting the needs of the population.

The planned autism centres are expected to support access to diagnosis, therapeutic services and research, while serving as regional hubs for families, healthcare professionals and educational institutions.

The initiative reflects the Federal Government’s determination to strengthen local capacity and improve support for persons with autism and related developmental conditions.

The minister assured stakeholders that the Federal Government would continue to pursue reforms that expand access to relevant education, strengthen institutional capacity and promote skills development.

Alausa commended the Chairman of the Federal Government Committee for the Advancement of Audiology, Occupational Therapy and Speech and Language Therapy, Dr. Victoria Amu, for her passion and dedication to duty.

He called on vice-vhancellors and other university administrators to work closely with the Ministerial Committee Chairman, Dr. Victoria Amu, the relevant regulatory agencies and professional bodies to facilitate the development of the proposed programmes and ensure that training meets appropriate academic and professional standards.

The minister reaffirmed the Federal Government’s commitment to building a responsive and inclusive higher education system that equips Nigerians with relevant skills, addresses critical manpower gaps and expands access to essential specialised services.

The initiatives form part of the administration’s broader efforts to strengthen human capital development, improve service delivery and ensure that Nigeria’s education system responds effectively to national priorities and the needs of its citizens.

World.title: Birmingham, UNILAG Bring UK Postgraduate Degrees Closer to Nigerians
World.content:
Iyke Bede

Nigerian students seeking internationally recognised postgraduate qualifications will have an opportunity to study programmes offered by a United Kingdom university without relocating abroad, following a new partnership between the University of Birmingham and the University of Lagos (UNILAG).

The universities have launched two one-year postgraduate programmes in Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Data Technologies, and Digital Media and Communications, which will be delivered in Lagos from September 2027.

The initiative, developed under a Transnational Education (TNE) arrangement in collaboration with the Federal Ministry of Education and the National Universities Commission, is designed to expand access to international higher education while developing skills relevant to Nigeria’s growing economy.

Speaking at the launch on Thursday, the Minister of Education, Dr Tunji Alausa, described the partnership as crucial to Nigeria’s tertiary education development.

“Our planned collaboration and partnership with the University of Birmingham is both timely and strategic at this critical phase of Nigeria’s tertiary education advancement. It is designed to consolidate and deepen the significant gains we have made in strengthening our university system, while expanding access to world-class, high-quality education anchored in global best practices,” he said.

The MSc in AI and Data Technologies will cover machine learning, deep learning, computer vision, large language models and AI ethics, preparing graduates for opportunities in fintech, healthcare innovation and business analytics.

The MA in Digital Media and Communications will focus on digital cultures, communication, power, identity and media ethics, while equipping students with research, content creation and broadcasting skills for careers in journalism and digital communications.

The Provost of the University of Birmingham, Professor Nick Vaughan-Williams, said the programmes would support Nigeria’s educational and workforce development needs.

“We’re proud to launch these programmes with our partners at UNILAG. Together we are supporting Nigeria’s tertiary education and talent needs, which are central to its ambitions for economic growth,” he said.

Echoing the emphasis on the partnership’s long-term value, the Vice-Chancellor of the University of Lagos, Professor Folasade T. Ogunsola, said the collaboration reflected the university’s broader approach to international partnerships:

“The University of Lagos-University of Birmingham TNE collaboration reflects UNILAG’s broader vision of reimagining partnerships built on mutual respect, co-creation, and shared responsibility.”

The British Council Nigeria described the arrangement as a more affordable and accessible route for Nigerian students to obtain UK postgraduate qualifications without studying abroad.

World.title: [Watch] Woman fights off Cape baboon attack in viral video
World.content:
A woman fought off a Cape Peninsula baboon attack in a viral video. Images via TikTok

A video of a woman who fought off a baboon that raided her car in an attack in Cape Town has racked up millions of views on TikTok

The video was recorded at Sir Lowry’s Pass.

WOMAN FIGHTS OFF BABOON IN CRAZY CAR RAID

In the clip, posted by @buusolakhe, a group of female friends is seen trying to ward off several baboons at a picnic spot at Sir Lowry’s Pass, which falls under the Cape Town Metropolitan area.



The troop attempted to raid the car in search of food.

The woman behind the camera films herself opening her door before yanking out one angry baboon, which proceeded to bite her on her right arm.

She screams for help from her friends and a SAPS police van, parked nearby.

In the comment section, South Africans were amazed at the woman’s bravery while confronting a baboon.

She revealed that she had sought medical attention for the animal bite.

Take a look…



WHAT TO DO WHEN YOU SPOT THE WILD ANIMAL

Cape Town is well known for its Chacma baboon population. City officials have urged residents and visitors to keep a safe distance from the wild animals.

Here are a few tips on what to do when you spot the animal whilst out and about…

Stay inside your vehicle.

Keep doors locked and windows and sunroofs closed. Baboons are intelligent animals who can open car doors and may climb through windows to steal food.

Don’t leave food lying around.

Food should never be visible through the windows. Pack bags and food items in the vehicle’s boot or under the seats.

Do not chase a baboon or try to retrieve stolen belongings

If a baboon steals your bag and possessions, the City advises the public to let the animals move away after searching the bag, then retrieve your belongings.

Leave if they appear aggressive

When picnicking, pack up and leave if nearby baboons appear aggressive.

Never feed or touch baboons.

Feeding is punishable by law. The City warns that people caught feeding baboons may face a fine of up to R10,000 and/or two years’ imprisonment.

World.title: Baas van die plaas: Franco Mostert shows off his farm
World.content:
Franco Mostert at his farm. Images via IG

Franco Mostert is the latest Springbok to show off his flourishing business move – farming. The Bok lock has ventured into growing his own fresh produce and managing a guest house.

FRANCO MOSTERT SHOWS OFF NEW BUSINESS VENTURE

On their Instagram accounts, Franco Mostert and his wife, Juan-Ri, have given their followers a look at their farming business, Sous Plaas.

The company grows and sells fresh produce, like lettuce, onions, carrots and beetroot to local supermarkets.



The couple also own their own farmhouse, a self-catering holiday accommodation, called Die Mostert Plaashuis in the North West.

On its official IG account, Sous Plaas posted a clip of Franco manning a tractor in an open field during his downtime.

“Baas van die plaas”, the company said of the Springbok, who has 85 test caps.



OTHER SPRINGBOKS TRANSITIONING INTO FARMING

Franco Mostert is one of several current Springboks who own farms.



Pieter-Steph du Toit’s family owns Kloovenburg Wine & Olive Estate in the Western Cape, which produces wine, grape juice, olives, and avocados.

Kwagga Smith owns a guest farm in Mpumalanga, which also cultivates maize, soy, pecans, and walnuts.

Retired Springbok Duane Vermeulen owns a walnut farm near his restaurant in the Free State.

World.title: Camps Bay beach trashed by beach-goers [video]
World.content:
Scenes of a littered Camps Bay have upset Cape Town residents. Images via IG

A clip of a littered Camps Bay beach, left by messy beach-goers, has left Cape Town residents fuming.

This comes amid growing criticism about an influx of rowdy crowds, including a group of matric students.

CAMPS BAY TRASHED BY PARTYING BEACH-GOERS

On social media, a viral video has captured the aftermath of a beach party, which reportedly took place at Camps Bay beach last weekend.



In the clip, the beach is littered with items such as a KFC bucket, plastic bottles, and even an empty ice cream container.

“Camps Bay on a Monday morning”, read the text across the video.

In the comments section, Cape Town residents expressed their anger and frustration.



Ben Botha: “If that’s what’s on the beach, think what’s in the water!”

Anke-Elize Strauss: “Our beautiful beaches are there for everyone to enjoy, a gift from our amazing Creator. But we also have a responsibility to look after them. So much rubbish ends up in our oceans, and it honestly makes me so sad to see how little respect people have for our beautiful country”.

Cheslyn Louw: “There needs to be stricter law enforcement on the beach, especially during the festive season period, and now from matriculants who come to enjoy their last break before final exams”.



CITY LAYS DOWN THE RULES

On social media, many local residents have complained that the rowdy parties at Clifton Beach and Camps Bay violate city bylaws.

According to a City of Cape Town document, beach-goers must refrain from the following…

Being in possession of or consuming any alcohol except on licensed premises or where a temporary liquor licence has been granted;

Being under the influence of alcohol, drugs, or any other dependence-producing substance;

Holding, convening, or organising any entertainment, display, performance, procession, public meeting, recreation, or event without the permission of the City or doing so in contravention of any condition attached to any such authorisation

Acting in a manner that poses a risk to life, human well-being or property;

Behaving in an improper, indecent, unruly, violent, or anti-social manner or causing a

disturbance;

Performing an indecent act.

World.title: Ramaphosa concerned about political killings ahead of elections
World.content:
President Cyril Ramaphosa says he is concerned about the spate of politically related killings ahead of the 2026 local government elections.

Ramaphosa made the remarks while addressing journalists on the sidelines of his election campaign in Cape Town on Sunday.

RAMAPHOSA WEIGHS IN ON POLITICAL KILLINGS

This week, two ANC members were shot dead and three others injured during a door-to-door campaign in Umgababa, south of Durban, in KwaZulu-Natal.

The killings come amid growing concerns about political violence ahead of the 4 November 2026 local government elections.

“Obviously, we are all disturbed about the political killings that are targeting people who are either campaigning, who are both representatives who should be elected, and also the mass killings. The police are on the heels of all those people who are perpetrating those murders.

“We cannot be a country that has the killings of people who other people may be opposed to. We want to bring those killings to an end,” he said.

AT LEAST 43 PEOPLE KILLED IN SUSPECTED ATTACKS

The killings come amid wider concerns about political violence ahead of the November 4 local government elections.

A report by the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organised Crime, published in October, recorded at least 43 people killed in suspected political assassinations across South Africa between January and September 2026.

The report recorded 45 suspected political attacks during that period, with the number of deaths already exceeding the organisation’s full-year totals for the 2021 local government election year and the 2024 national election year.

World.title: ‘You can have him’: Bernard Parker’s ‘baby mama’ claps back?
World.content:
Bernard Parker's alleged baby mama throws shade at him. Images via IG

Bernard Parker’s alleged baby mama, Kacha Stepanovic, has seemingly taken a swipe at him amid rumours he has rekindled his relationship with his wife, Wendy Parker.

Earlier this week, the former Kaizer Chiefs and Bafana player made headlines after posting a statement about his split from the Serbian woman, who is allegedly the mother of his baby daughter. In it, the 40-year-old issued an apology, hinting at being unfaithful

He has since issued a second statement, distancing himself from his initial comments.



BERNARD PARKER’S EX THROWS SHADE?

On her Instagram Stories, Kacha Stepanovic seemingly shaded her ex, Bernard Parker and his wife, Wendy.

Kacha shared a video, which she also reposted, about an individual who appeared unfazed over a confrontation with another woman. The tagline read: “That girl who doesn’t fight other girls over a man”.

“You can have him”, the individual in the video says to the other woman.



Kacha is likely referring to Wendy Parker, who recently changed her profile picture to one with her and her husband, Bernard Parker.

In 2015, Wendy made headlines over a viral video of her physical fight with Diski Divas reality TV show co-star, Nonhle Ndala.

Kacha Stepanovic’s cryptic post. Is it about ex, Bernard Parker?

Images via IG

WIFE WENDY MAKES A RETURN?

Her actions were spotted by eagle-eyed social media users.

World.title: Full list of public swimming pools now open in Joburg
World.content:
Joburg has reopened more public swimming pools ahead of summer, with 13 more scheduled to be open by Monday.

However, 26 pools across the metro are still undergoing repairs and maintenance, according to the City’s office for Community Development

As of Wednesday last week, the number of operational facilities increased from 13 to 20.



The City is targeting another 13 openings by Monday, 19 October. If successful, this would bring the total number of operational swimming pools in Joburg to 33.

“With most major hurdles substantially resolved, the City’s focus has shifted towards maximising operational capacity,” said Community Development MMC Thapelo Amad.

“This includes sustaining uninterrupted operations, maintaining safety standards and ensuring reliable service delivery ahead of the peak swimming season in November and December.”



The City also confirmed that qualified lifeguards and cashiers are available at Joburg’s reopened facilities.

Which Joburg swimming pools are now open?

The following 20 municipal swimming pools were listed as operational as of the 13th of October:

REGION SWIMMING POOL A Rabie Ridge B Linden B Verity Park B Roosevelt Park B Blairgowrie C Florida Lake C Davidsonville D Jabulani New Pool D Orlando D Pimville D Meadowlands D Noordgesig E Zoo Lake E Paterson Park F Pioneer Park F Rhodes Park G Lenasia South G Eldorado Park Extension 4 D Eldorado Park Extension 9 G Lenasia Extension 2 – Greyville

Public pools scheduled to be open by 19 October

The City identified a further 13 pools for scheduled openings between 14 and 18 October.



“Our phased in approach of reopening swimming pools is working and we anticipate opening 13 additional swimming pools by Monday 19 October, bringing the total to 33,” Councillor Amad announced.

Region Swimming pool D Dobsonville D Jabavu D Diepkloof D Power Park D Senaone E Sydenham E East Bank F Turffontein F Forest Hill F Crown Gardens F Yeoville F Malvern G Lenasia Extension 10

Despite the progress, operational challenges continue to hamper the reopening of certain municipal pools in Joburg.

Coronationville’s pool reopened but had to close again due to an electrical supply issue. Roodepoort’s pool has been affected by a faulty substation, while electrical damage and cable theft have delayed the opening of Florida North swimming pool.



Ivory Park’s newly-completed facility remains closed amid community-related employment demands and security concerns.

Meanwhile, Drieziek’s new public swimming pool is expected to open once snag-list items have been completed.

The City noted that 26 pools across Regions A to G were still undergoing repairs and maintenance, with contractors on site and a number of facilities nearing completion.



“Aquatics will continue monitoring facility readiness, and facilitating further swimming pool openings,” Amad added.

“We will continue engagements with community stakeholders to urgently resolve employment, vandalism and security problems.”

World.title: All grown up! Charlize steps out with two daughters [video]
World.content:
Charlize Theron and her two daughters Jackson and August. Images via IG

Charlize Theron and her two daughters turned heads at the Academy Museum Gala in Los Angeles on Saturday, 17 October.

The South-African born actress adopted Jackson (who now identifies as a girl) and August in 2012 and 2015, respectively.

CHARLIZE THERON AND TWO DAUGHTERS TURN HEADS AT EVENT

On Saturday, Charlize made an appearance at the Sixth Annual Academy Museum Gala in LA, where she received the Icon Award in celebration of her cinematic career.



While the blonde Benoni-born star walked the red carpet alone, she shared a sweet moment with her daughters, Jackson, 14, and August, 12.

Charlize and her model-like kids shared a warm embrace in a video captured by People magazine.

Both girls had their hair styled in long braids and wore black minidresses and strappy heels.



While they aren’t biologically related, it’s clear the girls inherited their style and grace from their South African mom.

WHY SHE CHOSE TO ADOPT

Over the years, Charlize Theron has spoken openly and honestly about her unconventional path to parenthood.



In an interview with Elle Magazine in 2018, the South African-born star revealed that she was intrigued with adoption from a young age.

She shared: “South Africa, orphanages were everywhere, and I wanted a brother or sister. I was always aware that there are so many children in this world who don’t have families. Adoption is a very personal thing – I know people whom I love dearly who don’t feel that they could raise another child as their own. I respect that.

“But for me -and I can’t be the only person out there- I never saw a difference in raising an adopted child versus my own biological child. I don’t feel like I’m missing out on something.



“This was always my first choice, even when I was in a relationship. I was very honest with my partners that I was open to having my own biological kids but that adoption had to be a part of my life. I felt that strongly about it”.

World.title: DA and ANC gunning for Cape Town
World.content:
CAPE TOWN - The race for Cape Town’s mayoral seat is heating up ahead of next month's polls.

ANC representative Jerimia Thuynsma claims the party managed the metro better than the DA when it last governed Cape Town before 2006.

The parties were facing off in eNCA's We The Nation election debate.

Thuynsma said, "The ANC governed the city for three years, and our delivery record in the three years is clearly much better than the DA. That's why you will be able to see that we delivered more houses... "We were in the process, as I indicated the last time, of getting people who are living in rental stock of the ANC to transfer the houses to them so that they can have ownership and have property that they can basically use. That of course got stopped when the DA came into power in 2006."

Geordin Hill-Lewis blasted the ANC, saying the only example of success that the ANC government can point to is more than 20 years ago.
