The legislature has already approved the regime’s plan to borrow money from major arms supplier Belarus, which will be used to import goods from Minsk.

Prior to Wednesday’s parliamentary approval, the regime had already raised nearly 14 trillion kyats through multiple treasury bill and bond auctions to finance its budget deficit for fiscal year 2026–27, according to Central Bank Deputy Governor Thet Htun Aung. He admitted the regime had also relied on treasury bond issuances and borrowing from the Central Bank to address budget shortfalls in previous years.

Analysts warn that borrowing from the Central Bank will accelerate inflation and the kyat’s depreciation. Currency traders report the dollar rose to 4,670 kyats in the unofficial market on Thursday, up from 4,450 kyats earlier this month, while the baht has risen from 129 to 139 kyats. Before the coup, the kyat was trading at less than 1,300 to the dollar.

“This surge is linked to the new loans. The market jumped from 4,400 to nearly 4,700 within days. Whether it will continue to increase, or decline—or if the regime will make arrests—remains to be seen,” one trader told The Irrawaddy. The regime has repeatedly arrested foreign exchange traders during currency spikes, accusing them of speculation and market manipulation.

The loan proposal has triggered fears that the revenue-deprived regime will simply print more banknotes to address the shortfall.

Deputy Finance and Revenue Minister Kyaw Htin explained that the regime has other plans to address the shortfall, apart from borrowing money. “We are working to reduce reliance on Central Bank financing to boost state revenue. We are developing taxation policies,” he told the parliament.

Recently, the regime has escalated its efforts to enforce remittance rules requiring Myanmar migrant workers to send at least 25 percent of their salaries back home at the official exchange rate of 2,100 kyats per dollar.

Officially, the Central Bank pegs the dollar at 2,100 kyats, while the trading rate between banks is 3,660 kyats and the market rate currently hovers at around 4,670 kyats. Meanwhile, the regime has restricted imports to reduce dollar spending, which has proved counterproductive for a war-ravaged economy heavily reliant on imports ranging from cooking oil and pharmaceuticals to fuel and fertilizer.

Rising dollar rates are expected to push up the cost of imported fuel, medicines, food, consumer goods and machinery, with knock-on effects for transport and production costs. Domestic industries face mounting pressure as expenses rise.

Meanwhile, the Belarus loan package, arranged through the Development Bank of the Republic of Belarus (DBRB) and Belinvestbank JSC, carries interest rates of between 2.25 and 9.33 percent. The loans will be used to import goods including capital goods from Minsk, but the total amount was not revealed.

Myanmar can receive loans in five currencies—the dollar, euro, Russian ruble, Belarusian ruble and Chinese yuan—said Kyaw Htin, who admitted exchange rate fluctuations would affect the amount of money Myanmar will actually receive.

Unlike concessional loans from Japan’s aid agency JICA—which carry a 40‑year repayment term at just 0.01 percent interest—analysts note that the Belarusian loan is a “tied” arrangement, warning the regime is locking itself into costly debt that will further deepen Myanmar’s economic crisis.

International organizations and Japan suspended development aid to Myanmar following the coup.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Launches ‘ASEAN Affairs’ Panel to Clinch Full Reintegration
World.content:
Myanmar coup leader Min Aung Hlaing has formed a new ASEAN Affairs Committee to “regain the country’s original role and rights” in the regional bloc, which continues to bar his regime from summits months after it rebranded as an “elected” government.

The committee’s inaugural meeting on Tuesday was chaired by Foreign Minister Tin Maung Swe, with representatives from the President’s Office and ministries of Defense, Home Affairs, Information, and Social Welfare also in attendance.

While the Foreign Ministry normally serves as the focal point for international relations, the new body includes the defense and home affairs ministries, underscoring the junta’s bid to institutionalize its efforts to reintegrate into the regional bloc.

Reintegration is crucial for coup leader Min Aung Hlaing, who is seeking international legitimacy after installing himself as president in April following an election widely denounced as a sham by Western nations and rights groups.

While individual members including Thailand have recognized Min Aung Hlaing’s presidency, ASEAN as a whole remains divided, prompting continuous regime demands for full integration as a “legitimate elected government.”

Tin Maung Swe told the meeting that Myanmar had suffered “discriminatory treatment” since 2021, when ASEAN excluded Min Aung Hlaing from top-level meetings for ignoring its Five‑Point Consensus agreed in Jakarta. The bloc’s peace plan calls for an immediate end to violence, dialogue among all parties, and humanitarian access—conditions the junta has refused to meet.

Tuesday’s meeting came just weeks ahead of the next ASEAN Summit in Manila. Since assuming the presidency, Min Aung Hlaing has made official visits to five bloc members, securing support for Myanmar’s reintegration from Laos, Thailand, Cambodia, Vietnam, and Malaysia. Analysts say the committee was formed in an effort to win over the remaining five members.

“The regime is attempting to win a majority consensus through bilateral engagement with individual member states,” said political analyst Htin Kyaw Aye.

“The committee is designed for this purpose. But it remains difficult for ASEAN to allow Myanmar’s return while there is no visible progress on the Five-Point Consensus.”

Since assuming office in April, the pseudo-civilian regime has dismissed the Five-Point Consensus as a non-binding declaration, before formally rejecting the peace deal through its rubber-stamp parliament.

The regime said Tuesday’s meeting tabled “Myanmar‑led approaches” to restore the country’s role in ASEAN—a statement reiterating defiance of the Five-Point Consensus spearheaded by an ongoing military campaign that has killed over 8,500 civilians since the coup.

While rights groups warn that countries hosting Min Aung Hlaing risk legitimizing a regime still committing atrocities, others have different views after more than five years of isolation has delivered no results.

Former Japanese prime minister Fumio Kishida told Nikkei Asia on October 12 that Japan should help Myanmar rejoin ASEAN. Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. recently hailed Min Aung Hlaing’s visits to fellow ASEAN countries as part of a “new approach” to resolving the country’s crisis. Meanwhile, Brunei and Indonesia plan to invite Min Aung Hlaing for official visits, according to junta spokeswoman Khaing Khaing Soe, leaving only Timor-Leste and Singapore standing firm against the regime.

As the bloc’s newest member, Timor-Leste has backed Myanmar’s pro-democracy movement while initiating legal action against the military regime in February over alleged war crimes. Meanwhile Singapore, which will take over the rotating chairmanship at year-end, recently affirmed that there can be “no political representation” for Myanmar at ASEAN meets.

Mon Mon Myat, a lecturer in the Department of Peace Studies at Thailand’s Payap University, said: “It appears that the Philippines wants to reintegrate Myanmar into the bloc before Singapore takes the chair next year. ASEAN countries that are stepping up their diplomatic engagement with Myanmar regime must exercise extra caution to avoid legitimizing war criminals.”

She added that ASEAN must set clear rules for accountability if the regime refuses to obey the Five-Point Consensus.

“Otherwise, the regime may secure full legitimacy as a leader of an ASEAN nation.”

World.title: Myanmar Regime Denies Drafting College Students Into Army
World.content:
Myanmar’s military regime has denied reports that university students must suspend their studies for two years to serve in the army, but fears persist among students and parents.

Earlier this month, a panic broke out when rumors said that young men selected in conscription lotteries must serve in the army even if they are registered university students, and those drawing numbers under 100 would be called up within three months.

Conscripts are selected randomly at ward levels by drawing lots from a box. Those with smaller numbers are drafted first, and those with larger numbers later.

In Mandalay, even high school students who just turned 18 were forced to participate in the conscription lottery last month, according to parents.

“High school students were also told to draw lots. I drew on my son’s behalf and got a large number, over 500,” said a mother from Mandalay. “But we are still really scared because of reports that university students would be called up.”

In denying the rumors, the regime’s central conscription committee this week cited Article 15 (a)(3) of the Conscription Law, which allows deferment for students in education. It said official newspapers “repeatedly stressed this point.”

But concerns persist as township administrative offices in regime-controlled areas including major cities like Naypyitaw, Yangon and Mandalay have called in lists of university and high school students, apparently separating out those with spectacles, health problems, disabilities or on long‑term medication.

In August, the regime centralized the draft, with regional and district authorities taking over management from township and lower-level conscription offices. Since early September, a new wave of lotteries have been held in wards and villages across Mandalay but not yet in Yangon.

“Ward offices summon us according to lists from the Population Department,” one young man said. “Everyone aged 18 to 35 including students must draw. In our ward alone, over 40 students were included. One 12th grader drew a number under 100, but officials said high school students would be granted temporary deferment.”

Previously, families with eligible young men could pay a monthly fee to the authorities for deferment, in theory so someone else could be paid to take their place. But the regime abolished the substitution fee in September, declaring that all those selected must serve in order of their lottery numbers.

The department also denied reports that ward offices are confiscating ID cards and smart cards of selected youths, requiring monthly check‑ins, and demanding parents sign pledges to prevent their sons’ escape.

A Mandalay conscription official told The Irrawaddy that the process strictly follows laws and regulations.

“Students who can prove they are genuinely enrolled, with proper documents and forms, are granted temporary deferment,” the official said.

According to the 2019 census, nearly 13 million people are eligible for conscription under the Conscription Law—6.3 million men and 7.7 million women. So far, about 140,000 men have been called up by the regime, assuming that around 5,000 recruits are drafted per batch.

When the long-dormant Conscription Law was revived in 2024, it forced a mass exodus of young people, and the regime has since been struggling to meet its quotas despite barring eligible men from working abroad and even snatching young men from streets and homes.

In Yangon, an eerie quiet descends after 8 p.m. as regime-backed thugs prowl the streets on the hunt for eligible young men to abduct, a practice that has swiftly degenerated into a black economy of kidnappings for ransom.

World.title: New Road Opens Gateway to East Kazakhstan’s Altai Wonders
World.content:
ASTANA — Glacier-covered peaks, alpine lakes, thermal springs and ancient burial grounds lie scattered across the East Kazakhstan Region’s Altai Mountains, where reaching some of the most remarkable destinations has long been an adventure in itself. A newly repaired 13-kilometer road section leading to Rakhmanov Springs is easing access to the region’s mountain landscapes and opening new possibilities for travelers.

According to the Kazakh Ministry of Tourism and Sports, approximately 446,000 tourists visited the East Kazakhstan Region in 2025, including more than 26,000 visitors to Katon-Karagai State National Nature Park. Yet exploring the region still requires careful planning, with long distances, mountainous terrain and seasonal conditions shaping the travel experience, local tour operators said.

Katon-Karagai: from Rakhmanov Springs to Muztau

Stretching across more than 643,000 hectares near Kazakhstan’s borders with Russia and China, Katon-Karagai State National Nature Park encompasses forests, alpine meadows, mountain rivers and glacial landscapes. Its attractions range from nature trails and cultural sites to remote locations requiring multi-day expeditions.

Alexander Myakinin of Altai Travel described the district as a suitable starting point for exploring the region, particularly for visitors with limited time.

“A three- to five-day itinerary allows visitors to discover the nature of the Altai, visit the national park, see mountain rivers, waterfalls and lakes, explore maral deer farms and cultural sites, and learn about the region’s history. There are numerous hiking trails of varying difficulty, so travelers can choose a route suited to their abilities,” Myakinin told The Astana Times.

Among the district’s principal attractions are Rakhmanov Springs, known for their naturally occurring radon-containing thermal waters. Located near Rakhmanov Lake, the destination attracts visitors interested in wellness retreats, hiking and mountain recreation. The surrounding area offers waterfalls, forest trails and viewpoints overlooking the Altai Mountains.

Access to the springs improved following the completion of repairs on a 13-kilometer section of the Oskemen-Altai-Ulken Naryn-Katon-Karagai-Rakhmanov Springs highway, which opened Oct. 4. According to the ministry, the previously unpaved mountain stretch could take motorists up to 2.5 to three hours to cross. The new road surface has eased travel along the section, which now includes designated stopping areas with mountain views.

For a shorter visit, local tour operator Svetlana Chakileva suggested a three-day route through Katon-Karagai, allowing time to explore Rakhmanov Lake and the springs. She also mentioned local apiaries and maral deer farms, where travelers can learn about beekeeping and deer breeding, two activities closely associated with the region’s rural economy.

More demanding adventures lead toward Muztau, also known as Mount Belukha, the highest peak in the Altai Mountains at approximately 4,506 meters above sea level. Surrounded by glaciers and mountain valleys, it attracts experienced trekkers and mountaineers. Nearby Yazevoe Lake offers views of the peak in clear weather, and longer expeditions lead toward remote waterfalls and glacial areas.

Myakinin said reaching Muztau’s foothills overland typically requires an eight- to 10-day expedition involving horseback travel. Helicopter excursions offer an alternative for seeing the mountain within a single day, subject to weather conditions and availability.

A new tourist route could also make the area more accessible to hikers. In September, Katon-Karagai National Park introduced the Altai Trails route, which begins near Rakhmanov Springs and continues through the Sarsembay tract toward the foot of Muztau. The route is intended to provide an alternative to existing trails affected by difficult terrain and border-zone restrictions.

The district’s appeal also extends to its archaeological heritage. Near the village of Berel, excavations have uncovered Saka-era burial mounds containing preserved horse remains, textiles, wooden objects and ceremonial artifacts dating back more than 2,000 years. The Berel State Historical and Cultural Museum Reserve introduces visitors to these discoveries and the burial traditions of ancient nomadic communities.

Beyond Katon-Karagai: mountain lakes, historic routes and winter trails

Travelers with more time can explore other parts of the East Kazakhstan Region, where high-altitude lakes, rugged mountain roads and recreational areas offer experiences distinct from those found in Katon-Karagai.

For a weeklong itinerary, Myakinin suggested visiting Lake Markakol, the Old Austrian Road and the Bukhtarma shoreline, with additional time in Oskemen, the regional capital. These destinations cover considerable distances, making transportation and the choice of route important considerations.

Situated approximately 1,447 meters above sea level between the Kurchum and Azutau mountain ranges, Lake Markakol stretches nearly 38 kilometers in length. Surrounded by forests and mountain slopes, the freshwater lake is known for its cold waters and uskuch, a fish found in the lake. The nearby Markakol State Nature Reserve protects wildlife and plant species, attracting visitors interested in hiking, photography and nature-based travel.

The lake can be incorporated into an expedition along the Old Austrian Road, a historic mountain route connecting the Katon-Karagai and Markakol areas. Built in the early 20th century by Austro-Hungarian prisoners of war, the road winds through remote mountain terrain and is now popular among travelers seeking off-road adventures. Chakileva suggested allowing five days for an itinerary incorporating this route, with the usual travel season extending from mid-June through late August, depending on weather and road conditions.

Elsewhere in the region, the Kiin-Kerish tract in Kurchum District offers an entirely different landscape. Its red, orange and pale-colored clay formations, shaped by erosion into hills and ridges, resemble a desert, contrasting with the forests and alpine lakes of the Altai.

For a more relaxed holiday, the Bukhtarma Reservoir along the Yertis River remains a popular summer destination, with beaches, boating, fishing and holiday accommodation along its shoreline, including the Samar area. According to Chakileva, lakeside recreation continues to attract visitors, and interest in more active experiences, particularly jeep tours, trekking and helicopter excursions, has also increased.

The choice of destination also depends on the season. Summer is particularly suited to mountain expeditions and water-based recreation, and September brings autumn colors to the forests and valleys. During winter, skiers, freeride enthusiasts and snowmobilers head to Ridder, a mountain town near the West Altai State Nature Reserve, as well as ski resorts near Oskemen, including Altai Alps and Nurtau.

Despite the popularity of Katon-Karagai, Myakinin highlighted that travelers should also pay closer attention to the western part of the Altai.

“The West Altai, especially the surroundings of Ridder, remains undeservedly overlooked. I consider it a compact version of Katon-Karagai. This destination has enormous tourism potential, with dense taiga forests, clear rivers, high-altitude lakes and established routes for hiking and winter recreation. I am sure that interest in this area will continue to grow in the coming years,” he said.

Easier access, but planning remains essential

Improving transportation remains an important part of tourism development in the East Kazakhstan Region, where some destinations are separated by 400-500 kilometers and mountain routes can be difficult to navigate.

Alongside road improvements, a new airport is under construction in Katon-Karagai District, with completion scheduled for the end of 2026. The project includes a 2,200-meter runway and a passenger terminal designed to accommodate up to 150 travelers per hour.

The airport is intended to improve connections with Kazakhstan’s major cities and reduce travel time to the district. However, scheduled passenger services have yet to be announced, and reaching individual attractions will still require ground transportation.

Local tour operators said advance arrangements remain essential, particularly during the peak summer season, when demand for accommodation, transportation and qualified guides can exceed availability.

“The biggest mistake when planning a trip is not planning it at all. People arrive and start looking for guides and vehicles on the spot. You need to research everything in advance, find a guide and book accommodation beforehand, because demand has grown significantly, while accommodation options are limited and there are not enough guides,” said Chakileva.

She added that traveling without a knowledgeable guide can affect both safety and the overall experience, particularly when visitors reach natural or historical attractions without understanding their significance.

Although Rakhmanov Springs can be reached by an ordinary passenger vehicle under suitable conditions, more demanding mountain routes may require four-wheel-drive transportation and experienced local drivers. Travelers should also prepare for rapidly changing weather, limited fuel availability and unreliable mobile coverage in remote areas.

Myakinin said temperatures can fluctuate sharply even in summer, making warm clothing and appropriate equipment essential. Some protected areas and border territories also require registration or advance permits, depending on the destination.

The cost of travel varies according to the itinerary and level of service. Myakinin estimated that one-day excursions and hiking trips start at approximately 20,000-30,000 tenge (US$45-65), while individual premium programs involving complex logistics or helicopter flights can cost 500,000 to one million tenge (US$1,100-2,200) or more. Chakileva said organized multi-day tours generally range from 50,000 to 100,000 tenge (US$110-220) per person per day, depending on accommodation, transportation and guide services.

As road improvements and new transport connections make the East Kazakhstan Region’s remote destinations more accessible, growing tourism also raises questions about preserving the natural environment. Asked which lesser-known attractions deserve greater attention, Chakileva offered a different perspective.

“I actually try not to talk publicly about such places because I believe some locations should remain undiscovered. Let people visit the places they already know about. As for the places they don’t know, I would rather keep it that way for now, because some areas should remain wild,” she said.

World.title: Kazakhstan Cannot Wait 202 Years For Gender Parity
World.content:
Editor’s note: The Astana Times continues a section featuring articles by our readers. As a platform that values diverse perspectives and meaningful conversations, we believe that this section provides space for readers to share their thoughts and insights on various topics that matter to them and the AT audience.

A girl born today in Central Asia will not live long enough to witness gender parity if progress continues at its historical pace. The World Economic Forum (WEF) released a 2026 Global Gender Gap Report, stating that closing the region’s gender gap could take 202 years. On its current trajectory, Central Asia would be the last region in the world to reach parity. The index is based on an established reasoning: economies are less competitive when they fail to develop and use the talents of their entire population. Kazakhstan presents a striking paradox, ranking fourth out of five countries of the region. Since the WEF began measuring gender gaps in 2006, the country has experienced substantial economic growth, rapid digitalisation and deeper integration into the global economy. It has nearly closed its gender gaps in education and health. Yet in political empowerment, only 12.3% of the gap has been closed. More strikingly, Kazakhstan’s overall gender-parity score remains within one percentage point of where it stood in 2006.

The paradox is not that Kazakh women have been left outside the country’s development. Quite the opposite. Women are economically active and deeply embedded in the institutions of the state. The problem is: representation did not automatically translate into authority and power. The bottleneck is visible in the statistics. While women make up a majority of Kazakh civil servants, their representation declines sharply as authority increases. As of January 2024, women accounted for 56% of Corps B administrative civil servants, but only around 12.9% of Corps A and around 8.3% of political civil servants. Women increasingly disappear on the way up. The reasons are clear and well known: gender stereotypes, unpaid care work and expectations about women’s roles.

Artificial intelligence could reinforce existing gender inequalities.

The International Labor Organization has found that female-dominated occupations are almost twice as likely to be exposed to generative AI, partly because of women’s greater concentration in administrative roles. These findings matter for a public sector in which women constitute the majority. Kazakhstan needs to ensure that traditional rungs of the career ladder are not eliminated without creating stronger pathways for women towards leadership roles.

The government has already laid the foundations for the solution. It has invested considerably in e-Qyzmet to digitize significant parts of recruitment and personnel administration to make HR processes more transparent and standardized. However, while women enter the civil service in large numbers, they still progressively disappear as positions become more powerful. The next task is to make that leadership pipeline visible. Among civil servants with comparable qualifications, competencies, and performance, do women and men progress at similar rates? If not, at what point do their careers begin to diverge? Technology can help institutions ask these questions systematically. HR analytics could identify where promising employees stall, who receives the assignments and experience that prepare officials for senior leadership.

This is not to say that gender should become a criterion for promotion, but rather an audit variable. AI could eventually strengthen this process by identifying capabilities that conventional career paths or solely human judgement may overlook. The purpose of technology should therefore not be to decide who deserves to lead, but to make the evidence behind human decisions more visible and accountable.

One may argue that the government cannot solve a problem that ultimately lies in society. Assumptions about leadership, family obligations and informal professional networks do not disappear because recruitment rules are formally neutral. Culture became a convenient explanation for institutional inertia. However, Kazakhstan cannot wait for social attitudes to evolve over generations. The right policies and strong institutions can potentially shape and change the culture to drive further progress.

Closing the gender gap is not only about justice. The government has invested heavily in women’s human capital. The economic question is whether the country is receiving the full return on that investment. A country that educates women, brings them into professional life and employs them throughout the machinery of government, but loses much of that talent before the highest levels of decision-making, is not only facing a gender-equality problem. It is facing a human-capital allocation problem. For Kazakhstan, the next phase of gender equality is therefore not primarily about getting women through the door. It is about turning existing representation into influence. The 202-year projection is not destiny. It is an extrapolation from the past. Whether Kazakhstan follows that trajectory will depend, in part, on the policies and institutions it designs now.

The author is Adilya Tugel, a graduate student at the Nazarbayev University Graduate School of Public Policy.

Disclaimer: The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the position of The Astana Times.

World.title: China’s Rise and Central Asia: What Will Next Ten Years Look Like?
World.content:
For much of my time as a journalist, the story of China’s rise has come with a familiar undertone of alarm. China is either becoming the next great global power, challenging the West, rewriting the rules of international politics or quietly building a parallel system that the rest of the world will eventually have to adapt to. All of these arguments have some basis. But I sometimes wonder whether we make the China story too simple, especially from Central Asia, where China is not some distant geopolitical competitor, but a country next door, a major trading partner and an increasingly visible part of our economic landscape.

So I wanted to ask a broader question: if China continues to gain economic and geopolitical weight over the next 10 years, what will that power actually look like by 2035, and what will it mean for Central Asia? I spoke to several experts and their answers were more nuanced than the usual China-versus-the-West narrative. The most interesting conclusion was not that China will necessarily replace the existing international order. It may not have to.

China may reshape the order without replacing it

Jiyang Dong, assistant professor at Nazarbayev University’s Graduate School of Business, made a point that immediately shifted the question for me. “Ironically, the key variables impacting China’s future role in the international system are not necessarily within China,” he said.

China’s policies, he said, are already laid out in successive five-year plans and implemented with consistency. What matters just as much is what happens elsewhere: whether the United States (U.S.) continues to retreat from multilateralism and whether institutions such as the World Bank and IMF continue to meet the development needs of the Global South.

If they do not, Dong believes, institutions in which China plays a central role could gradually become more important. He points to the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank as one example. That means China’s rise may not depend entirely on Beijing building a new system from scratch. It may also depend on whether existing institutions leave enough space for China and other emerging powers to build something alongside them.

Gulnar Shaimergenova, director of the China Studies Center in Kazakhstan, sees the process in similar terms. “I would rather speak not about the creation by China of a completely alternative world order, but about an attempt to change the balance and rules within the existing international system,” she said.

By 2035, she expects a more polycentric system in which China becomes one of the key centers of economic, technological and political influence. The real question, she said, is not whether one world order will simply replace another, but which institutions and norms will adapt to the new balance of power.

Deputy Chairman of the Institute of Foreign Policy Studies under Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs Amangeldy Tazhenov reaches a similar conclusion. China, he said, is not trying to “break” the existing system. It is pushing for its transformation and reform so that it better reflects current realities and the changing distribution of power.

But Ken Moriyasu, a senior fellow at Hudson Institute, offered a sharper interpretation of the same trend. For much of the post-Deng Xiaoping era, he noted, China largely adapted to an international system shaped by Western powers. Under Xi Jinping, the ambition is different.

“It is less about reforming China to fit the existing order and more about changing the order to fit China,” Moriyasu said.

At the same time, he cautions against assuming Beijing is confident it can simply build the order it wants. China also knows that its rise generates resistance and suspicion. That, he said, helps explain why Beijing continues to emphasize the UN and existing institutions while simultaneously promoting BRICS, the SCO and a more multipolar system.

“Beijing will preserve institutions that reinforce China’s status, seek to reshape institutions where Western influence remains predominant, and simultaneously build organizations, relationships and economic networks that give Beijing alternatives,” he said.

I find that distinction more useful than the familiar question of whether China is trying to become “the next U.S.” Perhaps China does not need to replace the system. It may simply need to become powerful enough to change the way the system works around it.

Central Asia is becoming more important for a different reason

This is where the discussion becomes more interesting for Central Asia. For years, China’s relationship with the region was discussed largely through the familiar vocabulary of trade, energy, resources and transport corridors. Those things still matter. But the strategic logic appears to be changing. Moriyasu calls the emerging logic “strategic resilience.” Much of China’s trade and energy still moves through maritime routes exposed to American naval power. Central Asia gives Beijing something the South China Sea cannot: a vast continental hinterland connecting China westward across Eurasia. “Central Asia matters to Beijing not only because of the energy, minerals and markets within Central Asia, but increasingly because of what lies beyond it. It connects China westward across the Eurasian landmass,” he said.

His forecast is striking: “I would expect Central Asia to move from China’s economic periphery toward the strategic center of China’s relationship with Eurasia.”

That changes the question because Central Asia’s value for China is no longer simply what Beijing can obtain from the region. It is also what the region allows China to reach. Jiyang Dong approaches this from a more economic perspective. “Central Asia’s greatest strategic significance hinges on its potential as a connectivity hub in the heart of Eurasia,” he said.

Without sufficient connectivity infrastructure, he notes, trade volumes remain limited, and resources remain effectively locked in the region. That is why projects such as the expansion of the Aktau container hub and the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway matter beyond their immediate economic purpose. They are helping turn Central Asia’s geography into an asset. Perhaps this is where we should stop thinking of infrastructure simply as infrastructure.

Infrastructure may be the new geopolitics

Moriyasu said something that stayed with me: “Infrastructure becomes the new hinge of geopolitics.”

“Once trade routes, pipelines, power grids and supply chains are built around particular networks, they begin to shape the economic choices available to countries using them,” Moriyasu said.

That is a much more subtle form of power than the geopolitics I grew up reading about. There is no flag going up. No alliance is announced. No military base appears. But the network changes. And once a country’s trade, logistics, power systems, digital infrastructure or industrial supply chains are deeply embedded in a particular network, those connections can begin shaping the choices available to it. This is also where my own perception of China has changed.

It is difficult to ignore the efficiency of some of the infrastructure projects I see around me. The LRT in Astana is a very concrete example. Whatever one’s broader political view of China may be, a functioning project creates a different impression than a political speech or diplomatic statement. This is where infrastructure can begin to operate as soft power. Not necessarily because Beijing tells people to admire China, but because people encounter its capabilities in practical ways: a railway, a road or a technology. Over time, that can produce something harder to measure but politically significant: familiarity, respect and, potentially, a certain degree of loyalty.

Tazhenov described China’s approach in similarly long-term terms, noting that Beijing tends to think in much longer horizons than many other countries. He also pointed to the growing visibility of Chinese economic activity in Kazakhstan: from infrastructure and roads to new enterprises and resource projects. That matters because soft power is usually discussed in terms of culture, education or films. Perhaps in the next decade, we will have to add infrastructure to that list.

The next phase may be about technology, not concrete

This is where the forecasts become even more interesting. Shaimergenova believes the development most underestimated today is the transition from physical infrastructure connectivity to technological and institutional connectivity. A few years ago, the China conversation in Central Asia focused on roads, railways, pipelines and energy. Today, she notes, the agenda increasingly includes AI, digital infrastructure, green technologies and critical minerals.

“Central Asia will be not only a territory through which flows between China and Europe pass, but increasingly a space where different technological, production and regulatory systems will intersect,” she said.

That is probably the part of the China story that deserves more attention. Dong sees another underestimated area: cooperation in non-fossil energy. Solar panels, wind turbines, energy storage, flexible grids and nuclear power could all become increasingly important as Central Asian economies grow and demand more electricity. In other words, China’s future role in Central Asia may be less about simply connecting the region to China and more about helping shape the systems through which the region itself develops.

More China: more choices, or fewer?

This is where the experts stop agreeing. Dong sees growing competition among major powers as potentially useful for Kazakhstan because it creates more room to advance national interests through different partners and financial systems.

Shaimergenova is more cautious. “The strengthening of competition among major powers provides Kazakhstan with additional opportunities for investment, technology, transport projects and access to different markets. But at the same time, the risk increases that economic, technological and even logistical decisions will increasingly be viewed through the prism of geopolitical choice,” she said.

Tazhenov is even more direct: “My opinion is that an aggravation of geopolitical rivalry is certainly unfavorable for Kazakhstan. It actually narrows the field for foreign policy maneuver.”

This may be the real paradox of the next decade. China’s rise can give Kazakhstan access to more capital, infrastructure, technology and markets. But if rivalry between China and the U.S. continues to harden, those same economic choices may increasingly be interpreted as political choices. The more interconnected Kazakhstan becomes with major external powers, the more important it is to remain capable of deciding where each connection leads.

What we may be underestimating

One idea kept returning throughout these conversations, even when the experts approached it from very different directions. It is not simply that China is becoming more present in Central Asia. The region and China are becoming more mutually interested in one another. Tazhenov believes this growing mutual interest, connectivity and economic complementarity is one of the least appreciated trends. For China, Central Asia offers transport routes, resources, energy and stability. For Kazakhstan and its neighbors, China increasingly offers markets, investment and technology. The relationship is therefore becoming more complicated than a simple story of a rising power expanding into a neighboring region.

It is also becoming a story of mutual dependence which is not automatically good or bad. Its consequences depend on who has the capacity to negotiate, diversify and create value of their own. That may be the most important question for Kazakhstan as we look toward 2035. Not whether China will become stronger or have more influence in Central Asia. It is already deeply embedded in the region’s economic geography. The more interesting question is what kind of region Central Asia becomes as that influence grows.

If the next phase is about technology, industrial capacity, energy systems, and digital infrastructure as much as railways and ports, then Central Asian countries will have to think beyond attracting projects. They will have to think about what they build themselves. Because by 2035, I suspect the China story in Central Asia will no longer be mainly about a powerful country coming into the region.

It will be about systems becoming intertwined: railways with ports, energy with technology, trade with digital payments, industrial projects with skills and education. There may be no dramatic moment when the old order ends, and a new one begins. The balance may simply look different one day because the underlying architecture has changed.

And perhaps that is the real foresight question: not whether China will reshape the world, but how much of Central Asia’s future architecture will be shaped by China, and how much Central Asia will be capable of shaping itself.

World.title: Kazakhstan, Cambodia Seek AI Cooperation and Stronger Trade Ties
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and Cambodia are looking to expand cooperation in artificial intelligence, energy, agriculture and trade, while exploring direct air links, as President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet held talks on Oct. 17.

The discussions marked the first visit to Kazakhstan by a Cambodian prime minister and came as the two countries mark 32 years of diplomatic relations. Tokayev said the visit could open a new chapter in bilateral ties, with both countries seeking to translate shared intentions into practical cooperation, Akorda reported.

“Kazakhstan considers Cambodia a reliable partner in Southeast Asia and an important link in expanding our partnership with ASEAN countries,” Tokayev said during the expanded-format talks.

He added that the countries would adopt a joint statement outlining their shared vision for future relations and sign several bilateral documents.

AI and digital government

Technology emerged as a key area for cooperation, with Tokayev highlighting opportunities in artificial intelligence and digital government. Hun Manet and his delegation were scheduled to visit the Alem.ai International Center to learn about Kazakhstan’s AI initiatives and technological developments.

Tokayev noted Kazakhstan’s progress in the United Nations E-Government Development Index and said the two countries could achieve significant results by combining mutual interest with political commitment.

“I am convinced that, given mutual interest and firm political will, we can achieve significant progress in expanding cooperation across many areas of mutual interest,” he said.

The two leaders also discussed energy cooperation. During their one-on-one meeting earlier in the day, Tokayev proposed exploring direct air links to facilitate tourism and people-to-people exchanges.

“Many Kazakh people would like to visit Cambodia and discover its attractions. We need to discuss the possibility of establishing direct air links between our countries,” Tokayev said.

Trade, agriculture and education

Hun Manet expressed Cambodia’s interest in expanding cooperation in food security, agriculture and manufacturing, alongside energy and digitalization.

He also emphasized the longstanding humanitarian ties between the countries, noting that more than 120 Cambodian students had studied in Kazakhstan. Many have since taken up senior positions in public administration, including as provincial governors, state secretaries and ministry officials.

“Our countries are connected by a shared history and strong people-to-people ties,” Hun Manet said.

Tokayev praised Cambodia’s socioeconomic progress and expressed support for its long-term development goals under Cambodia Vision 2050 and the Pentagonal Strategy.

The leaders also highlighted their constructive political dialogue and engagement at the international level, including through their respective permanent missions to the United Nations. Tokayev commended Cambodia’s support for Kazakhstan’s initiatives on several topics on the UN General Assembly agenda.

Both officials expressed confidence that the talks would help increase bilateral trade, strengthen business ties and create new opportunities for partnership.

In the presence of Tokayev and Hun Manet, the two sides exchanged six memorandums of understanding covering cooperation in artificial intelligence and digital development, digital government and information and communication technologies, trade and economic relations, culture and the arts, and tourism. The documents also established sister-city relations between Astana and Phnom Penh.

Earlier, Kazakhstan’s Ambassador to Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos Kanat Tumysh told The Astana Times that the countries were seeking to expand trade, explore investment opportunities and strengthen transport and technology cooperation.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s PARAQTA Platform Turns Reading Into Daily Habit
World.content:
ASTANA – A Kazakh digital platform called PARAQTA is helping readers build consistent reading habits through page tracking, personalized goals and interactive features, bringing together more than 8,400 registered users who have collectively read almost 1 million pages over the past year.

The platform was created by Yerdaulet Ayanuly, an engineer by profession who wanted to make reading a more accessible part of everyday life. Speaking on the Jibek Joly television channel’s program on Oct. 15, he said the project grew out of his own experience with books and efforts to build a reading community in Astana, reported Kazinform.

Ayanuly first joined a book club before organizing reading-related activities with volunteers. When the group struggled to find a suitable venue for meetings, the team opened a café for book lovers. Financial difficulties eventually forced it to close, but Ayanuly continued looking for ways to promote reading.

“It was a special, cozy place that was close to my heart. We held various creative events there and managed to bring together Astana residents who enjoyed reading. Closing the project was difficult, but I did not want to give up on the idea of developing a reading culture,” he said.

The team had previously used a Telegram bot to record the number of pages members read. Ayanuly later decided to turn the simple tracking tool into a dedicated website.

From page tracking to a reading community

Artificial intelligence helped him develop the first version of the website in three months. Over the following four to five months, he added features and improved the design, bringing the total development period to approximately eight or nine months.

PARAQTA allows users to set reading goals, record completed pages and track their progress, whether they read printed books or digital editions. Users can also access books directly through the platform’s online library, which currently contains 148 titles.

The collection includes Kazakh folk tales, Abai’s “Words of Edification”, works in Kazakh, Russian and English, and translated literature. According to Ayanuly, users show particular interest in Kazakh classics and national literature.

The platform also uses gamification to encourage readers to return regularly. Users earn stars for reading, which they can exchange for profile customization options and virtual room decorations. Personal accounts allow readers to track their activity and see their progress over time.

“We believe people should not be forced to read books. Instead, we need to find other ways to interest them,” Ayanuly said, explaining that small rewards can encourage users to read more consistently.

He cited four platform members who each read 60 books in a year as examples of how a regular reading habit can develop.

Digital tools and offline connections

PARAQTA offers both free and paid features. Paid options allow users to read the same book alongside other participants, compare reading progress and pace, join book clubs and take part in rankings. The platform has collected around 600 book reviews.

Beyond its digital functions, the project aims to connect readers offline. Astana’s book club currently has around 300 members, with people aged 20 to 25 among its most active participants. Members meet to discuss books and exchange perspectives on what they have read.

For Ayanuly, building this community is as important as developing the technology itself. He said books can influence how people think and understand the world, motivating him to share his enthusiasm for reading with others.

PARAQTA remains a small operation, with a team of two people. Ayanuly continues to work in his main profession as a design engineer while developing the platform, which began as a personal hobby and is gradually becoming an independent business.

The next step is to expand access through mobile applications. Ayanuly is awaiting approval to publish the iPhone version on the App Store, while an Android version is also planned. The application will be free to download, with paid subscriptions remaining available.

He believes that making reading convenient and rewarding is essential to building a stronger reading culture, particularly when digital platforms compete for people’s attention.

Kazakhstan’s wider reading initiative

PARAQTA’s development coincides with Kazakhstan’s broader efforts to promote reading. In September, Kazakh singer Dimash Kudaibergen joined the nationwide Reading Nation marathon in its Parasat category, which encourages reading through the personal example of public figures rather than competition for prizes. The marathon runs from Sept. this year to April 2027 and brings together participants including schoolchildren, students, teachers, families and civil servants.

World.title: Kazakhstan, Cambodia Seek to Expand Trade and Explore New Investment Opportunities, Ambassador Says
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and Cambodia are seeking to turn political dialogue into tangible economic outcomes by expanding agricultural exports, strengthening business ties and exploring transport and technology partnerships, Kazakhstan’s Ambassador to Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos said ahead of Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet’s visit to Kazakhstan.

“The principal expected outcome of the visit is agreement on practical next steps in priority areas and the creation of favourable conditions for new trade and investment projects,” Kanat Tumysh said in written responses to questions from The Astana Times.

Trade and investment potential

Bilateral trade reached $40.7 million in 2025, up from $33.8 million in 2024. In the first half of this year, it amounted to $20.6 million, up 1.4% year on year. Trade remains heavily weighted towards Cambodian exports, particularly textiles, knitwear, footwear and other consumer goods.

“The priority now is to realise more fully the potential of our partnership,” Tumysh said, identifying agriculture, food processing, tourism, construction, transport and logistics as promising areas.

At a meeting in Shanghai on July 17, Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and Hun Manet discussed cooperation in these sectors, as well as the textile industry and technology. Kazakhstan expressed readiness to increase supplies of grain, fertilizers and other agricultural products and share its expertise in advanced technologies.

Investment ties remain modest. No gross inflows of direct investment from Cambodia into Kazakhstan have been recorded, while gross outflows of direct investment from Kazakhstan to Cambodia amounted to $30,000 in January-June. As of Sept. 1, four legal entities with Cambodian capital participation were registered and operating in Kazakhstan.

“The presence of businesses with Cambodian capital does not automatically imply substantial direct investment inflows,” Tumysh said, adding that these companies could nevertheless provide a basis for stronger commercial ties.

Agriculture offers opportunities for two-way trade

Kazakhstan sees opportunities to supply Cambodia with wheat, fertilizers and other agricultural products, while importing Cambodian rice.

“Cambodia, in turn, can export its rice to Kazakhstan, and we are ready to purchase it. This offers an opportunity to develop mutually beneficial trade in both directions,” Tumysh said.

Cambodia has a population of approximately 17.8 million and imported around $34 billion worth of goods in 2025. Its agricultural exports that year reached approximately 14.9 million tons, worth around $5 billion, including rice, rubber, cassava, maize, cashew nuts and tropical fruit.

Expanding Kazakh agricultural exports will require identifying buyers, establishing product specifications and assessing transportation costs, certification requirements and seasonal demand.

“For grain, it would be useful to assess the requirements of flour mills and food-processing companies, including quality specifications and opportunities to supply both raw materials and processed products,” Tumysh said.

Fertilizer exports would require similar assessments of demand, registration procedures and potential local partners. Agricultural processing, packaging, storage and distribution could offer additional opportunities.

Kazakhstan’s total exports to Cambodia amounted to just $47,000 in 2024, with control and measuring instruments accounting for the principal export items. Confirmed figures for agricultural supplies in 2025 and the first half of 2026 are not yet available, and no quantitative targets for future shipments have been announced.

“At this stage, it is therefore appropriate to speak of exploring opportunities rather than guaranteeing supplies of a particular volume,” Tumysh said.

Transport and regional connectivity

Kazakhstan is working towards accession to the Treaty of Amity and Cooperation in Southeast Asia, also known as the Bali Treaty. Tumysh said Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia had supported the initiative, which Kazakhstan views as an important step towards strengthening engagement with ASEAN.

“We aim to translate this partnership into practical outcomes by expanding trade, strengthening business ties, exploring investment opportunities and improving transport connectivity between Central Asia and Southeast Asia,” he said.

One proposed step is to assess multimodal routes with exporters, importers, carriers and freight forwarders, comparing costs, delivery times, transshipment, storage and documentation requirements. Cambodia’s Sihanoukville port, its principal maritime gateway, could be considered in these assessments. However, no dedicated Kazakhstan-Cambodia transport corridor has been agreed.

The two countries also have experience with direct air services. In October 2024, SCAT Airlines launched charter passenger flights from Astana and Almaty to Sihanoukville to serve tourist demand, but the services were subsequently suspended. Their experience could inform future assessments of passenger demand and commercial viability.

Tourism remains another potential area for cooperation. Cambodia welcomed approximately 5.57 million international visitors in 2025, creating opportunities for engagement between tourism authorities, tour operators and airlines.

Digital cooperation and next steps

Both countries could also explore partnerships in digital technologies and public services. Kazakhstan has offered to share its technological expertise, while Cambodia is developing e-commerce, digital financial services and digital government services.

The institutional framework for cooperation has developed through a February 2025 memorandum establishing a mechanism for political consultations between the two foreign ministries and a May 29 intergovernmental agreement providing visa exemptions for holders of diplomatic and service or official passports.

Tumysh said the immediate priority was to arrange business meetings, exchange information on export offerings and import requirements, consult logistics operators and assess trial shipments.

“Realistic targets can then be set, with progress measured through signed contracts, repeat deliveries, investments actually made and the reliability of transport services. Ultimately, the guiding principle is a practical approach: moving from general expressions of interest to commercially sound solutions that deliver mutual benefits for businesses and strengthen links between the two regions,” Tumysh said.

World.title: IMF Expects Kazakhstan’s Inflation to Ease and Economic Growth to Accelerate in 2027
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s inflation is projected to decline to 8.2% in 2027, while economic growth is expected to accelerate to 4.9%, according to the International Monetary Fund’s (IMF) latest World Economic Outlook, released Oct. 13 at the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok.

The IMF forecasts inflation to fall from 11.4% in 2025 to 10.3% in 2026 before declining further next year. Economic growth is projected at 4.4% in 2026, rising to 4.9% in 2027.

The report also identifies Kazakhstan among the countries outside the Persian Gulf that increased oil production and helped the global market adjust to disruptions in supplies through the Strait of Hormuz.

Kazakhstan’s economic outlook

The IMF expects Kazakhstan’s unemployment rate to remain at 4.6% in 2026 before easing to 4.5% in 2027. The country’s current account balance is projected to remain positive at 0.5% of gross domestic product in 2026.

Kazakhstan is also mentioned in the report’s assessment of the economic effects of the artificial intelligence boom. The fund identifies the country among commodity exporters benefiting from increased exports of technology-related goods produced by major Asian manufacturing economies.

Oil supply and the Strait of Hormuz

The report examines how the conflict in the Middle East disrupted global energy markets, with supplies through the Strait of Hormuz nearly halted in the spring. The disruption affected a route responsible for approximately 20% of global oil supplies, pushing prices to $126 per barrel in late March, according to the information cited in the report.

The IMF said the market adapted partly because countries outside the Persian Gulf increased production. Brazil, Kazakhstan, the United States and Venezuela were among those identified as helping offset the supply shortfall.

The report’s global outlook remains closely tied to developments in the Middle East. The IMF assumes that the Strait of Hormuz will reopen in March 2027 and that shipping will return to previous levels by October 2027. Under this scenario, oil prices are projected to average $96 per barrel in 2026 and $87 in 2027.

Artificial intelligence supports global growth

The IMF raised its forecast for global economic growth in 2026 to 3.1%, up from 3% in its July projection. The global economy grew by 3.5% in 2025, while growth is expected to reach 3.4% in 2027.

The fund attributes the improved outlook partly to substantial investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure, which is helping offset the economic effects of higher energy prices and the prolonged conflict in the Middle East.

Economies building AI platforms and manufacturing the equipment needed to support them are among those receiving upgraded forecasts. The report highlights South Korea, Malaysia, Mexico and Thailand in this context.

According to Reuters, Petya Koeva Brooks, deputy director of the IMF’s Research Department, said the global economy would have grown more slowly in 2026 without measures taken by governments and businesses following the oil shock. These included drawing on inventories, finding alternative suppliers and reducing oil consumption.

However, the IMF cautions that the effects of these adjustments are weakening as the conflict continues.

The benefits of AI-related investment are also becoming increasingly concentrated. According to the report’s assessment cited by Reuters, 32 countries now account for 95% of global growth, compared with 54 countries in April. Since then, the IMF has downgraded its growth forecasts for 47% of the world’s economies.

Diverging growth prospects

The United States is projected to grow by 2.3% in both 2026 and 2027, supported by consumer spending, tax cuts and investment in AI. The IMF raised its 2026 growth forecast for the euro area from 0.9% to 1.1% and expects the United Kingdom’s economy to expand by 1.3%. Investment in AI is among the factors supporting these projections, alongside higher defense spending in Europe.

China’s economy is projected to grow by 4.5% in 2026 and 4% in 2027. Higher oil prices are weighing on domestic demand, although strong exports continue to provide support. India is expected to remain the fastest-growing major economy, with projected growth of 7% annually.

By contrast, the Middle East’s oil-producing economies face significant pressure. The IMF forecasts Saudi Arabia’s economy to contract by 3.3% in 2026, reversing its July projection of 1.7% growth. The fund also expects deep economic contractions in Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates.

Inflation and risks to the global outlook

Global inflation is projected to reach 4.7% in 2026 before easing to 4.1% in 2027. However, the outlook depends heavily on how the conflict in the Middle East develops and whether energy supplies recover as anticipated.

The IMF also highlights uncertainty surrounding AI investment. Faster adoption of the technology could add 0.6% to global gross domestic product by 2029. Conversely, if the expected productivity gains fail to materialize and investment falls sharply, global economic output could be 1.1% lower by 2028, with the United States facing a potential decline of 1.8%.

High public debt, particularly in advanced economies, presents another challenge. The IMF urges governments to rebuild fiscal buffers and establish credible plans to return public debt to sustainable levels.

“The global economy has proved resilient, but this resilience is reaching its limits, so we need to move from simply surviving to rebuilding,” the IMF’s chief economist, Silvana Tenreyro, said, according to Reuters.

World.title: News Digest: Foreign Media on Kazakhstan’s Regional Ties, AI Rules and Middle Corridor Plans
World.content:
ASTANA — The Astana Times has selected articles from global media outlets covering Kazakhstan. This week’s foreign media digest covers Kazakhstan’s partnerships with Azerbaijan and Belgium, proposed AI rules for newsrooms, and plans to expand Middle Corridor logistics infrastructure.

President Ilham Aliyev meets with Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and officially inaugurates Trans-Caspian Fiber Optic Cable

President of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev met with President of Kazakhstan Kassym-Jomart Tokayev on Oct. 15, reported Trend.

During the meeting, the sides hailed the successful development of the strategic partnership and allied relations between Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan.

They highlighted the successful organization of the 7th CICA Summit in Baku, adding that the event had provided a good opportunity to discuss cooperation among countries in the Asian region.

Subsequently, Presidents Ilham Aliyev and Kassym-Jomart Tokayev officially inaugurated the Trans-Caspian Fiber-Optic Cable Line in an online format.

Kazakhstan weighs AI rules for newsrooms amid growing digital risks

Kazakhstan is considering new rules governing the use of artificial intelligence in newsrooms, including requirements to label AI-generated content. The proposal was discussed at the tenth Astana Media Week, which also focused on digital threats and children’s online safety, reported AnewZ on Oct. 15.

“Dmitriy Mun, CEO of Q.AI, predicted that AI could generate much of the content for some radio programmes and commentary within two to three years.

With automated content expected to become more common, Mun argued that the real challenge for journalists would be earning public trust rather than simply delivering information.

Fact-checking, accuracy and editorial independence could therefore become crucial in distinguishing professional journalism from machine-generated content,” reads the article.

Kazakhstan and Belgium to open new chapter in their partnership

EU Reporter published an article on Oct.12, written by Kazakhstan’s Ambassador to Belgium Roman Vassilenko, exploring how the first Belgian state visit to Central Asia could strengthen Kazakhstan-Belgium ties through trade, investment, transport connectivity, and broader economic, academic and cultural cooperation.

“For Kazakhstan, relations with Belgium also have an important European dimension. Brussels combines bilateral diplomacy with dialogue with the European Union institutions. Transport connectivity, investment and resilient supply chains form a shared agenda in which Belgian expertise and Kazakhstan’s potential can, and do, complement each other,” reads the article.

Belgian royals in Kazakhstan: first state visit to Central Asia

Brussels-based VRT News released an article on Oct. 12 about the first-ever state visit to Central Asia by Belgium’s King Philippe and Queen Mathilde, aimed at strengthening bilateral cooperation with Kazakhstan in trade, critical minerals, technology, and science.

German logistics group Rhenus plans up to 14 terminals along the Middle Corridor

Global logistics company Rhenus Group plans to build a new multimodal hub in the Kazakh city of Aktau and develop up to 14 terminals along the Middle Corridor. This network will link Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan and Türkiye, and connect the route to the company’s infrastructure in Europe, reported Euronews on Oct. 9.

German logistics giant Rhenus Group is set to roll out a network of up to 14 terminals along the Middle Corridor, also known as the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR), with a new trimodal container terminal in Aktau.

Azerbaijan–Kazakhstan ties could reorient Central Asian integration

The five Central Asian presidents met with Azerbaijan’s Ilham Aliyev in Avaza on Oct. 8 for the Consultative Meeting of the Heads of State of Central Asia and the Republic of Azerbaijan, reported The Times of Central Asia on Oct. 12.

Azerbaijan’s participation brings a principal outlet for Central Asian trade into the six governments’ economic deliberations. Within their consultative format, the states can coordinate industrial projects with the transport services through which regional producers reach foreign markets. If Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan connect cross-Caspian transport more closely to industrial cooperation, the corridor could become an organizing axis for regional integration.

World.title: “No to torture!” Saturday march in Tbilisi. “Protests in Georgia” video podcast
World.content:
The “Saturday marches” are part of an ongoing protest movement that has continued in Georgia for 689 days.

Protesters are demanding that Georgia return to the path of European integration and that all political prisoners be released. They are also calling for the repeal of all anti-democratic laws passed by the ruling Georgian Dream party over the past two years.

Protesters and opposition parties point out that part of Georgian society still does not recognise the results of the parliamentary election held in autumn 2024. They are calling for early parliamentary elections.

Over the course of nearly two years of protests, dozens of people have been arrested. Many have been charged with criminal offences and sentenced to prison.

For the first time in independent Georgia’s history, the country has around 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the independent media outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti. She was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer.

The protests continue despite an intensifying crackdown on civil society and the media.

World.title: Georgia: Billionaire Ivanishvili meets ruling party leaders – what is known about their talks after silent video release
World.content:
Ivanishvili Georgian Dream meeting

On 17 October, a rare political event took place in Georgia.

Bidzina Ivanishvili, founder and honorary chairman of the ruling Georgian Dream party, chaired a meeting of the party’s political council, followed by a meeting of the parliamentary majority, at the party’s central office.

This was the first public appearance in several months by Ivanishvili, whom many consider Georgia’s “shadow” ruler.

Yet it could hardly be called an “appearance”. Ivanishvili himself said nothing to journalists. The party’s press office released only silent footage of the meetings.

What was discussed behind closed doors became known through three sources: Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze’s briefing, the party’s written statement, and a brief comment by parliamentary majority leader Irakli Kirtskhalia.

Kobakhidze emphasised that Ivanishvili had expressed “pain” over his former team-mates who are in prison. This likely refers primarily to former Prime Minister Irakli Gharibashvili, who for many years was considered Bidzina Ivanishvili’s closest and most loyal ally but has now been convicted of large-scale corruption.

However, in the party’s statement, this issue is presented in a different tone.

It is stated that corruption problems within the team have been “fully and effectively” overcome.

While the meetings were underway, citizens protested outside the building under the slogan “Georgia against Ivanishvili”. One of the banners read, “Supporting Georgian Dream = betraying the country”, while another said, “14 bloody years”, referring to the years Georgian Dream has been in power.

Who joined the political council

The only publicly announced decision from the meetings was to expand the political council. Parliamentary majority leader Irakli Kirtskhalia and Zurab Pataradze, head of the government of the Autonomous Republic of Ajara, joined the body.

Footage released by the press office shows Ivanishvili entering the meeting, shaking hands with MPs and taking his seat. Irakli Kobakhidze, parliamentary speaker Shalva Papuashvili, Tbilisi Mayor Kakha Kaladze and Irakli Kirtskhalia sat beside him at the head table. Ministers were also present.

According to Kobakhidze, both meetings addressed current domestic and foreign policy issues. The party statement referred to “political and economic processes” in the country. It also said time was devoted to initiatives and reforms recently announced by the government.

The context behind Ivanishvili’s meetings with ruling party leaders

Bidzina Ivanishvili rarely appears in public. He has been under US sanctions since 2024.

His participation in party meetings on 17 October came amid an apparent crisis within the government.

Former senior Georgian Dream officials have been arrested one after another on corruption charges.

The most high-profile case involves former Prime Minister Irakli Gharibashvili.

In January 2026, he was sentenced to five years in prison under a plea agreement. In August, prosecutors brought a new bribery charge against him.

Gharibashvili has been publishing letters from prison in which he accuses Irakli Kobakhidze and former Deputy Prime Minister Mamuka Mdinaradze. On August 27, Mamuka Mdinaradze resigned from his post and announced his departure from politics. He denied any connection to the letters.

Another important factor in the context of Ivanishvili’s meeting with ruling party leaders is that the Constitutional Court is due to hear the authorities’ case seeking to ban opposition parties in just a few days.

According to opposition representatives, hearings were scheduled for October 21, 22 and 23. In response, an alliance of nine opposition parties announced a rally in Tbilisi on 25 October under the slogan “Georgia without Ivanishvili. Georgia deserves better.”

Gharibashvili is Ivanishvili’s “heartache” – and the statement about “overcoming difficulties”

After the meetings at the ruling party’s office, journalists asked Irakli Kobakhidze whether the possibility of releasing former Prime Minister Irakli Gharibashvili from prison had been discussed.

Kobakhidze replied that there had not. According to him, Ivanishvili gave a general assessment of “the developments”.

“For all of us, including, of course, first and foremost, Bidzina Ivanishvili, what happened is painful, when events unfold this way and former members of the team are serving sentences for specific crimes (…)”, Kobakhidze said.

He added: “What happened is regrettable. It was, of course, something of a blow to the team.”

Gharibashvili was sentenced to five years in prison in January 2026 following a plea agreement. In August, prosecutors brought a new charge against him. According to the prosecution, the former prime minister accepted 750,000 lari (about $290,000) in bribes.

Gharibashvili’s lawyers say he denies the new charge.

There is no mention of “heartache” in the party statement’s account of the same subject. According to the statement, Ivanishvili reviewed the corruption challenges the team had faced in the past and said that “as a result of the effective work of the prime minister, the government team and the security apparatus, these challenges have been fully and effectively overcome”.

Kobakhidze: “Friendship is none of your business“

Kobakhidze said the team had also discussed Mamuka Mdinaradze, a former deputy prime minister who previously served as head of the State Security Service.

Mdinaradze resigned from his post on August 27 and announced his departure from politics. At the time, he denied that his resignation was connected to Garibashvili’s letters published from prison.

Kobakhidze declined to elaborate publicly. “Mamuka Mdinaradze has left politics”, he said, adding that he did not consider it appropriate to bring the issue to the fore in these circumstances. He said he remained in occasional contact with Mdinaradze. He did not give a direct answer when asked whether they were still friends.

“Why are you asking about friendship? Friendship is none of your business”, he told journalists.

Journalists also raised the issue of a controversial social media post by Georgian Dream party member Dito Samkharadze, who wrote that “rats” [informers] had been identified within the ruling party.”

Kobakhidze was asked whether Samkharadze also meant Mdinaradze and whether legal proceedings against him were expected.

“I don’t know what you’re referring to,” the prime minister replied. He said there was “no basis whatsoever” for such speculation.

Parliamentary majority leader Kirtskhalia: “Ivanishvili spoke mostly about Kobakhidze“

Journalists asked Irakli Kirtskhalia to comment on growing public speculation that Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze could soon resign.

According to him, Ivanishvili devoted more time to Kobakhidze than to anyone else, “expressing support and praise, which the entire team, of course, shares”.

“Ivanishvili said that the government is performing very well under Kobakhidze’s leadership, and that not only is there no reason for his resignation, but every day confirms that he is the best prime minister,” Kirtskhalia said.

He described the resignation rumours as gossip spread by the opposition.

Scandal over possible corruption in spending on the Patriarch’s funeral

At a press briefing, Irakli Kobakhidze addressed the main political issue: allegations of possible corruption in spending on the Patriarch’s funeral.

He said preliminary information from the Government Administration showed “no indication of any improper expenditure”. He also said a large portion of the allocated funds had been returned.

In September, speaking on Rustavi 2, Kobakhidze provided specific figures: according to preliminary data, 722,000 lari (about $275,000) of the 3 million lari (about $1,100,000) allocated had been spent. The questions he answered concerned former Culture Minister Tika Rukhadze’s possible involvement in the alleged embezzlement.

Kobakhidze said detailed information would be presented to the public in the near future. Asked whether investigative agencies should look into the matter, he replied:

“First, we will present detailed information to you, and if any questions remain on this issue, let us discuss them together.”

“Whatever they call us, we keep winning” – Kobakhidze on media restrictions

Irakli Kobakhidze also commented on restrictions on the use of various words and expressions in the media adopted by the Communications Commission.

On 9 October, Transparency International – Georgia reported that the Communications Commission had objected to expressions used by independent TV channels Formula and Pirveli. The commission compiled a list of 93 words and phrases that it banned from use, including “regime”, “oligarch” and “prime minister appointed by Ivanishvili”, according to TI. Fines for using words on the list were increased to 10,000 lari (nearly $4,000).

Kobakhidze explained the decision as necessary to uphold the principle of objectivity.

He said these rules had existed in legislation for years, but an enforcement mechanism had not previously been in place. News programmes are now required to maintain neutrality.

That requirement does not apply to programmes expressing their hosts’ own views, Prime Minister said.

“Nothing bothers us. We win elections and emerge victorious from every political confrontation. Whether they call us a regime or a dictatorship, we win either way”, Kobakhidze said.

News in Georgia

World.title: Are Armenia’s residents thrifty, and how do they prefer to keep their savings? Statistics and reality
World.content:
Are Armenians thrifty

Most residents of Armenia (50.4%) believe it is important to build up savings, according to a study conducted by the Central Bank titled “Assessment of the Financial Capabilities of Armenia’s Population: Barometer 2025”.

The Central Bank also sought to establish how people in Armenia tend to accumulate savings and where they prefer to keep their money. The findings showed that:

87.2% view savings not merely as idle capital, but also as an opportunity to invest and generate additional income;

57.6% continue to keep their savings at home, either because they consider it safer or because the amounts saved are relatively small;

Only 10.7% keep their savings in bank deposits.

The study revealed that people have widely differing views on how to manage their savings. Some even consider investing in their own homes a form of saving. They take out mortgages and allocate a portion of their income towards repayments.

Others prefer to buy land, cars or property, including outside Armenia. Relatively few people trust financial institutions, investment funds or the cryptocurrency market.

Personal story of successful investment

Artak Farmanyan invests his savings in three different areas – property, gold and cryptocurrency. Over the past three years, he has earned the highest returns from crypto assets, although the gold and property markets have also seen strong growth.

“Unlike traditional savings and investments, the cryptocurrency market has a very interesting logic and way of developing. The more you learn about it, the more fascinating it becomes. There is simply more risk involved than, for example, with a bank deposit or property,” Artak explains.
