World.title: WA news LIVE: Protesters arrested over Woodside platform stunt
World.content:
Two Greenpeace activists are in police custody this morning, arrested over a stunt on Woodside’s gas platform, hundreds of kilometres off the Pilbara coast.

Greenpeace activists deployed a massive sign off the Woodside platform. Greenpeace Australia

The climate change activists scaled the floating production unit on Saturday and attached themselves to the structure with climbing equipment in protest of Woodside’s plans to drill for oil and gas in the Scott Reef.

Greenpeace said four protesters travelled to the platform, and had planned to stay for as long as possible after setting up temporary tents.

However, yesterday, special police forces landed a helicopter on the platform and the activists were removed and taken into police custody.

World.title: Ben Simmons was on the verge of an NBA comeback after 538 days. A serious injury has derailed it
World.content:
SportBasketballNBA Ben Simmons was on the verge of an NBA comeback after 538 days. A serious injury has derailed it Roy Ward and Vince Rugari October 19, 2026 — 10:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Ben Simmons’ NBA comeback season has been derailed after the Australian star reportedly tore his Achilles tendon in training, just days away from what loomed as his first game for the Sacramento Kings. According to reports on Monday (AEDT), Simmons suffered the injury in practice with the Kings, who were due to open the new NBA season on Thursday against the Los Angeles Clippers, the last team he played for. Ben Simmons’ return to the NBA is over before it even started. AP The injury is expected to rule the 30-year-old out for the entire season, ending what former teammate and NBA All-Star Dwight Howard had forecast as the “greatest comeback story in NBA history” – just as ESPN was preparing to air a documentary on his return to basketball. Simmons sat out all of last season as he spent the year recovering physically and even turning his hand to competitive fishing, but showed signs of promise in his pre-season outings for the Kings, and shaped as a starter for them.



He had also expressed hope that a successful stint in the NBA would pave the way for him to play for the Australian Boomers at the 2028 Olympic Games in Los Angeles. But those dreams will have to be put on hold, with his 538-day absence from the NBA set to continue a while longer. Chicago star Josh Giddey. Getty Images The injury is a blow to not only Simmons personally, but one of the strongest Australian storylines in the NBA this season. Here’s a closer look at nine of the other players who will suit up in the league. Josh Giddey



Age: 24. Team: Chicago Bulls. Wage: $US25m. Seasons: Six. Giddey’s Bulls have brought in teenage rookie Caleb Wilson, who looks a future star. His high-flying ways should mesh perfectly with Giddey’s lob-passing. Watch out for some highlight-reel plays. But the Bulls are still a work in progress and play in a vastly improved Eastern Conference which should hinder their play-off hopes. Still, Giddey remains a nightly triple-double threat, and his outside shooting looks to have improved yet again. He should fit well under new coach Tiago Splitter, a former Brazilian international who played with Gregg Popovich’s San Antonio Spurs during the Tim Duncan era. Best case: I’ve always been high on Giddey’s talents and I still think he has the capacity to have some All-Star seasons entering his prime NBA years. If he is making his shots, sticking his passes and Wilson immediately produces at a high level, things could get very exciting in the Windy City. Worst case: If Giddey can’t make his shots and faces oppressive defences, then it could be a tough year in which his minutes and role diminish. If Wilson and other emerging Bulls develop slowly or regress, it will also have an impact on Giddey, who, as point guard, is meant to orchestrate his team’s attacks.



Dyson Daniels Age: 23. Team: Atlanta Hawks. Wage: $US25m. Seasons: Five. Daniels is one of the NBA’s elite defenders, and that should continue to be the case. His Hawks have made some shrewd moves this off-season and are capable of winning games in the much-improved East. Lu Dort, CJ McCollum and Aaron Wiggins should help the Hawks. Where Daniels’ season will likely be judged is by how well he shoots from three-point range and how much offence he can offer his side. Dyson Daniels of the Atlanta Hawks and Aaron Nesmith of the Indiana Pacers battle for the ball during preseason. Getty Images Best case: If Daniels is shining at both ends and the Hawks are soaring up the standings, he could well be a defensive player of the year contender and a potential All-Star. If Daniels can also bring his play-making and post game to the fore, then the sky is the limit for him and the Hawks.



Worst case: If Daniels can’t make his threes and struggles to create on offence, it could hurt his minutes and how much the team plays him in the clutch. Daniels has a lot of drive, so he would hate having to watch from the bench. Jock Landale (No.31) leaps for a rebound. AP Photo/Darren Abate Jock Landale Age: 30. Team: Atlanta Hawks. Wage: $US14.1m. Seasons: Six. The Hawks and Landale proved a great fit when he was traded there last season. He should have a meaty role in their big-man rotation with his outside shooting and tough play inside.



Best case: Landale is a capable scorer from inside and outside. If he can crack a starting centre spot and produce regular, reliable points and rebounds then it would be a dream campaign after years of being shipped around the league. Worst case: The Hawks bench Landale and rarely use him before trading him away or letting him go at season’s end. Landale is only on a one-year deal, so he would be back on the free-agent market heading into a World Cup. Tyrese Proctor Age: 22. Team: Cleveland Cavaliers. Wage: $US2.1m. Seasons: Two.



The Sydney-raised playmaker made a strong start to his NBA career last season, and his Cavs should be pressing for a deep play-off run this time around. He showed he could fill the back-up point guard role last season but faces stiff competition for minutes behind starters James Harden and Donovan Mitchell. Best case: Proctor becomes a super reliable threat off the bench who scores and creates as the Cavs storm to the NBA title. This could happen, but Proctor will know he needs to take every chance he gets to impress. Tyrese Proctor drives the baseline against Boston during preseason. Getty Images Worst case: Proctor spends the season stuck on the bench and making occasional visits to the G-League for court time. This could happen as well, considering the Cavs are in win-now mode. But Proctor has shown he can rise to the occasion. Johnny Furphy



Age: 21. Team: Indiana Pacers. Wage: $US2.3m. Seasons: Three. Furphy won plenty of fans with his high-flying dunks last season, but he sadly crashed to earth late in the season when he ruptured his anterior cruciate ligament in February. Furphy is making good progress in his recovery and the Pacers hope he can return in mid-season. Indiana forward Johnny Furphy poses for a photo on media day. AP Photo/AJ Mast Best case: Furphy comes back bigger and stronger and plays a role for the Pacers as they make a deep play-off run, with his three-pointers, defensive plays and dunks all standing out. Worst case: Furphy’s recovery takes longer than planned and he misses the full season.



Josh Green Age: 25. Team: Utah Jazz. Wage: $US14.1m. Seasons: Seven. Green had a wild off-season as he was traded from Charlotte to Minnesota in July before being traded to Utah in late August. It looks a promising situation as the young Jazz roster could use his defence and three-point shooting. Best case: Green takes a starting role with the Jazz and posts career numbers at both ends of the court as the Jazz rise into the play-offs. Utah guard Josh Green defends Spurs guard Ja’Kobi Gillespie during preseason. Getty Images



Worst case: Green is traded again and lands at a club that benches him. The Sydney-raised wing deserves a chance to show what he can do in the NBA, and he deserves some stability after a couple of years of being regularly traded. Phoenix big man Duop Reath poses in his new colours. Getty Images Duop Reath Age: 30. Team: Phoenix Suns. Wage: $US2.1m. Seasons: Four. Reath linked up with the Suns on a one-year deal and looks like he could earn some minutes as the team figures out where it sits in the Western Conference. Young Suns centre Khaman Maluach is poised for a breakout year, but the Suns could use Reath’s mix of outside shooting and active rim defence.



Best case: Reath emerges as a super reliable performer who is pressing Maluach and Oso Ighodaro for minutes at centre while posting career numbers in points, blocks and rebounds. Worst case: Reath rarely leaves the bench as new Suns coach Jordan Ott opts for other players before letting Reath go late in the season. Minnesota centre Rocco Zikarsky. NBAE via Getty Images Rocco Zikarsky Age: 20. Team: Minnesota Timberwolves. Wage: $US680,985. Seasons: Two.



The 221-cm big man is still learning his craft. The Wolves’ plan when drafting him last year was that he would spend last season and this season as a two-way player, moving between the G-League and NBA teams while building his body and skills. He looks to have made some improvement and posted good G-League numbers last season. Best case: Zikarsky bulks up, starts hitting his jump shots and is promoted to the main roster for a deep run to the title. He makes the FIBA World Cup roster and impresses for the Boomers. Worst case: Zikarsky barely seesthe NBA court all season and doesn’t progress as fast as the team hoped. LA Lakers forward Matisse Thybulle steals the ball from Sacramento’s Zach LaVine. Getty Images Matisse Thybulle



Age: 29. Team: Los Angeles Lakers. Wage: $US3.3m. Seasons: Eight. Thybulle has gone from Portland to the Lakers and will be in the spotlight as Luka Doncic and Austin Reeves look to take the Lake Show into a new era post LeBron James. Thybulle’s defence will be valuable, and much will be made about whether he is sticking his three-point shots and stopping his defender from playing help-defence on the Lakers’ stars. Related Article NBL Simmons, Giddey, Daniels, Paul? The next Aussie gun on the path to hoops stardom Best case: Thybulle winds back the clock to his Philly days and has an All-Defensive-team calibre season while also scoring and attacking the basket. Worst case: Thybulle’s shots miss and his confidence crumbles before injuries set in and ruin his season. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX opens higher, tech stocks weigh on Wall Street Alex Veiga Updated October 19, 2026 — 10:13am ,first published 5:26am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. The Australian sharemarket has made a bright start to the week, shrugging off a negative lead from Wall Street, which was hit by another slump in technology stocks. The S&P/ASX 200 was up 28.3 points, or 0.3 per cent, to 8835 in early trade. The Australian dollar was trading higher at US69.64¢. A broad sell-off in technology companies pulled stocks lower on Wall Street on Friday, capping off the market’s worst week since late June. The S&P 500 fell 1.1 per cent. Its roughly 2 per cent drop for the week wiped out its gains from last week, when it set an all-time high. Wall Street wrapped up its worst week since June with more losses. Bloomberg The Nasdaq composite, which is heavily weighted with technology stocks, sank 2.1 per cent and posted its first weekly loss in five weeks and its worst since June. The Dow Jones Industrial Average held up better, closing 0.3 per cent lower.



Slightly more than half of the stocks in the S&P 500 fell, but all but seven of the 75 stocks in the index’s tech sector closed lower. Among the biggest decliners were chip companies, reflecting mounting worries about how long the frenzy over the AI buildout will last. Related Article Analysis

Sharemarket ‘Only the sharks are left’: The $388 billion change shaking up the sharemarket Micron Technology fell 5.6 per cent, Advanced Micro Devices dropped 6 per cent, Broadcom lost 4.5 per cent and Intel gave up 5.8 per cent. Among the other tech companies that finished in the red were Meta, which fell 3.7 per cent, and Google parent Alphabet, which dropped 2.5 per cent. It’s been a choppy week for chipmakers and other big tech stocks central to the artificial intelligence industry. Investors are now worried that the companies, which have relied on debt markets to finance an investment spree into their technology, may not be able to keep borrowing and spending as heavily with yields in bond markets worldwide recently climbing to their highest levels in years.



Netflix’s stock fell 2.9 per cent a day after the company announced that Chief Content Officer Bela Bajaria will be replaced by Peter Rice. The news comes just days after Netflix said that it plans to lay off about 6 per cent of its workforce, amounting to nearly 1,000 positions. Energy stocks held up better than most. Exxon rose 2.5 per cent and Chevron added 2.6 per cent. European and Asian markets closed higher. In the bond market, Treasury yields held relatively steady. The yield on the 10-year Treasury slipped to 5.09 per cent from 5.10 per cent late Thursday. It had topped 5.30 per cent earlier this month and touched its highest level since 2002 because of worries about high inflation, signals of a strong U.S. economy and other factors. Yields are down despite reports this week showing that inflation at the consumer and wholesale level rose more in the U.S. than economists expected.



The reports could persuade the inflation-fighters at the Federal Reserve to hike their key interest rate before the end of this year. The central bank increased its key interest rate by a quarter-point to about 3.9 per cent in September, its first increase in three years. Related Article Energy Australia clashes with Asian energy giants over gas export crackdown Wall Street traders expect the Fed will keep its short-term rate unchanged at its policy meeting this month, but the odds of a rate increase at the December meeting have jumped to 74.3 per cent from 50.2 per cent a month ago, according to data from the CME Group. On Friday, Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh offered no fresh signals about potential interest rate policy moves by the Fed while attending a meeting of financial leaders in Bangkok. Elsewhere in the market, shares in Tesla fell 2.1 per cent after the electric vehicle company unveiled a new model of its Roadster sports car that can thrust itself up in the air.



Alcoa rose 2.5 per cent and The Travelers Cos. gained 1.5 per cent after the companies reported quarterly results that topped Wall Street forecasts. Expectations are high for growth in profits from all kinds of companies this reporting season, which began in earnest this week. That’s what’s allowed U.S. stocks to set records despite high inflation and the many other worries weighing on Wall Street. All told, the S&P 500 fell 84.62 points to 7,659.44. The Dow dropped 175.28 points to 52,002.41, and the Nasdaq declined 572.99 points to close at 26,140.03. In energy markets, oil prices remained elevated as the global oil supply continues to be under pressure without a deal between the U.S. and Iran to end the Iran war. Brent crude, the international standard, jumped 3.7 per cent to settle at $US109.86 per barrel. That is up from around $US72 a barrel in late February before the start of the war. Brent climbed into triple digits last month, the first time since July.



The national average for gasoline is at $US4.33 a gallon on Friday, according to AAA. While that’s lower than the $US4.37 a gallon that it averaged last month, it’s sharply higher than the $US3.06 a gallon from a year ago. Oil remains well-supported as uncertainties surrounding the situation in the Middle East and concerns over oil flows in the Strait of Hormuz had the market “pricing in a significant risk premium,” ING commodities strategists Warren Patterson and Ewa Manthey wrote in a commentary. Edmonton: A fire at a Canadian military base that killed at least four people and seriously injured dozens started with a smouldering grass fire that was whipped into a wall of flames by high winds, Canada’s Globe and Mail newspaper has reported. The fire then engulfed Canadian Armed Forces members at a firing range, the newspaper said, citing internal military communications. Loading The Canadian government on Sunday confirmed four deaths at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright but has not publicly commented on the cause of the fire, which took place about 4pm on Saturday (9am Sunday, AEDT) in a training area at the base as winds gusted up to 96km/h. Prime Minister Mark Carney said the fire was one of the worst peacetime tragedies ever for Canada’s armed forces on home soil.



“The nation is in mourning for those brave members of our armed forces whom we have lost,” Carney said, adding that he had ordered flags on federal buildings across the country to be lowered to half-mast to honour the victims. CBC, the government-funded national broadcaster, previously reported seven deaths at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, citing unnamed sources. Canadian authorities have said the situation continues to evolve and that they will not confirm casualty figures until next of kin have been notified. Internal military communications indicate that the fire “very seriously” injured 31 people, The Globe and Mail reported.



Soldiers and reservists at the base were preparing for a deployment to Latvia, the paper said. CFB Wainwright had 1310 military and civilian personnel stationed there as of 2021, according to census data. The base, one of Canada’s largest, is about 210 kilometres east of Edmonton in Alberta. National Defence Minister David McGuinty said on Sunday he would go to the city for briefings on the situation. Paramedics load an injured person into an ambulance at the Wainwright Health Centre as injured military members are treated after a fire. John Ulan/The Canadian Press via AP The base houses the Canadian Manoeuvre Training Centre, which runs training scenarios and exercises for the army. Carney said those affected in Saturday’s fire came from military bases across the country.



Military and civilian firefighters fought the fire through the night in “some of the worst conditions imaginable”, Carney said. Canadian officials are expected to address the public from Wainwright, which lies in a largely rural area, later on Monday (AEDT). Air ambulances from Edmonton and Saskatoon, which is about 300 kilometres from Wainwright, flew to the military base on Saturday, Carney said. Patients are being treated in Edmonton, Wainwright, Calgary and Red Deer, he said. Health staff in Edmonton said a “code orange”, or mass-casualty event, was declared to co-ordinate the medical response for patients being transported from Wainwright, CBC News reported. The town of Wainwright, with a population of about 6600, is just north of the base.



The municipality posted on social media that the fire had crossed the base fence into the nearby district, but no evacuation orders had been issued. It said on Sunday that the fire was not expected to spread beyond its current boundaries. Reuters Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Stax is back, saved by founders of sneakerhead marketplace
World.content:
Exclusive BusinessEntrepreneurshipInsolvency Stax is back, saved by founders of sneakerhead marketplace Jessica Yun Updated October 19, 2026 — 10:00am ,first published August 10, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

For the past a month and a half, the website of Australian activewear brand Stax has been replaced by a customer FAQ page that states: “SALE IS CLOSED”. The company, which was best known for form fitting activewear with minimal branding, collapsed in June after its lender, NAB, called in receivers to try to recover millions in debts owed to several parties. Streetwear entrepreneurs Justin Truong and Sandy Li, who have bought Stax, pose in their sneaker warehouse. Audrey Richardson But one day, and no one is quite sure when, the site will be back up and running. “This is a fresh start for Stax,” said entrepreneur and Stax’s new co-owner, Justin Truong. “This is such an iconic Australian brand that we want to give it another chance. It could have been sold off to a faceless corporation that could strip it for parts.”



Truong and wife and business partner Sandy Li-Truong have led a private investor group to acquire Stax in a rescue deal that makes them the new majority owners. The athleisure label left behind debts of $6.7 million to employees, creditors and the tax office after being handed over to receivers in late June. It is not clear what, if anything, those parties will get out of the sale; the Truongs declined to discuss the financials of the deal and were also coy about how exactly they would avoid the pitfalls of the retail trade, where Stax competes against numerous other brands such as Lululemon, LSKD and White Fox all offering very similar products. Related Article Fashion retail ‘Each party is owed money’: Stax orders in limbo, company up for sale “Our focus is really building this with strong foundations and rebuilding Stax, so we can earn the trust of the really incredible, valuable, loyal community that the brand has built along the way,” said Justin Truong. The couple do have experience in the industry as the owners of Pushas, an online sneaker, streetwear and collectibles reseller. The shoe fanatics started selling their own sneakers in 2017 to fund their increasingly expensive hobby and turned it into a global marketplace. With backing from Justin Kan, a co-founder of the massive streaming service Twitch, and Airtasker founder Tim Fung, it now turns over $10 million-plus a year selling several thousands of authenticated items such as Air Jordans, Yeezys and Labubus a week to collectors in Australia, New Zealand, the US and Canada.



In a crucial difference from Stax, Pushas sells other companies’ brands, not its own. The Truongs, who acquired Stax alongside a handful of family offices for an undisclosed sum, are not interested in running their new business themselves. They are expecting to sign the paperwork to announce a new chief executive who will build out a team to restart operations for the assets they have acquired, which include its trademarks, IP, and digital assets. “It won’t be an entirely new team,” Truong said. “We’ll see who in the previous team we’ll bring back. It’s good to have continuity.” He will sit on the board as chairman; the new Stax will run independently of Pushas. “As owners, we don’t want to overstep,” he said. The rescue deal transfers the activewear brand from the hands of one entrepreneurial married couple to another. Founded in 2015, founders Don Robertson and wife Matilda Murray built Stax from the ashes of a previously failed business, an online supplement brand that was liquidated. The pair’s pivot to selling hoodies, merchandise and luxury activewear under the Stax brand saw the married couple debut on The Australian Financial Review’s Young Rich List in 2022, and worth an estimated $70 million as of 2025. Stax expanded aggressively into physical stores in 2022 and operated at least eight, but closed six in 2025 after rent costs increased and customers tightened their wallets following rapidly rising interest rates and high inflation.



Pushas co-founders Justin Truong and Sandy Li. On July 13, the pair issued an apology through Instagram for the sudden collapse of the high-profile brand that had been spotted on Jennifer Lopez, Megan Fox, Hailey Bieber. “I want to know that we have heard you,” the pair wrote in a joint Instagram post in their first public comments about the collapse that infuriated hundreds of customers over delayed or missing orders. “We’re truly sorry for this and for not communicating earlier … Knowing that many of our customers have been impacted is something we carry every day.” Stax owed over $453,000 to employees and nearly $6.3 million to creditors, according to documents filed to the corporate regulator, including $123,858 to the tax office and $1.9 million to Chinese supplier Ningbo Mingna Garments. Google, Meta, and Scentre were also owed payments in the hundreds of thousands.



Truong argues any brand that achieved the size and reach of Stax is a great business. “Sometimes things happen,” he said. “Credit where credit is due, I think Don and Matilda built an amazing brand. There’s definitely a great business that that can be built from it.” Sandy Li-Truong said the trust customers had in Stax made the company appeal to her. The new entity will be run with “operational discipline”, and the couple are looking at support avenues for customers impacted by unfulfilled orders, she added. “While those orders pre-date our ownership of the business, we recognise the impact this has had on the STAX community and we want to explore what we can do as a gesture of goodwill.” FTI Consulting receiver Asjadi Hone said she was proud to facilitate the sale.



“The new owners will appoint a team to focus on rebuilding the brand while maintaining the product quality, inclusivity and community connection that has defined Stax since its launch.” The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. A public servant employed by Victoria Police to work on child abuse investigations has been charged with possessing and accessing child abuse material. Vincent Manner will face court in Bendigo on November 4 on 23 charges, including 10 counts of possessing and accessing child abuse material, two counts of misconduct in public office and 11 counts of failing to provide information under warrant. Vincent Manner. Facebook Manner, 57, worked as a digital forensics officer between June 2016 and August 2025 before he was stood down with pay. He resigned in November 2025, while still under investigation. The allegations against him sparked a year-long police audit in which dozens of active court cases had to be reviewed, and that caused some of them to be delayed.



Digital forensics officers are not sworn police members, but they support police by extracting data from digital devices which can then be presented in court as evidence. Related Article Justice Evidence in dozens of court cases under review after forensics officer arrested Manner was arrested in October 2025, after which police wrote to lawyers advising them they had “become aware of potential irregularities with the storage and/or extraction and examination of some devices” during an audit of the man’s work. These irregularities prompted police to assess at least 112 cases before Victorian courts that may have been impacted. This masthead has followed more than a dozen cases in which Manner had handled evidence as they reappeared before the courts. Some of those matters were adjourned multiple times as police needed time to re-extract evidence from the devices.



Manner was charged more than a year after his arrest. In their statement last week confirming the charges, Victoria Police said they had completed the reexamination of evidence known as Operation Turnberry. “At this stage it is believed all issues have been identified and reviewed and impacted parties have been notified,” a spokesperson said. Police would not confirm exactly how many cases had ultimately been disrupted, saying the matter was now before the courts. A Victoria Legal Aid spokesperson told this masthead it knew of at least eight cases that had been affected by the audit, almost all of them delayed. When the investigation was made public last year, the Centre Against Sexual Assault said it was worried the situation would deter victims from reaching out to support services or to police.



Jean*, of Shepparton, has been personally affected by the delays. She heard in October last year that a case being heard affecting her family would need to be audited, even though it had already been adjourned twice for unrelated reasons. Jean said the case was adjourned a further four times before police confirmed in May that the digital evidence hadn’t been corrupted. “Every time we’ve been following it, we’ve had to make the trip to Bendigo, which means time off work and the stress and trauma of being there,” Jean said, adding that the family’s attempts to seek intervention orders had also been delayed by the court process. “Because we don’t have resolution in this case, we’re still going through it.” *Not her real name. Jean’s name has been changed to protect her identity. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

Rail commuters have been caught in delays stretching as long as 40 minutes, after a signalling issue blocked half of the available lines at Eagle Junction.

Queensland Rail discovered the issue shortly after 6.30am.

About 40 minutes later Translink warned all northern lines except Ferny Grove were experiencing delays, including the Airport, Caboolture, Doomben, Redcliffe Peninsula, Shorncliffe, and Sunshine Coast lines.

Engineers fixed the issue just before 8am, with trains funnelled through two of the station’s four tracks for more than an hour.

The delays affected trains travelling north and south through the major rail station.

A man has been charged after allegedly threatening to shoot three people with a sawn-off shotgun during a confrontation over a stolen van in Dulwich Hill on Friday, before setting fire to the vehicle and fleeing on foot.

An hours-long lockdown began in the inner west suburb after 10.20am on Friday, when Jake Kermode, 32, was allegedly confronted over a stolen van taken from a nearby suburb days earlier.

Police had shut down the area as they combed Dulwich Hill for the gunman on Friday. James Brickwood

Kermode allegedly set fire to the van, near an apartment complex at Williams Parade and Constitution Road in Dulwich Hill, and waved the shotgun at three witnesses, before fleeing on foot with the weapon.

Nearby businesses, cafes and schools were put into lockdown on Friday as tactical police, along with the police helicopter, combed nearby streets for the alleged gunman. The lockdown was lifted about 3pm that day.

World.title: WA news LIVE: Protesters arrested over Woodside platform stunt
World.content:
Two Greenpeace activists are in police custody this morning, arrested over a stunt on Woodside’s gas platform, hundreds of kilometres off the Pilbara coast.

Greenpeace activists deployed a massive sign off the Woodside platform. Greenpeace Australia

The climate change activists scaled the floating production unit on Saturday and attached themselves to the structure with climbing equipment in protest of Woodside’s plans to drill for oil and gas in the Scott Reef.

Greenpeace said four protesters travelled to the platform, and had planned to stay for as long as possible after setting up temporary tents.

However, yesterday, special police forces landed a helicopter on the platform and the activists were removed and taken into police custody.

World.title: Ben Simmons was on the verge of an NBA comeback after 538 days. A serious injury has derailed it
World.content:
SportBasketballNBA Ben Simmons was on the verge of an NBA comeback after 538 days. A serious injury has derailed it Roy Ward and Vince Rugari October 19, 2026 — 10:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Ben Simmons’ NBA comeback season has been derailed after the Australian star reportedly tore his Achilles tendon in training, just days away from what loomed as his first game for the Sacramento Kings. According to reports on Monday (AEDT), Simmons suffered the injury in practice with the Kings, who were due to open the new NBA season on Thursday against the Los Angeles Clippers, the last team he played for. Ben Simmons’ return to the NBA is over before it even started. AP The injury is expected to rule the 30-year-old out for the entire season, ending what former teammate and NBA All-Star Dwight Howard had forecast as the “greatest comeback story in NBA history” – just as ESPN was preparing to air a documentary on his return to basketball. Simmons sat out all of last season as he spent the year recovering physically and even turning his hand to competitive fishing, but showed signs of promise in his pre-season outings for the Kings, and shaped as a starter for them.



He had also expressed hope that a successful stint in the NBA would pave the way for him to play for the Australian Boomers at the 2028 Olympic Games in Los Angeles. But those dreams will have to be put on hold, with his 538-day absence from the NBA set to continue a while longer. Chicago star Josh Giddey. Getty Images The injury is a blow to not only Simmons personally, but one of the strongest Australian storylines in the NBA this season. Here’s a closer look at nine of the other players who will suit up in the league. Josh Giddey



Age: 24. Team: Chicago Bulls. Wage: $US25m. Seasons: Six. Giddey’s Bulls have brought in teenage rookie Caleb Wilson, who looks a future star. His high-flying ways should mesh perfectly with Giddey’s lob-passing. Watch out for some highlight-reel plays. But the Bulls are still a work in progress and play in a vastly improved Eastern Conference which should hinder their play-off hopes. Still, Giddey remains a nightly triple-double threat, and his outside shooting looks to have improved yet again. He should fit well under new coach Tiago Splitter, a former Brazilian international who played with Gregg Popovich’s San Antonio Spurs during the Tim Duncan era. Best case: I’ve always been high on Giddey’s talents and I still think he has the capacity to have some All-Star seasons entering his prime NBA years. If he is making his shots, sticking his passes and Wilson immediately produces at a high level, things could get very exciting in the Windy City. Worst case: If Giddey can’t make his shots and faces oppressive defences, then it could be a tough year in which his minutes and role diminish. If Wilson and other emerging Bulls develop slowly or regress, it will also have an impact on Giddey, who, as point guard, is meant to orchestrate his team’s attacks.



Dyson Daniels Age: 23. Team: Atlanta Hawks. Wage: $US25m. Seasons: Five. Daniels is one of the NBA’s elite defenders, and that should continue to be the case. His Hawks have made some shrewd moves this off-season and are capable of winning games in the much-improved East. Lu Dort, CJ McCollum and Aaron Wiggins should help the Hawks. Where Daniels’ season will likely be judged is by how well he shoots from three-point range and how much offence he can offer his side. Dyson Daniels of the Atlanta Hawks and Aaron Nesmith of the Indiana Pacers battle for the ball during preseason. Getty Images Best case: If Daniels is shining at both ends and the Hawks are soaring up the standings, he could well be a defensive player of the year contender and a potential All-Star. If Daniels can also bring his play-making and post game to the fore, then the sky is the limit for him and the Hawks.



Worst case: If Daniels can’t make his threes and struggles to create on offence, it could hurt his minutes and how much the team plays him in the clutch. Daniels has a lot of drive, so he would hate having to watch from the bench. Jock Landale (No.31) leaps for a rebound. AP Photo/Darren Abate Jock Landale Age: 30. Team: Atlanta Hawks. Wage: $US14.1m. Seasons: Six. The Hawks and Landale proved a great fit when he was traded there last season. He should have a meaty role in their big-man rotation with his outside shooting and tough play inside.



Best case: Landale is a capable scorer from inside and outside. If he can crack a starting centre spot and produce regular, reliable points and rebounds then it would be a dream campaign after years of being shipped around the league. Worst case: The Hawks bench Landale and rarely use him before trading him away or letting him go at season’s end. Landale is only on a one-year deal, so he would be back on the free-agent market heading into a World Cup. Tyrese Proctor Age: 22. Team: Cleveland Cavaliers. Wage: $US2.1m. Seasons: Two.



The Sydney-raised playmaker made a strong start to his NBA career last season, and his Cavs should be pressing for a deep play-off run this time around. He showed he could fill the back-up point guard role last season but faces stiff competition for minutes behind starters James Harden and Donovan Mitchell. Best case: Proctor becomes a super reliable threat off the bench who scores and creates as the Cavs storm to the NBA title. This could happen, but Proctor will know he needs to take every chance he gets to impress. Tyrese Proctor drives the baseline against Boston during preseason. Getty Images Worst case: Proctor spends the season stuck on the bench and making occasional visits to the G-League for court time. This could happen as well, considering the Cavs are in win-now mode. But Proctor has shown he can rise to the occasion. Johnny Furphy



Age: 21. Team: Indiana Pacers. Wage: $US2.3m. Seasons: Three. Furphy won plenty of fans with his high-flying dunks last season, but he sadly crashed to earth late in the season when he ruptured his anterior cruciate ligament in February. Furphy is making good progress in his recovery and the Pacers hope he can return in mid-season. Indiana forward Johnny Furphy poses for a photo on media day. AP Photo/AJ Mast Best case: Furphy comes back bigger and stronger and plays a role for the Pacers as they make a deep play-off run, with his three-pointers, defensive plays and dunks all standing out. Worst case: Furphy’s recovery takes longer than planned and he misses the full season.



Josh Green Age: 25. Team: Utah Jazz. Wage: $US14.1m. Seasons: Seven. Green had a wild off-season as he was traded from Charlotte to Minnesota in July before being traded to Utah in late August. It looks a promising situation as the young Jazz roster could use his defence and three-point shooting. Best case: Green takes a starting role with the Jazz and posts career numbers at both ends of the court as the Jazz rise into the play-offs. Utah guard Josh Green defends Spurs guard Ja’Kobi Gillespie during preseason. Getty Images



Worst case: Green is traded again and lands at a club that benches him. The Sydney-raised wing deserves a chance to show what he can do in the NBA, and he deserves some stability after a couple of years of being regularly traded. Phoenix big man Duop Reath poses in his new colours. Getty Images Duop Reath Age: 30. Team: Phoenix Suns. Wage: $US2.1m. Seasons: Four. Reath linked up with the Suns on a one-year deal and looks like he could earn some minutes as the team figures out where it sits in the Western Conference. Young Suns centre Khaman Maluach is poised for a breakout year, but the Suns could use Reath’s mix of outside shooting and active rim defence.



Best case: Reath emerges as a super reliable performer who is pressing Maluach and Oso Ighodaro for minutes at centre while posting career numbers in points, blocks and rebounds. Worst case: Reath rarely leaves the bench as new Suns coach Jordan Ott opts for other players before letting Reath go late in the season. Minnesota centre Rocco Zikarsky. NBAE via Getty Images Rocco Zikarsky Age: 20. Team: Minnesota Timberwolves. Wage: $US680,985. Seasons: Two.



The 221-cm big man is still learning his craft. The Wolves’ plan when drafting him last year was that he would spend last season and this season as a two-way player, moving between the G-League and NBA teams while building his body and skills. He looks to have made some improvement and posted good G-League numbers last season. Best case: Zikarsky bulks up, starts hitting his jump shots and is promoted to the main roster for a deep run to the title. He makes the FIBA World Cup roster and impresses for the Boomers. Worst case: Zikarsky barely seesthe NBA court all season and doesn’t progress as fast as the team hoped. LA Lakers forward Matisse Thybulle steals the ball from Sacramento’s Zach LaVine. Getty Images Matisse Thybulle



Age: 29. Team: Los Angeles Lakers. Wage: $US3.3m. Seasons: Eight. Thybulle has gone from Portland to the Lakers and will be in the spotlight as Luka Doncic and Austin Reeves look to take the Lake Show into a new era post LeBron James. Thybulle’s defence will be valuable, and much will be made about whether he is sticking his three-point shots and stopping his defender from playing help-defence on the Lakers’ stars. Related Article NBL Simmons, Giddey, Daniels, Paul? The next Aussie gun on the path to hoops stardom Best case: Thybulle winds back the clock to his Philly days and has an All-Defensive-team calibre season while also scoring and attacking the basket. Worst case: Thybulle’s shots miss and his confidence crumbles before injuries set in and ruin his season. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX opens higher, tech stocks weigh on Wall Street Alex Veiga Updated October 19, 2026 — 10:13am ,first published 5:26am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. The Australian sharemarket has made a bright start to the week, shrugging off a negative lead from Wall Street, which was hit by another slump in technology stocks. The S&P/ASX 200 was up 28.3 points, or 0.3 per cent, to 8835 in early trade. The Australian dollar was trading higher at US69.64¢. A broad sell-off in technology companies pulled stocks lower on Wall Street on Friday, capping off the market’s worst week since late June. The S&P 500 fell 1.1 per cent. Its roughly 2 per cent drop for the week wiped out its gains from last week, when it set an all-time high. Wall Street wrapped up its worst week since June with more losses. Bloomberg The Nasdaq composite, which is heavily weighted with technology stocks, sank 2.1 per cent and posted its first weekly loss in five weeks and its worst since June. The Dow Jones Industrial Average held up better, closing 0.3 per cent lower.



Slightly more than half of the stocks in the S&P 500 fell, but all but seven of the 75 stocks in the index’s tech sector closed lower. Among the biggest decliners were chip companies, reflecting mounting worries about how long the frenzy over the AI buildout will last. Related Article Analysis

Sharemarket ‘Only the sharks are left’: The $388 billion change shaking up the sharemarket Micron Technology fell 5.6 per cent, Advanced Micro Devices dropped 6 per cent, Broadcom lost 4.5 per cent and Intel gave up 5.8 per cent. Among the other tech companies that finished in the red were Meta, which fell 3.7 per cent, and Google parent Alphabet, which dropped 2.5 per cent. It’s been a choppy week for chipmakers and other big tech stocks central to the artificial intelligence industry. Investors are now worried that the companies, which have relied on debt markets to finance an investment spree into their technology, may not be able to keep borrowing and spending as heavily with yields in bond markets worldwide recently climbing to their highest levels in years.



Netflix’s stock fell 2.9 per cent a day after the company announced that Chief Content Officer Bela Bajaria will be replaced by Peter Rice. The news comes just days after Netflix said that it plans to lay off about 6 per cent of its workforce, amounting to nearly 1,000 positions. Energy stocks held up better than most. Exxon rose 2.5 per cent and Chevron added 2.6 per cent. European and Asian markets closed higher. In the bond market, Treasury yields held relatively steady. The yield on the 10-year Treasury slipped to 5.09 per cent from 5.10 per cent late Thursday. It had topped 5.30 per cent earlier this month and touched its highest level since 2002 because of worries about high inflation, signals of a strong U.S. economy and other factors. Yields are down despite reports this week showing that inflation at the consumer and wholesale level rose more in the U.S. than economists expected.



The reports could persuade the inflation-fighters at the Federal Reserve to hike their key interest rate before the end of this year. The central bank increased its key interest rate by a quarter-point to about 3.9 per cent in September, its first increase in three years. Related Article Energy Australia clashes with Asian energy giants over gas export crackdown Wall Street traders expect the Fed will keep its short-term rate unchanged at its policy meeting this month, but the odds of a rate increase at the December meeting have jumped to 74.3 per cent from 50.2 per cent a month ago, according to data from the CME Group. On Friday, Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh offered no fresh signals about potential interest rate policy moves by the Fed while attending a meeting of financial leaders in Bangkok. Elsewhere in the market, shares in Tesla fell 2.1 per cent after the electric vehicle company unveiled a new model of its Roadster sports car that can thrust itself up in the air.



Alcoa rose 2.5 per cent and The Travelers Cos. gained 1.5 per cent after the companies reported quarterly results that topped Wall Street forecasts. Expectations are high for growth in profits from all kinds of companies this reporting season, which began in earnest this week. That’s what’s allowed U.S. stocks to set records despite high inflation and the many other worries weighing on Wall Street. All told, the S&P 500 fell 84.62 points to 7,659.44. The Dow dropped 175.28 points to 52,002.41, and the Nasdaq declined 572.99 points to close at 26,140.03. In energy markets, oil prices remained elevated as the global oil supply continues to be under pressure without a deal between the U.S. and Iran to end the Iran war. Brent crude, the international standard, jumped 3.7 per cent to settle at $US109.86 per barrel. That is up from around $US72 a barrel in late February before the start of the war. Brent climbed into triple digits last month, the first time since July.



The national average for gasoline is at $US4.33 a gallon on Friday, according to AAA. While that’s lower than the $US4.37 a gallon that it averaged last month, it’s sharply higher than the $US3.06 a gallon from a year ago. Oil remains well-supported as uncertainties surrounding the situation in the Middle East and concerns over oil flows in the Strait of Hormuz had the market “pricing in a significant risk premium,” ING commodities strategists Warren Patterson and Ewa Manthey wrote in a commentary. World.content:

Edmonton: A fire at a Canadian military base that killed at least four people and seriously injured dozens started with a smouldering grass fire that was whipped into a wall of flames by high winds, Canada’s Globe and Mail newspaper has reported. The fire then engulfed Canadian Armed Forces members at a firing range, the newspaper said, citing internal military communications. Loading The Canadian government on Sunday confirmed four deaths at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright but has not publicly commented on the cause of the fire, which took place about 4pm on Saturday (9am Sunday, AEDT) in a training area at the base as winds gusted up to 96km/h. Prime Minister Mark Carney said the fire was one of the worst peacetime tragedies ever for Canada’s armed forces on home soil.



“The nation is in mourning for those brave members of our armed forces whom we have lost,” Carney said, adding that he had ordered flags on federal buildings across the country to be lowered to half-mast to honour the victims. CBC, the government-funded national broadcaster, previously reported seven deaths at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, citing unnamed sources. Canadian authorities have said the situation continues to evolve and that they will not confirm casualty figures until next of kin have been notified. Internal military communications indicate that the fire “very seriously” injured 31 people, The Globe and Mail reported.



Soldiers and reservists at the base were preparing for a deployment to Latvia, the paper said. CFB Wainwright had 1310 military and civilian personnel stationed there as of 2021, according to census data. The base, one of Canada’s largest, is about 210 kilometres east of Edmonton in Alberta. National Defence Minister David McGuinty said on Sunday he would go to the city for briefings on the situation. Paramedics load an injured person into an ambulance at the Wainwright Health Centre as injured military members are treated after a fire. John Ulan/The Canadian Press via AP The base houses the Canadian Manoeuvre Training Centre, which runs training scenarios and exercises for the army. Carney said those affected in Saturday’s fire came from military bases across the country.



Military and civilian firefighters fought the fire through the night in “some of the worst conditions imaginable”, Carney said. Canadian officials are expected to address the public from Wainwright, which lies in a largely rural area, later on Monday (AEDT). Air ambulances from Edmonton and Saskatoon, which is about 300 kilometres from Wainwright, flew to the military base on Saturday, Carney said. Patients are being treated in Edmonton, Wainwright, Calgary and Red Deer, he said. Health staff in Edmonton said a “code orange”, or mass-casualty event, was declared to co-ordinate the medical response for patients being transported from Wainwright, CBC News reported. The town of Wainwright, with a population of about 6600, is just north of the base.



The municipality posted on social media that the fire had crossed the base fence into the nearby district, but no evacuation orders had been issued. It said on Sunday that the fire was not expected to spread beyond its current boundaries. Reuters Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Stax is back, saved by founders of sneakerhead marketplace
World.content:
Exclusive BusinessEntrepreneurshipInsolvency Stax is back, saved by founders of sneakerhead marketplace Jessica Yun Updated October 19, 2026 — 10:00am ,first published August 10, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

For the past a month and a half, the website of Australian activewear brand Stax has been replaced by a customer FAQ page that states: “SALE IS CLOSED”. The company, which was best known for form fitting activewear with minimal branding, collapsed in June after its lender, NAB, called in receivers to try to recover millions in debts owed to several parties. Streetwear entrepreneurs Justin Truong and Sandy Li, who have bought Stax, pose in their sneaker warehouse. Audrey Richardson But one day, and no one is quite sure when, the site will be back up and running. “This is a fresh start for Stax,” said entrepreneur and Stax’s new co-owner, Justin Truong. “This is such an iconic Australian brand that we want to give it another chance. It could have been sold off to a faceless corporation that could strip it for parts.”



Truong and wife and business partner Sandy Li-Truong have led a private investor group to acquire Stax in a rescue deal that makes them the new majority owners. The athleisure label left behind debts of $6.7 million to employees, creditors and the tax office after being handed over to receivers in late June. It is not clear what, if anything, those parties will get out of the sale; the Truongs declined to discuss the financials of the deal and were also coy about how exactly they would avoid the pitfalls of the retail trade, where Stax competes against numerous other brands such as Lululemon, LSKD and White Fox all offering very similar products. Related Article Fashion retail ‘Each party is owed money’: Stax orders in limbo, company up for sale “Our focus is really building this with strong foundations and rebuilding Stax, so we can earn the trust of the really incredible, valuable, loyal community that the brand has built along the way,” said Justin Truong. The couple do have experience in the industry as the owners of Pushas, an online sneaker, streetwear and collectibles reseller. The shoe fanatics started selling their own sneakers in 2017 to fund their increasingly expensive hobby and turned it into a global marketplace. With backing from Justin Kan, a co-founder of the massive streaming service Twitch, and Airtasker founder Tim Fung, it now turns over $10 million-plus a year selling several thousands of authenticated items such as Air Jordans, Yeezys and Labubus a week to collectors in Australia, New Zealand, the US and Canada.



In a crucial difference from Stax, Pushas sells other companies’ brands, not its own. The Truongs, who acquired Stax alongside a handful of family offices for an undisclosed sum, are not interested in running their new business themselves. They are expecting to sign the paperwork to announce a new chief executive who will build out a team to restart operations for the assets they have acquired, which include its trademarks, IP, and digital assets. “It won’t be an entirely new team,” Truong said. “We’ll see who in the previous team we’ll bring back. It’s good to have continuity.” He will sit on the board as chairman; the new Stax will run independently of Pushas. “As owners, we don’t want to overstep,” he said. The rescue deal transfers the activewear brand from the hands of one entrepreneurial married couple to another. Founded in 2015, founders Don Robertson and wife Matilda Murray built Stax from the ashes of a previously failed business, an online supplement brand that was liquidated. The pair’s pivot to selling hoodies, merchandise and luxury activewear under the Stax brand saw the married couple debut on The Australian Financial Review’s Young Rich List in 2022, and worth an estimated $70 million as of 2025. Stax expanded aggressively into physical stores in 2022 and operated at least eight, but closed six in 2025 after rent costs increased and customers tightened their wallets following rapidly rising interest rates and high inflation.



Pushas co-founders Justin Truong and Sandy Li. On July 13, the pair issued an apology through Instagram for the sudden collapse of the high-profile brand that had been spotted on Jennifer Lopez, Megan Fox, Hailey Bieber. “I want to know that we have heard you,” the pair wrote in a joint Instagram post in their first public comments about the collapse that infuriated hundreds of customers over delayed or missing orders. “We’re truly sorry for this and for not communicating earlier … Knowing that many of our customers have been impacted is something we carry every day.” Stax owed over $453,000 to employees and nearly $6.3 million to creditors, according to documents filed to the corporate regulator, including $123,858 to the tax office and $1.9 million to Chinese supplier Ningbo Mingna Garments. Google, Meta, and Scentre were also owed payments in the hundreds of thousands.



Truong argues any brand that achieved the size and reach of Stax is a great business. “Sometimes things happen,” he said. “Credit where credit is due, I think Don and Matilda built an amazing brand. There’s definitely a great business that that can be built from it.” Sandy Li-Truong said the trust customers had in Stax made the company appeal to her. The new entity will be run with “operational discipline”, and the couple are looking at support avenues for customers impacted by unfulfilled orders, she added. “While those orders pre-date our ownership of the business, we recognise the impact this has had on the STAX community and we want to explore what we can do as a gesture of goodwill.” FTI Consulting receiver Asjadi Hone said she was proud to facilitate the sale.



“The new owners will appoint a team to focus on rebuilding the brand while maintaining the product quality, inclusivity and community connection that has defined Stax since its launch.” The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. A public servant employed by Victoria Police to work on child abuse investigations has been charged with possessing and accessing child abuse material. Vincent Manner will face court in Bendigo on November 4 on 23 charges, including 10 counts of possessing and accessing child abuse material, two counts of misconduct in public office and 11 counts of failing to provide information under warrant. Vincent Manner. Facebook Manner, 57, worked as a digital forensics officer between June 2016 and August 2025 before he was stood down with pay. He resigned in November 2025, while still under investigation. The allegations against him sparked a year-long police audit in which dozens of active court cases had to be reviewed, and that caused some of them to be delayed.



Digital forensics officers are not sworn police members, but they support police by extracting data from digital devices which can then be presented in court as evidence. Related Article Justice Evidence in dozens of court cases under review after forensics officer arrested Manner was arrested in October 2025, after which police wrote to lawyers advising them they had “become aware of potential irregularities with the storage and/or extraction and examination of some devices” during an audit of the man’s work. These irregularities prompted police to assess at least 112 cases before Victorian courts that may have been impacted. This masthead has followed more than a dozen cases in which Manner had handled evidence as they reappeared before the courts. Some of those matters were adjourned multiple times as police needed time to re-extract evidence from the devices.



Manner was charged more than a year after his arrest. In their statement last week confirming the charges, Victoria Police said they had completed the reexamination of evidence known as Operation Turnberry. “At this stage it is believed all issues have been identified and reviewed and impacted parties have been notified,” a spokesperson said. Police would not confirm exactly how many cases had ultimately been disrupted, saying the matter was now before the courts. A Victoria Legal Aid spokesperson told this masthead it knew of at least eight cases that had been affected by the audit, almost all of them delayed. When the investigation was made public last year, the Centre Against Sexual Assault said it was worried the situation would deter victims from reaching out to support services or to police.



Jean*, of Shepparton, has been personally affected by the delays. She heard in October last year that a case being heard affecting her family would need to be audited, even though it had already been adjourned twice for unrelated reasons. Jean said the case was adjourned a further four times before police confirmed in May that the digital evidence hadn’t been corrupted. “Every time we’ve been following it, we’ve had to make the trip to Bendigo, which means time off work and the stress and trauma of being there,” Jean said, adding that the family’s attempts to seek intervention orders had also been delayed by the court process. “Because we don’t have resolution in this case, we’re still going through it.” *Not her real name. Jean’s name has been changed to protect her identity. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

Rail commuters have been caught in delays stretching as long as 40 minutes, after a signalling issue blocked half of the available lines at Eagle Junction.

A man has been charged after allegedly threatening to shoot three people with a sawn-off shotgun during a confrontation over a stolen van in Dulwich Hill on Friday, before setting fire to the vehicle and fleeing on foot.

An hours-long lockdown began in the inner west suburb after 10.20am on Friday, when Jake Kermode, 32, was allegedly confronted over a stolen van taken from a nearby suburb days earlier.

Police had shut down the area as they combed Dulwich Hill for the gunman on Friday. James Brickwood

Kermode allegedly set fire to the van, near an apartment complex at Williams Parade and Constitution Road in Dulwich Hill, and waved the shotgun at three witnesses, before fleeing on foot with the weapon.

Nearby businesses, cafes and schools were put into lockdown on Friday as tactical police, along with the police helicopter, combed nearby streets for the alleged gunman. The lockdown was lifted about 3pm that day.

World.title: FNRL clears $300k debt and pays World Cup player allowances
World.content:
The Fiji National Rugby League (FNRL) says all players and officials competing at the 2026 Rugby League World Cup (RLWC) have been paid for their pool game commitments.

FNRL executive chairman Rajesh Singh confirmed to RNZ Pacific that every one of the Fiji Bati and Fiji Bulikula players and officials were paid before the teams left for Australia last week.

He said the FNRL is now debt-free, after the organisation cleared its outstanding debt.

Singh said the pre-tournament payment of allowances and clearing of debts were two positive achievements for the FNRL following financial restructures in the past six months.

"We've cleared our debts, which was around $300,000 (NZ$225,000)," he said. "And the players and officials have been paid for all their pool games at the World Cup. If they advance to the next round, we'll make sure they'll get paid for it."

Singh said the results have come after the streamlining of expenses and restructuring of the organisation's financial system following audits.

"I'm grateful to the dedicated staff at the FNRL office for their commitment and sacrifice," he said.

Fijian players huddle ahead of the Men's Rugby League World Cup Group A match between Fiji and the Cook Islands at McDonald Jones Stadium in Newcastle, Sunday, 18 October 12026. AAP / Photosport

The Bulikula took the New Zealand Kiwi Ferns to the wire in their opening clash in Newcastle, Sydney on Sunday, only losing 18-12 in the end, with the Kiwi Ferns managing a converted try two minutes from fulltime.

The Bati defeated Cook Islands 40-12 to open their campaign with a convincing win.

Singh said the initial performances were promising, although he believes the second round of matches will be tougher for both teams.

The Bulikula will take on Papua New Guinea in Port Moresby on Saturday. The PNG Orchids won their first game with a 58-4 thrashing of France at home on Saturday.

The Bati take on world champs Australia, who pipped New Zealand 24-22 on in their RLWC opener last Thursday.

Disparity addressed

Meanwhile, Rugby League Players Association president and Dolphins' forward Feleti Kaufusi has told Australian media that the pay disparity between Australian and other international players needs to be addressed.

Australia is paying AU$40,000 to players for their World Cup commitment, which is an agreement between the Rugby League Players Association (RLPA) and the Australian Rugby League Commission (ARLC).

Other international teams have been tagged at A$850 per match.

Kaufusi said he would formally address the issue in the next Collective Bargaining Agreement (CBA).

"I want more equality in the prizemoney. It is something we will raise in the next CBA," Kaufusi was reported in the Australia media as saying.

"Australia is always going to get first preference, which is fine, but we need to get to a stage where it is a lot more even.

"It may not be the same, but it should be somewhere thereabouts."

Meanwhile, the Pacific Island teams are in action again this upcoming weekend.

In the women's competition, Fetu Samoa, who played brilliantly despite losing to Australia last weekend, will take on Wales in Sydney on Friday evening.

PNG hosts Fiji at home in Port Moresby on Saturday.

World.title: Coalition by Christmas? Don't bet on it
World.content:
Audio player for " Weekly interview with Prime Minister, Christopher Luxon " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/politics_election-2026/2017956%2Fcoalition-by-christmas-don-t-bet-on-it

Weekly interview with Prime Minister, Christopher Luxon Morning Report Download MP3 7m

Christmas could come and go before New Zealand gets a new government, with neither Christopher Luxon nor Chris Hipkins willing to promise a coalition deal before the festivities are over.

On Monday, both prospective prime ministers refused to put a deadline on coalition talks, raising the prospect of Christmas being swallowed up by political horse-trading.

Asked on RNZ's Morning Report about the timeframe, Luxon was non-committal.

"I'm hoping that we can get something put together before Christmas - would be ideal. But frankly, it'll take as long as it takes."

Luxon indicated formal negotiations would likely wait until the final vote count was released on 27 November, nearly three weeks after polling day.

"We'll probably need to wait for that to come back, and then you'll see negotiations commence," he said.

"That's why I'm asking New Zealanders first and foremost to think very intentionally about how they want to vote."

Hipkins was similarly reluctant to make promises, telling reporters at Parliament it would depend on what voters delivered.

"We've got to play the cards that the voters deal us. If you want a good, decisive outcome, vote for one. Vote Labour.

"Give us the strongest possible hand in those post-election discussions."

On Sunday, Hipkins said he would make it a priority to get a deal done before Christmas, but he could not guarantee it.

"It's one of the later elections that we've had in recent times, and that could, depending on the outcome, make it more challenging."

In 2023, it took National, ACT and New Zealand First 41 days after voting day and 21 days after the final count to sign their coalition agreements.

The same timetable this year would take us to 18 December - just one week before Christmas.

World.title: Wellington family shaken after pedestrian breaks windscreen of car with them inside
World.content:
A Wellington family has been left shaken after a pedestrian threw an object at their car while they were travelling through Mount Victoria Tunnel tunnel.

Olivia Fuller was in the car on Sunday around 5pm with her two young children while her mother was driving from the Hataitai end of the tunnel towards the Basin Reserve.

She said she saw a pedestrian throw something at their windscreen about a third of the way through the tunnel.

"And then the next thing I knew it just smashed into our windscreen," she said.

Although no one was injured, Fuller said her six-year-old daughter was upset by what happened.

"We had sunglasses on and things, which was lucky because there was glass everywhere."

Fuller said glass had gone 'everywhere' but no one had been hurt. Supplied

The family continued driving out of the tunnel before heading home and contacting police.

"My daughter was very scared and she tends to stress out about stuff, so I didn't want to freak her out. I tried to stay calm and just get her inside before I called the police."

Fuller said she fears the consequences could have been much worse if the object had broken through the windscreen, potentially injuring or killing someone in the car.

Fuller said she was concerned others could be hurt. Supplied

She said her mother was visiting from out of town, and the incident has left the family shaken.

Fuller regularly uses the tunnel about four times a week and is concerned another motorist could be seriously hurt.

"It just concerns me that people were doing that and they might hit someone else and they might not be as lucky as we were," she said.

She is trying to get CCTV footage from the tunnel.

Police said the report is at assessment stage and that it is fortunate no one was injured, given the potential consequences.

World.title: Labour pledges social media ban for under-16s
World.content:
*Correction: An earlier version of this story incorrectly said Labour promised to implement the ban in its first 100 days

Labour is pledging to get an under-16 social media ban to select committee in its first 100 days and set up an online watchdog that can fine technology giants that break new rules.

If back in government Labour says it will give people more control of their internet feed by platforms to allow users to choose between an algorithm-driven feed or posts only from accounts people follow.

The new rules would mean users could switch between those feeds at any time.

There would also be a new 'Digital Duty of Care' law that would require platforms to "identify risks and protect Kiwis from harmful content and addictive designs".

Any breaches of these new rules would be assessed by a new independent online regulator, which would have powers to "enforce safety standards, investigate harmful practices and take action against companies that break the rules'.

The new duty of care law would cover stronger protections for under-18s against harmful content, bullying and design features that encourage excessive use or damage self-esteem, the party says.

It would also have "stronger protections against deepfake abuse, including non-consensual sexual images, and powers to take down harmful nudify apps and sites".

Lastly the new law would cover reponsibilities for companies and make platforms identify risks, detail what they're doing to keep people safe and fix the problems when things go wrong.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins says big technology companies have too much power when it comes to New Zealanders' online experience. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

The government introduced a bill to ban social media for under-16s in August but it did not have support from National's coalition partners New Zealand First or Act.

It was introduced so close to Parliament rising for the election that National's Christopher Luxon and Erica Stanford said it would not get its first reading this term.

Labour said it would support the bill at first reading to allow it to go to select committee but the Leader of the House Louise Upston made clear it would not go before the House as there wasn't enough time.

Addressing reporters at Parliament, Labour sought to differentiate its proposed social media ban from the National Party's policy.

Labour MP Reuben Davidson said National's efforts were little more than "a PR exercise" given it refused to progress legislation before the end of this term.

"We're committed to having that first reading of the bill within the first 100 days. To getting that into the select committee process. To getting things started.

"It can't just be announcements. It has to be action."

Davidson said Labour's policy also featured a "Digital Duty of Care" law to be introduced in its first year in power, putting basic responsibilities on the companies running online services.

Labour MP Reuben Davidson. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

"National have talked a big game about online safety, but it's not a game. It's real lives."

Labour leader Chris Hipkins said politicians had traditionally been slow to respond to technological advances and needed to "urgently" get on top of the new digital environment.

He pointed to statistics showing one in three teenagers spending five or more hours a day on social media: "that's an explosion".

Hipkins said big technology companies had too much power when it comes to New Zealanders' online experience.

"Social media is part of everyday life. It helps us stay connected, share ideas and keep in touch with the people we care about."

"At the same time, scams are becoming more sophisticated, fake images and videos are harder to spot, and a lot of parents are worried about what their children are seeing," he said.

"Parents shouldn't have to take on big tech on their own."

New Zealand First leader Winston Peters dismissed Labour's social media ban as "a naive solution to a genuine issue".

"Throwing out simplistic sound bites denies the reality that banning social media in its entirety means either banning VPNs or using digital ID for everyone - otherwise it's a fool's errand and meaningless."

World.title: Samoan PM accused of being 'a leader who believes he is above the law'
World.content:
A former editor of Samoa's only independent daily newspaper has characterised Samoan Prime Minister La'aulialemalietoa (La'auli) Leuatea Schmidt as a "dictator" under whose leadership the "law has been compromised".

Shalveen Chand, who led the Samoa Observer as its editorial chief, has accused La'auli of a "lack of accountability and transparency", "intimidation" of journalists and "nepotism" since coming to power.

"La'auli ... made a promising start when he was elected prime minister in September 2025," Chand wrote in an op-ed for the Cook Islands News, where he now works as a senior journalist.

"In his first press conference, he made a promise to be transparent and accountable. A promise that he never intended to keep, which has now resulted in the banning of Samoa's only independent publication from government events, government officials not being accountable to the media, bullying and assault on journalists, including on me in front of his house."

In his piece, Chand said that intimidation was among the reasons he had to leave Samoa and his job in Apia and move the the Cook Islands.

La'auli has been at odds with the Samoa Observer over what he has previously stated as the newspaper's lack of "factual, accurate and impartial articles with integrity and professionalism".

As a result, La'auli arbitrarily banned the news outlet from attending and covering him or government events in the public interest.

"I pray that the temporary suspension will produce a fruitful way forward for not only the Samoa Observer but all other media outlets to maintain the highest standards of professionalism as prescribed in the Media Code of Ethics," the prime minister said in a statement at the time.

La'auli has been at odds with the Samoa Observer. Facebook / The National University of Samoa

Chand said that the rule of law has been compromised in Samoa.

"Corruption was already rife; however, when you add in a leader who believes he is above the law, the rule of law starts becoming non-existent. The Australian Broadcasting Corporation has dubbed La'auli as the 'Trump of the Pacific', and his behaviour often mirrors that of the American," he wrote.

Chand also claimed that there have been serious breaches of due process, including in top-level government appointments.

"It is worrying when merit is no longer a requirement to hold a top civil service position. Nepotism is rife, and his own children are acting as if the nation were the family business.

"This was seen a few weeks ago when La'auli's son snatched a camera off a reporter and deleted photos, saying it was against the law to photograph his father. Last time it was checked, no such laws existed."

The incident Chand was referring to occurred late last month, when La'auli's son took the camera of a female Samoa Observer journalist and deleted photographs taken by her of La'auli.

The Samoan government issued a statement following a media backlash and defended the action, saying that the ban on the Samoa Observer was still in place.

"My toddler and wife have often been victims of these attacks, even though my spouse's political allegiance is with La'auli," Chand wrote.

"Yes, she's Samoan, and she occasionally reminds me of how 'Sleeping with the Enemy' can be viewed in a whole new context. But I am thankful that despite being critical of the media, she has always stood up for me whenever I have been targeted, either physically or on social media."

Chand said he has been approached those who questioned "why I was against their prime minister".

"It is hard to make some people understand that it was no personal attack on the leader but a journalistic attempt to keep him honest, accountable and transparent."

"Many times, these physical confrontations have been met with my personal bodyguard, my wife, willing to throw a few combinations like David Tua."

World.title: Support from political parties for Working for Families reform
World.content:
Audio player for " Do I know enough about my financial state to retire? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/personal-finance/2017178%2Fsupport-from-political-parties-for-working-for-families-reform

Do I know enough about my financial state to retire? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 17m

There is support across the political spectrum for changes to Working for Families that could reduce the chances of people ending up with surprise debt.

A review last year proposed a number of changes for the scheme, including more regular assessments of household income.

At present, many people do not realise they are being overpaid Working for Families credits until the end of the tax year, at which point they may owe significant sums of money.

Inland Revenue said it was still working with other government agencies to understand potential issues and to develop possible options for some of the proposals in the discussion document, including a shorter period of assessment.

It has already implemented changes to the Working for Families residency rules and an Approved Information Sharing Agreement with Customs to support those rules will come into force from April.

A spokesperson for National said it was continuously looking for ways to improve and modernise systems and schemes and that included Working for Families.

"There are a range of measures we are looking at that aim to do this. Currently a family needs to estimate how much income they will earn over the tax year and if this changes it can mean they need to make repayments. One option could be to make assessments on a more regular basis to lower the chances of this happening, and therefore lower debt owed, but the pros and cons need to be fully understood. These possibilities are currently under consideration and therefore no decisions have been made."

Deborah Russell, Labour's revenue spokesperson said families should not be hit with surprise debt when their circumstances changed or if the calculations were wrong.

"We would like to see Inland Revenue do more work to help people to understand their obligations, but we would also like to see National rethink its staff cuts at IR. Ordinary Kiwis are working hard and going backwards under this government, and National's cuts to Inland Revenue jobs will unfortunately just make this problem worse."
